0.title: How to Behave in the Household of God
0.overview:
First Timothy is a letter from a seasoned apostle to a young pastor — and it is as practical and urgent as anything Paul ever wrote. Timothy had been left in Ephesus to deal with a crisis: false teachers were infecting the church with 'different doctrine,' with myths and endless genealogies, with a distorted use of the law and a spiritualised asceticism that forbade marriage and certain foods. Paul's letter is his pastoral briefing for a young man who has been given a very hard assignment in a very important city.

Ephesus was the capital of the Roman province of Asia — a commercial and religious metropolis, home to the great temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. It was a city Paul knew intimately: he had spent nearly three years there on his third missionary journey (Acts 19–20), and the church he planted was one of the most strategic in the Roman East. Now, years later, that church was in danger. The false teachers were not outsiders; they had come from within — perhaps former elders or teachers who had 'made shipwreck of their faith' (1:19–20). Timothy's task was to confront them, silence them, and restore the church to sound doctrine and ordered life.

The letter's great themes weave together seamlessly. There is the primacy of sound doctrine — 'the glorious gospel of the blessed God' (1:11) — against which every false teaching must be measured. There is the ordering of the church: prayer, worship, the qualifications of overseers and deacons, the care of widows, the honour due to elders. There is the call to godliness — a word that appears more often in 1 Timothy than in any other New Testament letter — the practical Christlikeness that is the goal of all authentic teaching. And there are the five 'trustworthy sayings' (1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Tim 2:11; Tit 3:8) — compact theological summaries that sound like early confessions of faith, already familiar in the church before Paul wrote them down.

Did Paul write the Pastoral Letters? Many scholars think a later follower wrote them in his name, arguing that their vocabulary and style differ from Paul’s other letters, that their church order with elders and deacons looks later, and that their travels cannot be fitted into Acts. But each letter names Paul as author, they were received as his by the early church, and the church order they describe is simple: plural elders and deacons, which Paul appointed from his first journey (Acts 14:23; Phil 1:1). Differences of style suit an older apostle writing to trusted co-workers on new subjects. And the travels fit if Paul was released from the imprisonment with which Acts ends, as the early church believed, and then travelled again, to Macedonia (1:3), Crete (Titus 1:5) and elsewhere, before a final arrest. The more likely conclusion is that Paul wrote them, in the mid-60s.

And what was Timothy’s role? Not a bishop of Ephesus in the later sense, but Paul’s delegate, sent with apostolic authority for a time, Until I come (4:13), to correct false teaching and see that qualified elders led the church (3:1–7; 5:17–22).

Above all, this is a letter about the church as 'the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth' (3:15). The church is not a voluntary association or a religious club; it is the family of the living God, called to hold up the truth in a world drowning in falsehood. That is what gives urgency to every instruction about doctrine and order and godliness: the stakes are not institutional but cosmic. The household of God must be governed well — because the God who indwells it is the blessed and only Sovereign, King of kings and Lord of lords (6:15).

1.title: The Glorious Gospel and the Worst of Sinners
1.overview:
Paul left Timothy in Ephesus to stop certain men teaching a different doctrine: myths, genealogies and confident talk about the law that produced endless speculation instead of love. The law is good, Paul says, when used for its purpose: to convict sinners, measured by the gospel of God’s glory.

Then Paul turns to himself as the proof of that gospel: if Christ’s patience reached a persecutor, it can reach anyone. The chapter ends with a charge to Timothy to fight the good fight.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An official greeting to a son in the faith: Paul writes under orders, and gives mercy before instructions.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Our Saviour, and Mercy Added

The Pastorals call the Father ‘Saviour’ (salvation was his design, as the Son accomplished it), and only the letters to Timothy add ‘mercy’ to grace and peace: compassion for a struggling minister.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A young, unwarlike Timothy (4:12; 2 Timothy 1:7) needed the apostolic commission standing behind him.

Now: ‘Christ Jesus our hope’ tells anyone in a hard post where to look when the situation offers nothing to look at.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, To Timothy, my true child in the faith: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Timothy 1 sets out why the letter was written and what is at stake. Paul had left Timothy in Ephesus to silence men teaching a different doctrine, myths, genealogies and a misuse of the law, which bred arguments instead of love from a pure heart, a good conscience and sincere faith (vv. 3–7). The law is good when used lawfully, to expose and restrain sin, and its list of sins tracks the Ten Commandments (vv. 8–11). Then Paul offers his own story as the proof of the gospel he guards: a blasphemer, persecutor and violent man shown mercy, because Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom he is the foremost; and the memory bursts into praise of the King of the ages (vv. 12–17). He closes by charging Timothy to fight the good fight, unlike Hymenaeus and Alexander, who made shipwreck of their faith and have been put out of the church (vv. 18–20). A chapter about false teachers turns out to be a chapter about mercy, because the only safe guardian of the gospel is a man who knows he needed it more than anyone.

The setting. 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy and Titus are called the Pastoral Letters, because they are written to Paul’s co-workers about leading churches. After his first Roman imprisonment (Acts 28), Paul seems to have been released and to have travelled again, around AD 62–64, leaving Timothy in Ephesus and Titus in Crete. Timothy, son of a Jewish believing mother and a Greek father (Acts 16:1; 2 Timothy 1:5), had served alongside Paul for well over a decade, and was still relatively young (4:12), perhaps timid (2 Timothy 1:7), and often unwell (5:23). Ephesus, where Paul had spent three years (Acts 19; 20:31), was now troubled by exactly the false teachers he had warned its elders about at Miletus: from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things (Acts 20:29–30). The wolves had come, and some of them were wearing the elders’ clothes.

An apostle of Christ Jesus. An apostle (apostolos) is one sent with authority, carrying the word of the one who sent him. The letter is personal, a father writing to a son, but it is also official: apostolic instruction for the church, so that you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God (3:15). Timothy would read it to the church, and the men he had to correct needed to know that these instructions carried Christ’s authority and not merely an old friend’s opinion.

By command of God. The word is epitagē, a command, the word used of royal orders issued by someone with the authority to compel. Paul did not volunteer and was not elected; he was commanded. That matters to a young man, probably not a fighter by temperament, left with a job he did not choose. Neither of them is in charge of this church. They are both under orders.

God our Saviour. Here Saviour is said of the Father, a title characteristic of these letters (2:3; 4:10; Titus 1:3; 2:10; 3:4), and there is no confusion in it: the Father is Saviour in that salvation was his design and his will before the world began; the Son in that he accomplished it. It also echoes the Old Testament, where the LORD is the Saviour of Israel and there is no other (Psalm 106:21; Isaiah 43:3, 11). And it had an edge in Ephesus. Emperors were hailed as saviours on coins and inscriptions, and Artemis, whose temple dominated the city, was given the title saviour by her worshippers too. Paul gives the title to the living God alone, in the opening line of a letter that would be read aloud a short walk from her altar.

Christ Jesus our hope. Not our example or our teacher, though he is both: our hope (Colossians 1:27). Christ is not merely the one who gives hope; he is the hope, and the phrase faces forward. What we wait for is not first a place or a feeling but him: to see him, to be like him and to be with him for ever (1 John 3:2; Colossians 3:4). Every other good thing we hope for is held inside that one. Before he names a single problem, Paul names the direction to look: to anyone left in a hard post, the job, the family, the illness they would leave tomorrow if they could. The one who commands is the same one who is coming back.

My true child in the faith. The word is gnēsios: genuine, legitimately born, the real thing as against a counterfeit. Timothy was Paul’s spiritual son, probably converted through Paul’s first visit to Lystra, where Paul was stoned and left for dead (Acts 14:6–20), and he had grown to be genuinely like his father in faith and service: I have no one like him, who will be genuinely concerned for your welfare (Philippians 2:20–22). Ephesus was full of men who wanted to be teachers (v. 7); Timothy is the genuine article, and Paul says so publicly. It is a father’s hand on a nervous son’s shoulder in front of the whole room.

Grace, mercy, and peace. A small alteration in the greeting, and a tender one. Paul’s letters to churches say grace and peace; mercy (eleos) is added only in the letters to Timothy (some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add it at Titus 1:4 as well). Grace is God’s favour to the undeserving; mercy is his pity on the miserable, his compassion toward the struggling; peace is the wholeness and reconciliation that follow. It is the right word for a tired minister. A man carrying a congregation like this one needs to be told that God’s disposition toward him is not measured by how well he is coping. Mercy is what God gives to people who are not coping, and he gives it first, before the instructions.

From God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. One preposition, “from”, governs both the Father and Christ. They are the single source of grace, mercy and peace, and only God gives these. So without stopping to argue it, Paul places Christ on the side of God and not of creatures. The man who will call himself the foremost of sinners later in this chapter prays to a Saviour who is himself God.

Did Paul really write this letter? Many modern critical scholars doubt that Paul wrote the Pastoral Letters, pointing to differences of vocabulary, church organisation and theology from his earlier letters. But the letters claim Paul as author repeatedly and personally (1:12–16; 2 Timothy 4:9–21); the early church received them as Paul’s (Marcion, who cut much else from his Bible, left them out, but they are echoed by Polycarp and named as Paul’s by Irenaeus); differences of vocabulary are well explained by different subject matter, a different stage of life, and possibly a different secretary (perhaps Luke, who alone was with him, 2 Timothy 4:11); and a pseudonymous letter with forged personal details, such as the request for a cloak and some parchments, would have been regarded as a deception and rejected. Scholars still debate the question, and the arguments deserve a fair hearing; but the case against Paul is not compelling. We receive them as Paul’s, and as Scripture.

Is this letter for me if I am not a pastor? Yes. It is addressed to Timothy, but it was read to the whole congregation, and most of it concerns them: how they pray (chapter 2), whom they choose as elders and deacons (chapter 3), how they treat widows, older men and younger women (chapter 5), what they do with money (chapter 6). A church member needs to know what sound teaching sounds like, so that he can recognise it and test what he hears; what a faithful elder looks like, so that he can choose one and honour him; and how God wants his household run, because he lives in it. Reading a letter to a minister is also the best way to learn how to pray for one.

How do I find, or become, a spiritual father or mother? Timothy had a mother and grandmother who taught him the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15), and then Paul. You do not need an apostle. Look in your own church for an older believer whose life you respect, and ask for an hour: to read the Bible together, to talk about how they have walked with Christ, to pray. Most will be surprised and glad. And if you are older, do not wait to be asked. Pick one younger believer, of the same sex where the friendship will be close, and simply begin: invite them to a meal, ask how their soul is, open the Scriptures. Paul did not run a programme. He took a young man with him.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy came from Lystra, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, and joined Paul on his second journey. The letter seems to come from after the events of Acts, probably after Paul’s release from his first Roman imprisonment, in the early to mid 60s AD.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With no thanksgiving, Paul goes straight to the problem: teaching that breeds speculation instead of love, and a misuse of the good law, measured against the gospel entrusted to him (vv. 3–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
What Teaching Is For

The telos of the whole charge is love (v. 5). Paul is not setting doctrine against love but saying what doctrine is for — and the law, good when used lawfully (v. 8), convicts sinners and drives them to Christ rather than feeding speculation.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul diagnoses the Ephesian teaching by its output: endless speculation rather than God's household well run (v. 4).

Now: The vice list of vv. 9–10 must be read where Paul put it: five verses before he calls himself the foremost sinner alive.

verseByVerse.quote: As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain at Ephesus so that you may charge certain persons not to teach any different doctrine, nor to devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculations rather than the stewardship from God that is by faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No thanksgiving. In most of his letters Paul begins by giving thanks for his readers; here he goes straight to the problem in the third verse. Among Paul’s letters Galatians and Titus are the clearest others without one, and in Galatians the gospel itself was being abandoned. That omission is itself a measure of how serious things were at Ephesus. Paul loves this church: its elders wept and embraced him when they parted at Miletus (Acts 20:36–38), but a father who sees a fire in the house does not begin with pleasantries.

Remain at Ephesus. The word for urged (parakaleō) means appealed, pleaded; remain (prosmeinai) means stay on. Paul had asked him face to face to stay, and now he puts the charge in writing, where Timothy can reread it on hard days. This journey to Macedonia is not recorded in Acts, which supports the view that Paul was released after his first imprisonment and travelled again.

Charge certain persons. The word for charge (parangellō) means to command, to give an order with authority, and with its noun it is a key word in this letter (1:5, 18; 4:11; 5:7; 6:13, 17). Timothy is not asked to start a discussion with these men. He is to tell them to stop. And note “certain persons” (tisin): Paul knows exactly who they are and does not name them yet, perhaps hoping they will repent before their names are written down for ever. He will name two at the end of the chapter. Some were probably elders of the church itself, just as he had warned (Acts 20:30).

Any different doctrine. One compound verb, heterodidaskaleō, found in the New Testament only in this letter: to teach other-ly, to teach a different thing. It does not necessarily mean teaching outright falsehood. It means teaching something of a different kind from what was handed down (6:3). There is a fixed body of truth, the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3), and a teacher’s job is to deliver it, not to improve it.

Myths and endless genealogies. To devote themselves (prosechō) is to be absorbed in. Myths (mythoi) are fables, invented stories; genealogies (genealogiai) are lists of ancestry. The precise content is debated. The false teaching seems to have had a Jewish flavour (v. 7; Titus 1:14; 3:9): elaborate speculations built on the Old Testament family trees and legends, like the imaginative expansions found in some later Jewish writings, and possibly early speculation about chains of spiritual beings between God and the world. Paul does not bother to describe it: he diagnoses teaching by its output, not its content.

Endless. That word (aperantos) is the giveaway: without limit, never reaching a conclusion. Some subjects never conclude, and that is their attraction: they make the pursuer feel sophisticated and never require him to do anything. A man can spend twenty years on the names in a genealogy and never once be told to forgive his brother.

Speculations rather than the stewardship. Here is the diagnosis, two words set against each other. Speculations (ekzētēseis) are controversial questions, open-ended enquiry that never lands; their fruit was argument and division, not faith and love (6:4–5; 2 Timothy 2:23). Stewardship (oikonomia) is the management of a household: the ordered, practical administration of what God has entrusted to someone, and more widely God’s own plan, his way of running his household and saving his people, received and carried out by faith. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV (godly edifying), read oikodomē, edification, building up, but the better reading is stewardship. The contrast is between human speculation and God’s revealed way of salvation.

A plan with a Head. Paul’s word for God’s stewardship, oikonomia, is the word he used when he wrote to this same church about God’s purpose: a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth (Ephesians 1:10). God’s household order has a centre, and the centre is Christ. That is why the genealogies were never meant to be endless. In Scripture they run somewhere, and they serve the story of Christ: Matthew’s list walks down the generations from Abraham and stops at Jesus, who is called Christ (Matthew 1:16). The false teachers kept the family trees and lost sight of the Son they were written to reach.

What are the myths and genealogies today? Anything that turns the Bible into raw material for a system it does not teach, and keeps people busy without making them holy. Date-setting for the Lord’s return and charts that decode current events. Hidden numerical codes in the text. Conspiracy theories baptised with proof-texts. Endless online controversies whose main fruit is a following. Elaborate claims about angels and demons, or about the hidden meaning of names, that Scripture never makes. The test is Paul’s: where does it lead? If it leaves you more anxious, more superior and more argumentative, and no more prayerful, loving or obedient, it is speculation, however clever it sounds.

How do I tell healthy study from speculation? Healthy study stays with what Scripture actually says, reads each passage in its setting, and is content to stop where the Bible stops (Deuteronomy 29:29). It aims at the questions the text is answering, not the ones it leaves aside. It makes you know Christ better and love people more. It can be deep and demanding: Paul’s own letters are not light reading. But it lands. You close the book with something to believe, to repent of or to do. Speculation never lands, and its favourite questions are the ones God chose not to answer.

Should I stay in a hard church? Paul asked Timothy to stay in a difficult place, and that is a word to those of us who leave too quickly. A church with problems is not a reason to go; a church with problems may be exactly where God wants a faithful member. But this is not a rule that you must stay anywhere at any cost. Timothy stayed in order to correct error, and he had an apostle’s authority behind him. If the gospel itself has been abandoned and the leaders will not hear correction, or if you or your children are being harmed and the church will not act, leaving is not unfaithfulness. Take counsel from mature believers before you decide, and leave, if you must, without bitterness.

For worship. Our God does not leave his household guessing. The men in Ephesus could have searched the family trees for a lifetime and found only more questions; God himself has opened the one secret that matters, and its name is Jesus. His plan was not discovered by clever readers but announced to sinners, and it is received not by speculation but by faith, so that a slave who could not read a genealogy could know the Head of the whole household as well as any scholar, and better than the teachers of the law.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the leading city of the province of Asia, where Paul had spent about three years.

verseByVerse.quote: The aim of our charge is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The aim of our charge. This is the key sentence of the paragraph. The word for aim is telos: the end, the goal, the point of the whole exercise. Everything Timothy has been left in Ephesus to do, all the charging and correcting and teaching, exists to produce something. The point of sound doctrine is not winning arguments but producing a certain kind of person.

Is love. Not correct opinions, not a settled congregation, not the defeat of the opposition. Love (agapē): self-giving love for God and for others, in sharp contrast with the speculations of verse 4, which produced quarrels. That is a startling thing to write at the head of a letter about to spend six chapters on doctrine, church order and false teachers. Paul is not setting doctrine against love. He is telling us what doctrine is for. A theology that does not arrive here has failed on its own terms, however correct it is.

Love with a face. Paul does not leave the word undefined. Ten verses later he names the love this charge exists to reproduce: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1:15); and in the next chapter, the man Christ Jesus gave himself as a ransom for all (2:5–6). By this we know love, John writes, that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers (1 John 3:16). A doctrine that is accurate about the cross and cold toward people has learned the facts of Calvary without its shape.

A pure heart. Love issues from (ek, out of) three springs, and each blocks a specific counterfeit. Pure (katharos) means clean, unmixed. The heart in Scripture is the centre of the person: thought, desire and will together. A pure heart is one cleansed by God (Psalm 51:10; Acts 15:9) and wholly given to him, the heart Jesus said would see God (Matthew 5:8): the affections uncontaminated, wanting one thing. Without it you get love as a performance, done for an audience or for what it returns.

A good conscience. Conscience (syneidēsis) is the inner moral awareness, the faculty that sits in judgment on our own actions. A good conscience is one that does not accuse us, because we have been cleansed by Christ’s blood (Hebrews 9:14; 10:22) and are walking in obedience: an inner court with nothing unresolved in it. The phrase recurs in these letters (1:19; 3:9; 2 Timothy 1:3), and at verse 19 a wrecked conscience is what sinks a man; the false teachers had consciences seared as with a hot iron (4:2). Without a good conscience you get love as compensation: the busy kindness of someone avoiding something.

A sincere faith. Sincere (anypokritos) means un-play-acted, without a mask; the hypokritēs was the actor on the Greek stage. Paul uses the same phrase of the faith that lived first in Timothy’s grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice and now in him (2 Timothy 1:5). Without it you get love as religion: the correct behaviour of a person who does not actually trust God.

What does teaching grow? So Paul’s test for teaching is not merely whether it is true, though it must be, but what it grows. The false teachers were producing speculation and controversy; the charge was given to produce people who love, out of clean hearts, clear consciences and unfeigned faith. Hold any teaching you are drawn to, and any you are inclined to fight about, against that measure.

What it does not mean. It does not mean doctrine is unimportant so long as people love. Love here is the fruit of sound teaching, not a replacement for it: the same chapter that names love as the goal will hand two men over to Satan for false teaching. Nor does it mean love is merely a feeling. It flows from a heart, a conscience and a faith that God has renewed.

Does love mean I should never confront false teaching? No. This verse comes in the middle of a command to stop false teachers, and it explains why the command was given. Error harms people, and love will not stand by and watch sheep being harmed. The father who lets his child drink poison because correcting him feels unkind does not love him. What love changes is the manner: gently, patiently, without quarrelling, correcting opponents in the hope that God may grant them repentance (2 Timothy 2:24–25). Love also changes the aim. You are not trying to win; you are trying to heal.

How can I have a good conscience when mine keeps accusing me? A good conscience is not one that has never been guilty. It is one that has been cleansed. Bring the specific thing to God, confess it plainly, and believe what he says: the blood of Christ purifies our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). Where you have wronged someone, put it right as far as you can. Then refuse to keep paying for what Christ has paid for. If the accusation returns after you have confessed, it is no longer your conscience doing its proper work; it is the accuser, and you answer him with the cross. And keep your conscience tender by obeying it quickly the next time it speaks.

On a Tuesday. Recall the last theological conversation you had that grew heated, and run Paul’s three springs over it: was I wanting God’s glory and the other person’s good, or wanting to win; arguing loudly about one thing to avoid another; performing? Then, as one whose conscience Christ’s blood has cleansed, do one thing that verse 5 would recognise: write to that person, or pray for them, or ask their forgiveness for the tone if not the content.

verseByVerse.quote: Certain persons, by swerving from these, have wandered away into vain discussion, desiring to be teachers of the law, without understanding either what they are saying or the things about which they make confident assertions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By swerving from these. The verb is astocheō: to miss the mark, to shoot wide. The image is an archer, and the target was named in verse 5. These men are not described as enemies who attacked the target from outside. They aimed at it and missed. They were church people with ambitions to teach, and they went wide, which is a more uncomfortable diagnosis than malice, because it can happen to anyone who stops checking where he is pointing.

Vain discussion. Wandered away (ektrepō) is to turn aside, used of turning off a road, and in medical writers of a limb wrenched out of joint. Vain discussion (mataiologia) is empty talk, idle chatter. Not false talk necessarily; empty. Like a dislocated limb, their teaching still moved, but it could no longer bear weight.

Desiring to be teachers of the law. Teachers of the law (nomodidaskaloi) is the word used of the Jewish teachers of the law, such as Gamaliel (Luke 5:17; Acts 5:34). And the order of the sentence is the whole diagnosis. First comes the desire to be a teacher. The content is secondary: a subject was needed, and the law provided one. Paul is describing men who wanted the standing that comes with teaching and then went looking for something to teach, which is the reverse of how it should work and is not confined to the first century.

Confident assertions. The double ignorance is precisely observed: they do not understand their own words, nor the matters they pronounce on. Yet the pronouncing is confident. The verb (diabebaioomai) means to insist strongly, the tone of a man who has settled the question. That combination, certainty without comprehension, is the reliable signature of this kind of teacher. Confidence in the truth is not the fault; Paul himself can say, I know whom I have believed (2 Timothy 1:12). But genuine understanding usually makes a person more careful, not less. The more a man truly knows of God, the more often he says, I do not know.

Paul had been this man. These lines come from someone who knew the type from the inside. Before Damascus, Saul of Tarsus was as confident in the law as any man of his generation: a Pharisee, advancing beyond his contemporaries, as to righteousness under the law blameless (Galatians 1:14; Philippians 3:5–6). And he understood neither what he was saying nor the things he asserted, because the law he taught was pointing to the Christ he was hunting. Six verses later he will say he acted ignorantly in unbelief (1:13). What cured him was not a better argument but a meeting: the risen Jesus spoke his name. It is still the only cure for certainty without comprehension, and it lets Paul write of these men with severity but without contempt.

Is it wrong to want to teach? No. Paul will say in 3:1 that if anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task. The difference is in what is wanted. One man wants the work: to feed people, to make Christ known, to see a church grow in love. Another wants the platform: to be listened to, quoted, deferred to. You can usually tell which you are by what happens when someone else is asked instead of you, and by whether you are willing to learn before you teach (James 3:1). A good teacher is first a good listener to Scripture and to wiser people.

How do I know if I am confident without understanding? Three signs. You find it easier to explain why others are wrong than to explain the passage in front of you. You have never seriously read the best case for the view you oppose. And you are rarely heard to say, I am not sure, or, I was wrong about that. The remedy is not timidity. It is to sit longer with the text before you speak, to check your reading against the faithful teachers of the church, and to hold firmly what Scripture says plainly and lightly what it does not.

verseByVerse.quote: Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law is good. Paul now guards himself against a misunderstanding. He has just dismissed the would-be teachers of the law, and someone could easily conclude that the problem is the law itself: that the Old Testament is the difficulty and the sooner the church is clear of it the better. Marcion drew that conclusion in the second century, and many have drawn it since; Paul heads it off at once. The law (nomos), here the Law of Moses and especially its moral commands, is good (kalos): excellent, fine, beautiful. It is holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12), because it reflects the character of the God who gave it. It is not on trial here.

If one uses it lawfully. There is a deliberate play in the Greek: nomos used nomimōs. The law must be used law-fully. The false teachers were using it as a source of speculation, or perhaps as a ladder of merit; its proper use is to expose and restrain the sin of the lawless.

Where the lawful use leads. A law used lawfully does not leave a man admiring his own record; it sends him to a Saviour. Paul knew it from his own life: the commandment that promised life proved to be death to him (Romans 7:10), and it drove him to Christ, who is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4). Used as God meant it, the law is the guardian that walks a sinner to the door and hands him over to Christ (Galatians 3:24). The false teachers made it a puzzle and so never arrived there.

Where Christians differ: what is the place of the law for Christians? Some say the Old Testament law has no role for Christians at all; others make it a way of earning favour with God. Faithful Christians weigh this differently, and some who love the gospel are wary of any talk of law for believers because they fear it breeds legalism. Verdict: The Reformed tradition, following Scripture, speaks of three uses of the moral law. First, it shows us our sin and drives us to Christ (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:24). Second, it restrains evil in society (the use in view here, vv. 9–10). Third, it guides believers in grateful obedience (Romans 13:8–10; Ephesians 6:2). The ceremonial laws are fulfilled in Christ and no longer binding (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1–14); the civil laws of Israel expired with Israel’s state, though their principles of justice remain instructive. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, remains God’s will, but it is never the way of justification.

The remedy for bad use is good use. The false teachers’ law never accused, restrained or guided anyone; it only entertained. Yet the instinct when something good is being handled badly is to withdraw it: to stop teaching it, to treat the subject as dangerous. Some churches have done this with election, with the law, with the Lord’s Supper, with the Holy Spirit. Paul does not respond to the abuse of the law by abandoning the law; he responds by explaining what it is for. Good use always costs more effort than avoidance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we are saved by keeping the law. No one is justified by works of the law (Galatians 2:16). Justification is acquittal in God’s court: the sinner is not made sinless overnight but pardoned and accepted, because Christ’s obedience and death are counted as ours (Romans 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Every commandment was kept, perfectly and gladly, by the Son. Nor does it mean the law is bad because it cannot save. The fault lies in us, not in the law: what the law could not do, weakened by the flesh, God did by sending his own Son (Romans 8:3).

If I am not under the law, why should I read it? Because you are not under it as a covenant of works, a way of earning life, but you are still under God, and the law tells you what he loves. A believer reads the commandments the way a child reads a letter from his father: not to find out how to be adopted, but to learn how to please the one who already adopted him. Christ did not abolish the law but fulfilled it (Matthew 5:17), and the Spirit writes it on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). The same commandments that once condemned you now describe the family likeness the Spirit is forming in you.

Do I need to keep the food laws, festivals and sacrifices? No. Those belonged to the ceremonial law, which was a shadow of the things to come, and the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). The sacrifices pointed to his one sacrifice and ended when it was offered (Hebrews 10:1–14). The food laws marked Israel off from the nations, and Christ has made the two one (Mark 7:19; Ephesians 2:14–15). You read those chapters to see Christ in them, not to obey them as rules. The moral law is different, because it is grounded in God’s own character and in creation, and it is repeated throughout the New Testament. The Sabbath commandment needs a word of its own. This commentary holds that its rest is fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10), so that Christians gladly set the Lord’s Day apart for worship and rest as a gift, not under rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience on it (Romans 14:5); many godly brothers in the Westminster and 1689 tradition hold it as a continuing Sabbath, and they are to be honoured.

On a Tuesday. Read the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:1–17) this week, slowly, once for each use. First as a mirror: where do they show you your sin? Take that to Christ. Then as a fence: thank God for the restraint his law has placed on the world you live in, on your street, your courts, your own worst impulses. Then as a path: choose one commandment and ask what it would look like to keep it gladly, as love for God and neighbour, before Friday.

verseByVerse.quote: understanding this, that the law is not laid down for the just but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and sinners, for the unholy and profane, for those who strike their fathers and mothers, for murderers, the sexually immoral, men who practice homosexuality, enslavers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not laid down for the just. Here is the proper use, and it deserves its weight. Laid down (keitai) is a legal term: set, enacted, on the statute book. Paul does not mean a righteous person may ignore God’s commands. He means the law in its convicting and restraining function, as accuser, as the thing that arraigns you, is not aimed at people already doing what it requires. Its sharp edge is directed against wrongdoing. Those justified in Christ do not live under the law’s condemnation (Romans 8:1), though they delight in its moral content (Romans 7:22).

The lawless and disobedient. Then the list, and its shape is deliberate. It falls into two halves that track the two tables of the Ten Commandments, the traditional division into duties toward God and duties toward neighbour. The first six words come in three pairs, describing sin against God: lawless and disobedient (those who reject authority), ungodly and sinners (those without reverence for God), unholy and profane (those who treat sacred things as common, trampling what God calls holy). That is the first table, the commandments about God.

Who strike their fathers. Now the second table, sins against neighbours, and these run in the order of the commandments. The words (patrolōais kai mētrolōais) mean literally father-killers and mother-killers, or those who beat their parents: the fifth commandment, honour your father and your mother, at its most violent extreme (Exodus 20:12; 21:15). Murderers follow: the sixth commandment (Exodus 20:13).

Men who practice homosexuality. The seventh commandment, broadened to all sexual sin. The sexually immoral (pornoi) are those who engage in any sexual relations outside marriage. Men who practise homosexuality translates arsenokoitai, a compound of male and bed. It appears first in Paul’s letters and he may have coined it, and its parts come straight out of the Greek translation of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, which forbid a man lying with a male as with a woman: arsenos koitēn, a male bed. It refers to same-sex sexual acts, not only to exploitative forms. The historic Christian reading has been the plain one, and it should be stated plainly rather than smuggled or softened.

Where Christians differ: same-sex relationships. Some argue that Paul condemned only exploitative or abusive practices, such as pederasty, and not loving, committed same-sex relationships. Many who argue this are moved by love for gay friends and family, and the question deserves care. Verdict: The word arsenokoitai comes from the Levitical prohibition, which concerns the act itself, regardless of the relationship. Romans 1:26–27 describes mutual desire, not only exploitation. Scripture consistently teaches that sexual union belongs to the marriage of one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6): Jesus roots marriage in creation itself, God making them male and female, not in the customs of a culture. This is held with compassion: same-sex attraction is a real struggle for many, it is not itself the same as acting on it, and all of us stand in this list as sinners. The hope is the same for all: “And such were some of you. But you were washed” (1 Corinthians 6:11).

Where Paul put it. But it should also be stated in this list, which is where Paul put it, alongside liars and men who hit their parents, and five verses later he will call himself the foremost sinner alive. The list does not single out one sin as worse than all others. This is a passage about who the law arraigns, and the answer includes the writer. Any use of verse 10 that leaves the user feeling comfortable has misread the paragraph it sits in.

A list of people Christ came for. The list does not have the last word, and Paul will not let it. Six verses on, the same pen writes that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1:15), using the very word that stands in this catalogue (v. 9). Every kind of person named here is the kind of person the Son of God came for: the parent-beater, the murderer, the sexually immoral, the slave-trader, the respectable liar. The law arraigns the lawless so that the gospel can acquit them, and it can acquit them only because Christ became a curse for us and bore the sentence himself (Galatians 3:13).

Enslavers. The eighth commandment, do not steal, in its most extreme form. Enslavers (andrapodistai) are kidnappers, slave-traders, men who steal human beings to sell them. The law punished man-stealing with death (Exodus 21:16). Note what Paul counts as the worst form of theft: not a purse but a person. And Paul, writing inside an empire built on slavery, puts slave-trading in a list of things contrary to sound doctrine. Scripture condemns the trade that built so much of history’s slavery, including the Atlantic trade that men professing Christ carried on for three centuries against the plain words of this verse.

Liars, perjurers. The ninth commandment, false witness. Perjurers (epiorkoi) are those who swear falsely, the lie told under oath where justice depends on the truth.

Sound doctrine. The catalogue was never meant to be complete; the list is representative. And then a word that will become a refrain in these letters. Sound (hygiainousa, related to our word hygiene) is a medical word: healthy, whole, wholesome (6:3; 2 Timothy 1:13; 4:3; Titus 1:9; 2:1). Paul’s standard for teaching is not merely accuracy but health: doctrine that makes people well. False doctrine is a disease that spreads like gangrene (2 Timothy 2:17). And Paul does not say these sins are contrary to good manners, but to sound doctrine. What a church believes and how its people live are one organism, and sickness in either spreads to the other.

What if I am a Christian who experiences same-sex attraction? It means you are not in this list for your temptations; you are in Christ, and the list is about practice. Being tempted is not sin: our Lord was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Your calling is the one every Christian has, to say no to sexual sin and yes to Christ, whether in faithful celibacy or, for some, in marriage to someone of the opposite sex. That is costly, and the church must not pretend otherwise. It must be a family to you: homes open to you, friendships deep enough to carry the weight, no jokes or contempt tolerated. Many faithful believers walk this road, and Christ is not ashamed to call them brothers and sisters.

Did the Bible approve of slavery? Not of the slavery most people picture. The trade that seized Africans and shipped them across the Atlantic was man-stealing, and this verse and Exodus 21:16 condemn it outright. Old Testament servitude among Israelites was mostly a form of working off debt, limited in time and protected by law (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12–15; 23:15–16). The law also allowed foreigners to be held permanently (Leviticus 25:44–46), a hard text Christians should not hide: like divorce, it was an institution the law regulated and restrained because of hardness of heart rather than one it created (Matthew 19:8). In the New Testament Paul did not lead a revolt against Roman slavery, which would have been swiftly crushed, but he planted the gospel that dissolved it: masters and slaves equal in Christ (Galatians 3:28), a runaway sent back as a beloved brother (Philemon 16), slaves told, on the most likely reading, to gain their freedom if they could (1 Corinthians 7:21). The Christians who fought to end the trade were reading these verses rightly.
verseByVerse.note: The list follows the order of the Ten Commandments, from the first table (God) to the second (neighbour).

verseByVerse.quote: in accordance with the gospel of the glory of the blessed God with which I have been entrusted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In accordance with the gospel. This is the standard against which the whole chapter has been measuring. The myths and genealogies, the confident assertions, the misuse of the law: all of it is judged by whether it accords with this. What is sound doctrine (v. 10)? Whatever agrees with the gospel. And the law and the gospel are not at war. The law exposes sin; the gospel announces the remedy.

The gospel of the glory. The phrase is often quoted as the glorious gospel, as the KJV renders it, and that is not quite what Paul wrote. Literally it is the gospel of the glory: the gospel that concerns God’s glory, that displays it, that has it as its content. God’s glory is not an adjective describing the message but the thing the message is about. And the glory is seen in a face: the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God (2 Corinthians 4:4, 6). What does that mean in practice? At the cross you see his holiness, which would not overlook sin, and his love, which paid for it himself, both at full strength at once (Romans 3:25–26). No other message shows you so much of God.

The blessed God. A phrase Paul uses only in this letter (here and 6:15). The word is makarios, the same word that opens each of the Beatitudes: happy, supremely fortunate. Applied to God it means he is perfectly and self-sufficiently happy: not needing anything, not waiting on circumstances, complete in himself, the Father delighting in the Son and the Son in the Father in the fellowship of the Spirit from all eternity. He was entirely blessed before he made anything, and the gospel is the overflow of that fullness rather than the remedy for a lack.

Entrusted. The verb (pisteuō, here in the passive) is the language of a deposit placed in someone’s keeping, the same idea he will press on Timothy at the end of the letter: guard the deposit (6:20; 2 Timothy 1:12–14). Paul did not devise this message and does not own it; he received it by revelation of Jesus Christ (Galatians 1:11–12). He is holding something for its owner, which is the only posture from which anyone can safely correct anybody else’s doctrine. And that word turns the paragraph. Paul has been describing men who wanted to be teachers. Now he remembers that he was made one, and the memory sets off the most personal passage in the letter.

Is it irreverent to call God happy? No; it is Paul’s own word, and it guards us against two errors. One pictures God as stern and joyless, tolerating us with a frown, so that the Christian life becomes a matter of keeping a grim master satisfied. The other pictures him as needy, as if he made us because he was lonely and saves us because he could not bear to be without us. Neither is the God of the Bible. He is holy and he is happy, and these are not in tension: his joy is joy in what is good. That is why his commands are not burdensome, why his presence is fullness of joy (Psalm 16:11), and why the servant who is faithful is told to enter into the joy of his master (Matthew 25:21).

verseByVerse.ref: 1:12–17 – Christ Jesus Came to Save Sinners
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s own conversion is the gospel told as a life: mercy to a persecutor, a trustworthy saying, and a doxology (vv. 12–17).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Present Tense of Verse 15

‘Of whom I am the foremost’, not was. Nearness to light shows more dust, not less, and only a man who sees himself so can correct others without contempt.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The persecutor became the pattern (v. 16): Christ's patience with him is the outer limit that no later case exceeds.

Now: The doxology of verse 17 comes from a man remembering his own conversion and unable to finish the sentence without worship.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank him who has given me strength, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to his service, though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief, and the grace of our Lord overflowed for me with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who has given me strength. The thought of the gospel entrusted to him makes Paul stop and give thanks, and the first thing he thanks Christ for is strength. The verb (endynamoō) means empowered, put power into. Paul’s ministry was not his own achievement but Christ’s power in him (Philippians 4:13; 2 Timothy 4:17).

In the flow. Verses 12–17 can look like a detour from the false teachers, but they are the heart of Paul’s answer to them. The men of verse 7 wanted to be teachers of the law; here is a man who had been the most zealous teacher of the law in his generation, telling what actually happened to him. His story is the gospel of verse 11 told as a life, and it prepares the charge to Timothy (vv. 18–20): the man who must silence error is to do it as one who has himself been shown mercy.

He judged me faithful. Judged (hēgeomai) is considered, regarded; faithful (pistos) is trustworthy. That is an extraordinary thing for this man to say. It was not because Paul had earned it; he was a persecutor. Christ, by grace, made him trustworthy and then entrusted him with the work (1 Corinthians 7:25). The Lord does not find faithful men; he makes them, and then he treats them as what he has made.

Appointing me to his service. Service (diakonia) is ministry, the word from which deacon comes. A gracious appointment, given on the Damascus road: he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name (Acts 9:15; 26:16).

Formerly a blasphemer. Three words, and they escalate: in word, in deed, in attitude. Blasphemer (blasphēmos): he had spoken against the name of Christ, and worse, had tried to force others to do it (Acts 26:11). Persecutor (diōktēs): he had hunted people down; Acts records him approving an execution and going house to house dragging off men and women to prison (Acts 8:1, 3; 9:1–2; Galatians 1:13). Insolent opponent is hybristēs, related to our word hubris: the violent, arrogant man who takes pleasure in hurting and humiliating people. It is the ugliest of the three, and Paul chose it about himself.

I received mercy. The verb (eleeō) is passive: he was shown pity. He did not find mercy, earn it or ask for it. On the road to Damascus he was not seeking Christ; he was seeking Christians.

Ignorantly in unbelief. This needs care, because it can be misread as an excuse, and Paul is not making one; he has just used three brutal words about himself. He did not fully know what he was doing: he thought he was serving God (Acts 26:9; Romans 10:2). In the Old Testament there was provision for sins committed unwittingly, and none for sins committed with a high hand, in deliberate defiance (Numbers 15:27–31). Paul is saying he was on the first side of that line: catastrophically wrong, and sincerely so. Not innocent. Reachable. Jesus prayed for the men who crucified him in the same terms: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34).

Grace overflowed. The verb is enormous: hyperpleonazō, super-abounded, flooded beyond measure. Where his sin had been extreme, grace was more extreme. Grace did not merely match his sin; it overwhelmed it, as where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Romans 5:20).

Faith and love. Something came with the flood. Faith and love were not what Paul contributed in response; they arrived in it. Faith in place of his unbelief; love in place of his violence. Both are found in Christ Jesus, given through union with him. Union with Christ means that by faith a person is joined to him so closely that what is his becomes ours: as a branch draws its life from the vine, so faith and love flow into us from him (John 15:4–5). The man who had neither was given both, which is the exact answer to the question raised by verse 5, where love from sincere faith was named as the goal of everything. Here is where such love comes from. It is not produced by teaching alone. It is poured in by grace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s ignorance earned or caused God’s mercy, as if ignorance made him deserving. Ignorance is not innocence; Paul still calls himself the foremost of sinners (v. 15). His sin, though terrible, was not the deliberate, knowing rejection of the Spirit that Jesus calls unforgivable (Mark 3:28–29). Mercy remained possible, and God freely chose to give it. Paul’s conversion was God’s sovereign, effectual call (Galatians 1:15–16): a call that does not merely invite but brings the person, so that God speaks and the dead heart answers, as Saul’s did on the road.

Could I have committed the unforgivable sin? If you are worried that you have, you have not. The sin Jesus warned of (Mark 3:28–30) was committed by men who watched the Spirit’s work in Christ and deliberately called it the devil’s, and who were so hardened that they had no desire to repent. It is a settled, knowing hostility to Christ, not a single dreadful thought, a terrible season of backsliding, or a past as violent as Paul’s. The very fear that you have gone too far is evidence that the Spirit is still at work in you. Paul blasphemed, persecuted and enjoyed hurting people, and he was received. Come to Christ now, and you will find that he does not cast out anyone who comes (John 6:37).

Can God really use someone with my past? Look at who wrote this. God did not merely forgive Paul and leave him in a back pew; he put him in the front line, among the very people he had hunted. Your past does not disqualify you from belonging to Christ or from serving him. It may shape how you serve: some offences have lasting consequences, and some roles, such as eldership, require a good reputation over time (3:2, 7). But grace does not only pardon; it appoints. The stories you are most ashamed of may be the ones God uses to show someone else that there is hope.

On a Tuesday. Name the most hostile person you know toward Christ: the relative who mocks, the colleague who sneers, the public figure who rages. Pray for them today by name, and pray for more than their restraint. Pray that Christ would do to them what he did to Saul. Then thank him, specifically, for what you were when he found you.

For worship. Christ went looking for his fiercest enemy and turned him into an apostle. He did not wait for Saul to soften; he met him at full speed on the road to Damascus, with letters of arrest in his bag, and spoke his name. Grace overflowed, and it is still overflowing. Not one of his people was found worthy. Every one was made so.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying is trustworthy. Trustworthy (pistos) is the same word Christ used of Paul in verse 12. This is the first of five such formulas in the Pastoral Letters (3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8), and it appears to flag a line already in circulation: something the churches said, perhaps sang or taught to new believers, which Paul now endorses with his apostolic authority.

Full acceptance. The phrase (pasēs apodochēs) means total welcome, wholehearted reception. This truth is not only to be agreed with but embraced with the whole self, the way a starving man does not merely agree that bread is nourishing.

Came into the world. He was somewhere else first. It is a claim to his pre-existence made in passing (John 1:9; 3:17), and to what the church calls the incarnation: the eternal Son did not stop being God, but took to himself a real human body and soul, so that one person is truly God and truly man (John 1:14; Philippians 2:6–7). He left the glory he shared with the Father and walked into a world of sinners, not to inspect them but to save them.

To save sinners. The purpose of his coming: not merely to teach or to set an example, but to save, to rescue from sin and its penalty (Matthew 1:21; Luke 19:10). And to save sinners: not the promising, not the religious, not the nearly good. Jesus said it himself: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners (Mark 2:17). This is the gospel in a sentence, and the only qualification for it is the one thing everyone has.

The foremost. Then Paul adds words of his own, and they are the reason the verse is unforgettable. Foremost (prōtos) is first, chief, worst. And the tense is the thing. Not was the foremost, which is what we would expect after verse 13’s list of past crimes. I am. Decades into an apostleship, having planted churches across the empire and written much of the New Testament, Paul’s settled estimate of himself is present tense. Mature believers see their sin more clearly, not less: the least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9), the very least of all the saints (Ephesians 3:8), and now the foremost of sinners.

Nearness to light. This is not theatrical humility, or a man fishing for contradiction, nor a statistical claim to be the worst man who ever lived. It is what happens to self-knowledge over a long life with God. Nearness to light shows you more dust, not less. John Bunyan took the title of his own spiritual autobiography from this verse: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners. And John Newton, the slave-ship captain who became a minister of the gospel, is remembered as saying near the end of his life that his memory was nearly gone, but he remembered two things: that he was a great sinner, and that Christ was a great Saviour.

How Paul uses it. And see how it functions here. Paul is about to discipline two men (v. 20), and he does it from this position. A man who genuinely considers himself the foremost sinner in the room can correct other people without contempt, and is the safest kind of man to do it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ came to save everyone without distinction in such a way that all will be saved; he came to save sinners, and those he came to save he actually saves (Matthew 1:21; John 10:11, 27–29).

Isn’t it unhealthy to call myself the worst of sinners? Not when it is said the way Paul says it, in the same breath as Christ Jesus came to save. Self-hatred looks at sin and stops there; it ends in despair or in self-punishment. Paul looks at his sin in order to look at his Saviour, and it ends in a doxology two verses later. Nor is it a false humility that refuses to see God’s work in you: Paul also says he worked harder than all the apostles, though it was not he but the grace of God (1 Corinthians 15:10). The healthy Christian holds both: I am a great sinner, and I am greatly loved. Each truth keeps the other from going wrong.

What if I do not feel that bad? The question is not how you compare with Paul, but how you stand before God. A respectable sinner is still a sinner, and the danger of feeling not that bad is that you never come to Christ as one who needs saving. Paul’s first opinion of himself was that he was blameless (Philippians 3:6); that was his worst condition, not his best. The door of this verse is marked Sinners, and the only people who cannot go through it are those who think the sign does not apply to them.

On a Tuesday. When you next find yourself despising someone, the political opponent, the neighbour, the church member who has failed publicly, say this verse under your breath with your own name in it. It changes the tone of what you say next. And if you are carrying a sin you think is too heavy for this verse, read it again: it does not say Christ came to save sinners, except for the worst. The worst signed it.
verseByVerse.note: The first of five “trustworthy sayings” in the Pastoral Letters.

verseByVerse.quote: But I received mercy for this reason, that in me, as the foremost, Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life. To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His perfect patience. God had a reason for choosing such an enemy, and the reason was you. Display (endeiknymi) is to demonstrate, to put on show. Perfect patience (tēn hapasan makrothymian) is all his long-suffering, the whole extent of it: long-temperedness, the slowness to boil that endures provocation. Christ was patient with Saul for the whole time Saul was doing his worst. That patience is not indifference to sin; it gives time for repentance (Romans 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9).

An example. The word (hypotypōsis) is a pattern, a sketch, an outline drawn so that others can see the shape of a thing: the prototype. Paul’s conversion is the template. If Christ’s patience stretched to a man who hunted his people and tried to make them curse his name, then nobody who comes after can reasonably say their case is too hard. Paul’s biography stands as a kind of outer limit: a case as bad as any was received. Whatever anyone brings, it has already been exceeded.

To the King of the ages. Then the sentence breaks into praise, and note where the doxology comes from. It is not attached to a doctrine of God in the abstract; it erupts out of the memory of his own conversion. Paul thinks about what he was and what he received, and cannot get to the end of the paragraph without worshipping. That is a fair test of whether the gospel has been understood or merely learned. King of the ages (basileus tōn aiōnōn): the eternal King, ruler over all the ages of history. He governs every era, including this troublesome one in Ephesus, and including yours.

Immortal, invisible, the only God. Immortal (aphthartos) is literally incorruptible, not subject to decay, unlike everything else Timothy is dealing with: the church, the false teachers, his own body with its frequent illnesses. Invisible (aoratos): no one has ever seen God in his essence (John 1:18; 1 Timothy 6:16). That is exactly the difficulty of pastoral work: the one you serve cannot be seen, while the opposition is entirely visible. The only God: there is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4), and in a city whose economy ran on the temple of Artemis, that is not a philosophical statement but a stand. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add wise, the only wise God, probably borrowed from Romans 16:27; the earlier reading is the only God.

Forever and ever. The phrase (eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn) is to the ages of the ages, one of the strongest phrases Greek has for endlessness. The King of the ages receives glory for the ages of the ages. And Amen: so be it, it is true. Paul expects the congregation to say it back.

Is it fair that a man like Saul should be forgiven? No, and that is the point: mercy is never fair, or it would not be mercy. But it is not unjust either. God did not pretend Saul’s violence had not happened. Every blow he struck at Christ’s people was a blow at Christ himself (Acts 9:4), and Christ bore the punishment for it on the cross, so that God is just when he forgives (Romans 3:26). The objection usually hides something in us: the elder brother’s complaint that the prodigal gets a feast he did not earn (Luke 15:28–30). Nobody at that feast earned it. The only people who stay outside are the ones who insist on being paid what they deserve.

What if I was converted quietly as a child? Is my story worth anything? Yes. Paul’s story is the outer limit, set there so that the worst may hope. But a child brought up in the faith and kept from great sins has received just as much mercy; it was simply given earlier, before the damage could be done. Being kept is as much grace as being rescued. Your story displays Christ’s patience in a different way: patience with all the small, stubborn sins of a long ordinary life, and faithfulness through every year of it.

If God is invisible, how can I know him? Because the invisible God has made himself known. John says that the only Son, himself God and at the Father’s side, is the one who has made the unseen Father known (John 1:18). Christ is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), and whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). You meet him in the Scriptures, which testify to Christ, and you know him by faith, through the Spirit, who opens the eyes of your heart. The invisibility of God is not his absence. It is his greatness: he is not one more object in the world, and he cannot be captured in an image, but he has come close in his Son.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The charge handed on to Timothy, and a warning from two men whose faith was wrecked (vv. 18–20).
verseByVerse.theology:
Which Goes First: Conduct or Doctrine

In verse 19 the conscience goes first and the faith goes down after it; and even the severest discipline, handing over to Satan, is remedial: ‘that they may learn’ (v. 20).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy was to fight by the prophecies once made over him (compare 4:14).

Now: Shipwreck is what happens when a man keeps sailing while ignoring what his conscience tells him about the rocks.

verseByVerse.quote: This charge I entrust to you, Timothy, my child, in accordance with the prophecies previously made about you, that by them you may wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience. By rejecting this, some have made shipwreck of their faith, among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This charge I entrust. Paul returns to where the chapter began, and the vocabulary of deposit returns with it. The charge is the word of verse 5: the commission to guard sound doctrine. Entrust (paratithēmi) is to deposit with someone for safekeeping. As the gospel was entrusted to Paul (v. 11), he now entrusts the charge to Timothy, who must later entrust it to faithful men who will be able to teach others also (2 Timothy 2:2). That is how it has always travelled: one faithful person to another, down every generation, until it reached you.

The prophecies. We are not told what was said when Timothy was set apart (4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6), but he is to fight by it, to use it as ammunition on hard days. When a man wonders whether he should be doing this at all, one answer is to remember what was said when he began.

The good warfare. Wage warfare (strateuomai) is to serve as a soldier, to fight a military campaign. The military note will come back (6:12; 2 Timothy 2:3–4; 4:7). Ministry here is not administration; it is a campaign, and there is an enemy, fought in the strength Christ gives (v. 12). Good (kalē) means noble, worth fighting.

Holding faith and a good conscience. Holding (echōn) is keeping, not letting go. These are the two things named back in verse 5, and here they are two weapons. They belong together. When conscience is violated, faith soon suffers.

Shipwreck. Rejecting (apōtheomai) is thrusting away, deliberately pushing aside, and what is rejected is the good conscience. Paul, who had been shipwrecked three times before he ever sailed for Rome (2 Corinthians 11:25; Acts 27), uses a vivid image: they deliberately threw overboard their conscience, and their faith broke up on the rocks.

The conscience goes first. The order is one of the most practical things in the chapter. The conscience goes first, and the faith goes down after it. Paul does not describe men who reasoned their way out of Christianity and then began living badly. He describes men who rejected a good conscience, who kept doing what they knew to be wrong, and whose doctrine followed their conduct onto the rocks. Wrong living has to build itself a theology eventually, and it usually manages one. Not everyone who leaves the faith takes this road, and honest doubts deserve honest answers; but Paul’s order is a warning worth heeding, because some who say they lost their faith for intellectual reasons lost their conscience first.

Hymenaeus and Alexander. Two names, after twenty verses of certain persons. Hymenaeus later taught, with Philetus, that the resurrection had already happened, and upset the faith of some (2 Timothy 2:17–18). Alexander may be the coppersmith who did Paul great harm (2 Timothy 4:14), though the name was common.

Handed over to Satan. The phrase is severe, and it is used elsewhere of putting someone outside the church’s fellowship (1 Corinthians 5:5): out of the sphere where God’s people gather under Christ’s protection, and back into the world, the domain of darkness where Satan operates (Colossians 1:13). This is excommunication, the most serious act of church discipline, though not a curse to hell.

A defeated enemy on a short chain. Handing a man over to Satan could only be remedial if Satan is not free, and he is not. At the cross Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them (Colossians 2:15). The devil still prowls, but inside the limits his conqueror sets, as Paul learned when a messenger of Satan was made to serve his good (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). Timothy fights under a Captain who has already won the battle that decides the war, and even the enemy’s ground can become a school in which Christ teaches a blasphemer to stop.

Learn not to blaspheme. But read the purpose clause, because it changes the colour of the whole thing. Learn (paideuō) is to be disciplined, trained, as a child is trained. It is remedial, not punitive. Even excommunication aims at restoration: experiencing life outside the church might bring them to their senses and to repentance. And note the word blaspheme. Their false teaching dishonoured God, and it is what Paul called himself in verse 13, before he received mercy. Blasphemy is not merely rude talk about religion. It is treating as common the name of the holy God, which the third commandment guards (Exodus 20:7), and false teaching does it inside his own house. He hands them over hoping for what happened to him.

Where Christians differ: do prophecies like these continue today? Charismatic and Pentecostal Christians see the prophecies over Timothy as a model for prophetic words in churches today. Verdict: The New Testament prophets belonged to the foundation-laying era of the church, alongside the apostles (Ephesians 2:20), when Scripture was still being given. With the completion of the canon, God guides his church through the sufficient written Word, not through new revelations (Hebrews 1:1–2; Jude 3). This is held charitably: brothers who differ often love Christ deeply, and God still guides through his Word, wise counsel, providence, and the inward witness of the Spirit to Scripture. But no word claiming to be prophecy may add to or stand alongside Scripture.

What were these prophecies? Spirit-given words, in the apostolic age, that marked Timothy out for his ministry, probably spoken when the elders laid hands on him (4:14). They belonged to that founding time. Today the church recognises a man’s call to ministry by his gifts, character and fruit, tested by Scripture, not by new prophecies.

Were Hymenaeus and Alexander true believers who lost their salvation? Arminian Christians, who hold that a true believer can finally fall away, read made shipwreck of their faith that way. The more likely reading is that they held the faith outwardly but never truly trusted Christ; as John says of such people, if they had been of us, they would have continued with us (1 John 2:19). Paul’s discipline was meant to bring them to repentance, that they might learn not to blaspheme. The warning is for every believer to hold faith and a good conscience.

What if I am afraid my own faith could be shipwrecked? The fear itself is a good sign; the men in this verse were not afraid, they were careless. Christ keeps his sheep, and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28), and he keeps them by means, one of which is this warning. So do what verse 19 says. Keep your conscience clean: when it accuses you, do not argue with it or bury it; take the thing to the cross, confess it and turn from it. Keep near the means of grace, the Word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of the church. And tell a trusted believer when you are drifting. Ships rarely sink in one wave; they take on water slowly, and someone who loves you can see the list before you can.

What does church discipline look like today? It begins quietly, as Jesus taught: a private word, then one or two others, and only then the church (Matthew 18:15–17). Most discipline ends at the first step, with repentance and restoration. Excommunication is the last step, for serious, unrepented sin or for persistent false teaching, and it is carried out by the church under its elders, not by individuals. It means the person is no longer received as a member or at the Lord’s Table. It does not mean hatred or shunning in every form: you may still greet them, and you should pray for them and call them back, warning them as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:14–15). And it must never be used to silence the victims of abuse or to protect leaders; that is a perversion of it.

In a sentence. The gospel is handed on to be fought for, and the fight is lost first in the conscience, which is why even the church’s severest discipline aims at bringing the wrecked back.

On a Tuesday. Is there one thing you have been doing that you know is wrong and have stopped thinking about? That is where shipwrecks start. Name it to God today, at the cross, and if it involves another person, put it right this week. A sin you hate and keep fighting is a different thing: the fight itself is the Spirit’s work, and the conscience that grieves over it is still afloat.

For worship. The gospel has come down to us through a long chain of trembling hands, Paul to Timothy, Timothy to faithful men, and on through every century, and not one link was strong in itself. Christ kept it. Paul knew what it was to be on a ship breaking up in the surf, and to see every soul on board brought safe to land as God had promised (Acts 27:24, 44). Even his discipline is mercy, a hand reaching after the wanderer, and the blasphemer who wrote these lines is the proof that it can bring him home.
verseByVerse.note: To hand someone “over to Satan” means putting him out of the church, in the hope that he will be brought to repentance.
