2.title: One Mediator, Many Prayers
2.overview:
Paul turns to the church’s gathered life. First, prayer for everyone, including rulers such as Nero, because God our Saviour desires all people to be saved, and there is one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom. Then conduct in worship: men are to pray without anger or quarrelling; women are to be adorned with good works rather than displays of wealth.

Finally the most debated verses: women are to learn, but not to teach or exercise authority over men in the church, and Paul grounds this in creation, not in Ephesian culture. This commentary holds the complementarian reading, respectfully stated, and insists that a restriction on a role is never a verdict on a person’s worth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Prayer comes first: every kind of prayer, for every kind of person, rulers included. Paul grounds it in the heart of the gospel: one God, one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom, and Paul sent as his herald to the nations.
verseByVerse.theology:
‘Desires All People to Be Saved’

Verse 4 has been read as all kinds of people, or, often in the Reformed tradition, as God’s revealed will (what pleases him and what he commands) set beside his decreed will (what he has purposed to happen). Either way there is one mediator, and his ransom is a substitute’s (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Under Nero, the church was told to pray, and give thanks, for kings (v. 2; compare Jeremiah 29:7).

Now: The aim is modest: a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified. Paul thought that enough to pray for.

verseByVerse.quote: First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Timothy 2 sets the church’s public worship in order. First, prayer (vv. 1–7): the church is to pray for all kinds of people, even rulers who might persecute it, because God our Saviour wants all kinds of people to be saved, and there is one God and one mediator, Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all; Paul was appointed to carry that message to the Gentiles. Second, men and women in worship (vv. 8–15). Men are to pray with holy hands, without anger or quarrelling. Women are to adorn themselves with good works rather than display, and to learn quietly and submissively; Paul does not permit a woman to teach or exercise authority over men in the church, and he grounds this not in culture but in creation and the fall (vv. 11–14). He closes with a hard sentence about women being saved through childbearing if they continue in faith, love and holiness (v. 15). At the centre of it all stands the one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself.

The setting. The false teachers in Ephesus seem to have been exclusive in outlook (perhaps thinking salvation was for a spiritual elite or for Jews), contentious in spirit, and particularly influential among some women (5:13–15; 2 Timothy 3:6–7). They may also have forbidden marriage (4:3). Paul’s instructions answer each of these: pray for everyone, because God’s salvation reaches all kinds of people; stop quarrelling; women are to learn, but not to take over the teaching office; and marriage and motherhood are good. When Paul wrote, the emperor was Nero (AD 54–68), who would soon begin persecuting Christians.

First of all. Having dealt with the false teachers, Paul turns to how the church is to conduct itself, and the first item is not strategy against the opposition, but prayer, and prayer for outsiders. First of all (prōton pantōn) means first in importance, not just first in a list: prayer is the church’s first priority in worship. And then (oun) connects to chapter 1: in the light of the battle for the truth, the church must pray. A church fighting error without praying for the world has already lost something the false teachers wanted it to lose.

Four kinds of prayer. The four words overlap but are not identical. Supplications (deēseis) are requests arising from need, the asking of someone who lacks something. Prayers (proseuchai) is the general word, the God-ward address. Intercessions (enteuxeis) carries the idea of approaching a superior on someone else’s behalf, a word used of bringing a petition before a king. And thanksgivings (eucharistiai), the surprising one, since those to be prayed for, and given thanks for, include Nero. Together they describe full, rich, many-sided prayer: not a brief mention of the government before the real business, but the church on its knees, bringing the world before the throne.

For all people. No one is excluded from the church’s prayers: friends and enemies, believers and unbelievers, rulers and slaves, Jews and Gentiles. The context, which immediately names kings, shows that Paul means all kinds and classes of people, not least those we might be tempted to leave out.

For kings. Kings includes the emperor; high positions are places of authority: governors, magistrates, officials. A church in Ephesus is to pray, and to give thanks, for the emperor who would shortly use Christians as living torches in his gardens, and under whom, as the early church remembered, Paul himself would be executed. The instruction is unqualified, and it matches what he wrote to Rome about governing authorities (Romans 13:1) and what Jeremiah told the exiles about Babylon: seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you, and pray to the LORD on its behalf (Jeremiah 29:7). God’s people have usually lived under governments they did not choose, and this is the standing instruction.

A peaceful and quiet life. Peaceful (ēremos) is tranquil, free from outward disturbance; quiet (hēsychios) is calm, settled within. The purpose is modest. Not that the church may prosper or gain influence, but peace and quiet: room to get on with living well, a setting in which the church can worship and the gospel can spread without hindrance. That is a smaller ambition than a modern church often has for its nation, and Paul thought it enough to pray for.

Godly and dignified. Godliness (eusebeia), reverent devotion to God shown in life, is a key word of these letters, used ten times. Dignified is seriousness, a life worthy of respect. The purpose of peace is not comfort but godliness. Paul does not ask for quiet so that Christians can be left alone to enjoy themselves. He asks for it so that they can be holy in public, and so that their neighbours can see what a life given to God looks like.

Praying for the power that judged him. Later Paul reminds Timothy of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession (6:13). The church’s Lord stood before a Roman governor, was condemned by Roman authority and nailed up by Roman soldiers, and he prayed for the men who did it (Luke 23:34). A church that prays for Nero is doing what its Master did. And it prays through him: its supplications and intercessions reach God only because there is one mediator between God and men (v. 5), who lives for ever to intercede for his people. Our prayers for rulers ride on his prayers for us.

What do I actually pray for a ruler I think is wicked? Pray what Paul prays. For their salvation first: Nero was beyond the church’s reach, but not beyond God’s, and the prayer that a persecutor might be converted was answered spectacularly in Paul himself. For wisdom and justice in their decisions. For restraint on their evil, and for protection of the weak who suffer under it. For peace, so that the church can worship and the gospel can run. And give thanks for whatever good they do, and for the order that even a bad government preserves, because the alternative is chaos. You can pray all this without pretending to admire them.

Does praying for rulers mean I must never oppose them? No. Praying for a ruler is not the same as agreeing with him. Christians may vote, campaign, protest lawfully and speak out against injustice, as the prophets confronted kings and Paul appealed to Caesar for his rights (Acts 25:11). Where a ruler commands what God forbids, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). But prayer changes the spirit in which we do all this. It is very hard to hate a man you have prayed for by name every week, and very hard to put your hope in politics once you have spent time before the King of the ages.

On a Tuesday. Pray today, by name, for your head of state, your local leaders, and one public figure you find hard to like. Pray for their good and their salvation, and thank God for one specific good thing that has come through them.

For worship. The Lord who rules the kings of the earth is never threatened by them. He turned the heart of Cyrus, humbled Nebuchadnezzar, and used a Roman census to bring his Son to Bethlehem. And his church, praying for Nero in a house in Ephesus, was not a frightened minority pleading for its life. It was a royal priesthood interceding for the world, under a King whose kingdom no emperor could touch.
verseByVerse.note: Christians were to pray for rulers such as Nero, under whom they would later suffer.

verseByVerse.quote: This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Good and pleasing. The logic connects: pray for everyone, because God’s saving concern reaches everyone. God delights in such prayer because it fits his own character as Saviour. The church’s prayers are to be as wide as God’s desire.

Who desires all people to be saved. All people is the same phrase as verse 1. God is not grudging toward sinners. He is a saving God, whose heart is open to all kinds of people, including kings who persecute and Gentiles whom the false teachers may have excluded. This is one of the most discussed sentences in the New Testament, because it sits beside the Bible’s equally clear teaching that God chooses and that his purposes do not fail.

The knowledge of the truth. Knowledge (epignōsis) is full knowledge, recognition. The truth is the gospel (2 Timothy 2:25; 3:7; Titus 1:1). Salvation comes through knowing and believing the truth, not apart from it. This is why prayer and preaching go together: God saves people by bringing them to know the truth, and he brings them the truth by sending people to tell it.

The desire with tears in it. To see what God’s desire for the lost looks like, look at his Son. Jesus wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41–42) and said, How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing (Matthew 23:37). Those were real tears over real people. The same Lord said that he would lose none of all that the Father had given him (John 6:39). Both are true in one Christ, and many Reformed preachers have pointed to those tears as the clearest window onto the sincerity of God’s call. The knowledge of the truth that God wants people to reach is, in the end, the knowledge of this Saviour.

Where Christians differ: if God desires all to be saved, why are not all saved? Arminian Christians argue that God wills to save every individual equally and that his grace enables everyone to believe, so that the difference lies in each person’s free response: God does his part, and each person decides. Universalists argue that, since God desires it, all will eventually be saved. Verdict: Universalism contradicts Scripture’s plain teaching on final judgment (Matthew 25:46; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). As for the Arminian view, Scripture distinguishes between what God desires in the sense of what pleases him and what he commands (his revealed will), and what he has decreed will happen (his decretive will). God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 18:23; 33:11) and sincerely calls all to repent; yet he has, for wise and holy reasons, chosen to save some and not all (Romans 9:18; Ephesians 1:4–5). Two further points help. First, all people in context means all kinds of people, including rulers and Gentiles (vv. 1–2, 7), as all often means in Scripture (Titus 2:11; compare Revelation 5:9). Second, God’s desire here is the ground for the church’s universal prayer and preaching: we do not know who the elect are, so we pray for and preach to all, knowing that God is pleased to save through that means. The Reformed view does not make God less loving; it makes him the sovereign author of every salvation. Arminian brothers and sisters hold their view out of a real concern for God’s love and human responsibility, and they preach the same crucified Christ; the difference is serious, but it is a difference within the family.

Two ways of speaking about God’s will. The distinction is not an evasion invented for this verse. Scripture itself shows both at work in one event: the cross was the most wicked act men ever committed, which God commanded them not to do, and it was the very thing his hand and his plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:27–28). God genuinely takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked; he genuinely commands all people everywhere to repent (Acts 17:30); and he has also purposed to save a people, and he will not lose one of them. We cannot see how all of this fits together in the mind of God. We are not asked to. We are asked to believe both, and to pray accordingly.

The pastoral force. Paul is not writing a lecture on the divine will. He is telling a small, harassed congregation that there is nobody they may treat as beyond praying for: not the magistrate who fined them, not the emperor, not the neighbour who reported them. Whichever reading you hold, the church must pray for everyone and preach to everyone.

If God has chosen whom he will save, why should I pray and evangelise? Because God ordains the means as well as the end. He has chosen to save people through the prayers and the preaching of his church, just as he has chosen to grow crops through farmers. Paul believed in election more firmly than anyone, and he was the great missionary of the early church; election was what gave him confidence that his preaching would not be wasted (Acts 18:9–10; 2 Timothy 2:10). You do not know who God’s elect are, and you are not meant to. You are meant to pray for everyone and tell everyone, and to trust that God will use it.

How can I be sure the offer includes me? Because it is addressed to you. The gospel does not say Christ died for the elect, find out if you are one. It says come, believe, repent, and everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:13). You never have to look into God’s secret decree to know whether you may come. You look at his open invitation, and you take him at his word. Everyone who has ever come to Christ has been received, and you will not be the first to be turned away.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person you have quietly decided will never be saved: the hardened relative, the mocking colleague, the man in the news. You were once as far off yourself, and someone prayed for you. Begin again today, and add one name from a group your church usually forgets.

verseByVerse.quote: For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For there is one God. This gives the reason for praying for all (vv. 1–4), and it has the ring of something already in circulation: compact, balanced, easily memorised. Paul is very likely quoting a confession the churches used. One God is the Shema, the first line of Israel’s faith (Deuteronomy 6:4), and it lands with force in Ephesus, a city whose economy ran on the temple of Artemis and whose riot in Acts 19 was a two-hour chant: Great is Artemis of the Ephesians. Since there is only one God, he is the God of Gentiles as well as Jews (Romans 3:29–30), of rulers and slaves alike. He is not the tribal God of one group, and so the church must pray for every group.

One mediator. A mediator (mesitēs) is a go-between, one who stands in the middle and brings two estranged parties together. Sinners are separated from a holy God; a mediator is needed who can represent both sides. And the word one is doing heavy work. It excludes every other candidate: not angels, not the speculative intermediary beings the false teachers seem to have been fascinated by, not Mary, not the saints, not a priest, not the church itself. Christ alone (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; Hebrews 8:6; 9:15; 12:24). There is a single point of access, and it is a person.

The man Christ Jesus. Not the Son, not the Lord: the man (anthrōpos, a human being). A mediator must have a genuine footing on both sides, and Paul presses the human side because that is the side in question. To represent humans, the mediator had to be truly human; to bring us to God, he had to be truly God (Hebrews 2:14–17; John 1:1, 14). He is one person in two natures. And note the tense of the phrase: Paul does not say the mediator was a man. He remains a man now, in heaven, in the risen body that showed Thomas the marks of the nails (John 20:27), and he always lives to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25).

Who gave himself. Christ’s death was voluntary self-giving (Galatians 1:4; 2:20; Titus 2:14). The phrase rules out any picture of a reluctant victim. He was not taken; he handed himself over, and he said he had authority both to lay his life down and to take it up again (John 10:18). The ransom was a gift, not a seizure.

A ransom for all. The word is antilytron, rare, and not found in any earlier Greek writing that survives: lytron, a ransom price, the word Jesus used of himself (Mark 10:45), with anti, in place of, fixed on the front. A substitute-ransom: a ransom price paid in place of another. Jesus did not merely pay for us; he stood where we were standing. It is substitution, and the rest of Scripture shows what kind: penal substitution, which means that he bore in our place the penalty we owed, to set us free. The penalty is real and the substitute is real: the punishment that God’s holy justice required for our sin fell on Christ instead of us (Isaiah 53:5–6; 1 Peter 2:24).

Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Many hold that Christ died for every individual equally, making salvation possible for all, with each person’s decision determining whether it becomes effective. Verdict: In context, all means all kinds of people, Jews and Gentiles, rulers and subjects (vv. 1–2, 7), as when Revelation 5:9 says he ransomed people “from every tribe and language and people and nation.” Scripture teaches that Christ’s death was a real ransom that actually frees those for whom it was paid, not a mere possibility. He laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:11, 15), for the church (Ephesians 5:25), for many (Mark 10:45). A ransom paid for someone who is never released would be a ransom wasted. This is definite atonement: Christ died with the intention and effect of saving all whom the Father had given him. Yet his death is of infinite worth, sufficient for the whole world, and so the gospel is to be offered freely and sincerely to every person. Many faithful Christians, some Reformed among them, hold that Christ died for every person alike, wanting to honour the Bible’s wide invitations; they preach the same Saviour, and this is a disagreement among brothers.

At the proper time. Christ’s self-giving is God’s witness to his saving purpose. At the proper time (kairois idiois) is literally at its own appointed seasons. Kairos is the right moment, not merely a date. History was not marking time until something happened; it was being brought to a particular hour. At the right moment God sent his Son, the fullness of time (Galatians 4:4), and now in this age the message is proclaimed (Titus 1:3).

To whom was the ransom of verse 6 paid? Not to the devil, as some early writers suggested, as if God owed Satan anything. The ransom was paid to the justice of God. Our debt was to God’s law, which we had broken, and the penalty was death (Romans 6:23). Christ paid it by bearing that penalty himself, so that God could be both just and the one who justifies the person who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). The Father did not extract the price from an unwilling Son, and the Son did not buy a reluctant Father’s love. The Father so loved the world that he gave, and the Son gave himself. The whole Trinity planned and paid the ransom.

Can I pray to Mary or the saints to help me? No, and you do not need to. They were sinners saved by the same mediator, and they are not commanded or promised to hear our prayers. Scripture never directs a single prayer to anyone but God. More than that, you need no one to soften Christ toward you, because he is not hard. He is a high priest who sympathises with our weaknesses, and he invites us to draw near to the throne of grace with confidence (Hebrews 4:15–16). Go to him directly. Ask fellow believers to pray for you, as Paul did; but bring your prayers to God through Christ alone.

Is it not arrogant to say there is only one way to God? It would be, if Christians claimed to have found the way by being cleverer or better than others. The claim is the opposite: none of us could find the way, so God opened one himself, at the cost of his Son. Every view of salvation draws a line somewhere; even the belief that all roads lead to God shuts out those who think otherwise. And if there were another way, the cross would have been needless (Galatians 2:21): God did not give up his Son for something that could be had another way. So the gospel is narrow in its door and wide in its welcome. There is one mediator, and anyone at all, of any nation or past, may come through him by faith (Romans 10:13–14).

On a Tuesday. When you pray today, ask whether you approach God as if you need to make yourself presentable first, or as if you had no standing at all. Neither is right. You come through a mediator who has already brought you near. Begin your prayer by naming him: I come through Jesus Christ, who gave himself for me.

verseByVerse.quote: For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Preacher and apostle. For this is the testimony of verse 6, Christ the ransom. The ransom was for all kinds of people, Gentiles included, and Paul’s own commission is the proof that God meant it. He was sent specifically to the outsiders. Three titles, and they are not synonyms. A preacher (kēryx) is a herald: the man who announces a king’s decree in the public square, whose job is accurate delivery and who has no licence to edit. An apostle (apostolos) is an authorised messenger, one sent with authority. A teacher (didaskalos) is the one who explains and instructs over time. Announcing, authorisation, patient explanation: the three together describe the whole task.

Appointed. The verb is tithēmi, set or placed: God placed Paul in this ministry. Set that against 1:7, where the men causing the trouble were desiring to be teachers of the law. One man was placed; the others placed themselves. The whole difference between apostolic ministry and religious ambition lies in who did the placing, and it explains why Paul can insist on his credentials in one breath and call himself the foremost of sinners in the next. He is not defending a position he took.

I am not lying. The parenthesis is a solemn assertion like Romans 9:1, and nobody had accused him in this sentence. The protest is about what he has just claimed. That God desires all to be saved, that the ransom was for all kinds of people, and that Paul is teacher of the Gentiles: these were the fighting words of his ministry. He had been mobbed in Jerusalem for less; the crowd listened to him until the word Gentiles, and then shouted for his death (Acts 22:21–22). The false teachers in Ephesus wanted to be teachers of the law (1:7), and the church needed to hear Paul’s credentials affirmed. The protest tells us that even here, late in his life, this was still the contested ground.

A teacher of the Gentiles. Paul’s special calling was to the Gentiles (Galatians 2:7–9; Acts 9:15). In faith and truth could mean faithfully and truthfully, or teaching the faith and the truth. Either way, it is not in speculation, which is what the rivals dealt in (1:4). The two nouns are the atmosphere his teaching is conducted in: trust toward God, and honesty about what is actually so.

The herald’s voice is Christ’s. A herald speaks in another’s name, and Paul knew whose. Writing to this same church, he said that Christ came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near (Ephesians 2:17). The Gentiles of Ephesus never saw Jesus in Galilee, yet Paul says Christ preached to them, because when his herald announced the ransom, the King himself was speaking. The risen Lord who stopped him on the Damascus road and sent him to open the eyes of the Gentiles (Acts 26:16–18) was making his own voice heard through him in every market square.

What he will fight for. The man who has just called himself the foremost of sinners, and who elsewhere refuses to defend his own reputation, will fight for this. He does not much mind what people think of him. He minds a great deal that they believe the Gentiles are genuinely included. And if you are not Jewish, he was fighting for you.

The apostolic office. The apostolic office was unique and foundational: the apostles were witnesses of the risen Christ, sent by him in person (Acts 1:21–22; 1 Corinthians 9:1), and the church is built once for all on their foundation (Ephesians 2:20), so the office has not continued.

Does God still call people to preach? Yes, though not as apostles. The church still needs heralds and teachers, and God still gives them (Ephesians 4:11; Romans 10:14–15). A call to preach is not normally a voice or a vision. It is a desire for the work, the gifts and character Scripture requires (3:1–7), and the recognition of the church, which tests a man and sets him apart. If you sense that desire, talk to your elders, ask them to test you, and take every opportunity to serve and learn. And whether or not you are called to preach, you are called to speak of Christ to the people around you.

On a Tuesday. The gospel reached you along a chain of heralds that runs back to Paul: someone told someone, across twenty centuries, until someone told you. Give thanks for the last link in that chain, and think of the nations that have come to your own street: the family from overseas, the international student, the colleague from another faith. A herald announces the King’s message to whoever is in the square.

verseByVerse.ref: 2:8–15 – Men and Women in the Assembly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Conduct in the gathered church: men praying without anger, women adorned with good works rather than display, and the teaching and governing office kept for qualified men, on grounds Paul takes from creation and the fall. The section ends with the hard promise that women will be saved through childbearing if they continue in faith, love and holiness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Contested Passage, Read Slowly

The crux of verse 12 is authentein; this commentary reads it as plain authority, with the thing itself restricted rather than only its abuse, and Paul grounds it in the order of creation (vv. 13–14), an order that concerns function, not worth (Genesis 1:27; Galatians 3:28).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The braided hair, gold and pearls of verse 9 imported social rank into the assembly; Paul replaces that currency with good works, which nobody can outspend.

Now: Whatever a church concludes about who teaches, a restriction on a function is never a verdict on a person.

verseByVerse.quote: I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling;
verseByVerse.commentary:
I desire then. Desire (boulomai) is a word of authoritative direction: not a preference but an apostolic instruction. And then draws it out of what he has just said: since God desires all to be saved, and there is one mediator, here is how the church is to pray.

That in every place. In every place likely means every place where the church gathers, all the house churches in and around Ephesus, and beyond them the churches generally (1 Corinthians 1:2). There is an echo of Malachi’s promise that in every place incense will be offered to God’s name among the nations (Malachi 1:11). Paul is not describing a local Ephesian arrangement but what he expects of the churches everywhere, which matters for how his instructions to men and women are read.

The men should pray. The men (tous andras) are males specifically, not people in general. Paul now addresses men and women in turn. Men are to lead the congregation in public prayer. This does not forbid women from praying in church (1 Corinthians 11:5), but it gives men a particular responsibility to lead. Paul’s first instruction to Christian men is not to take charge but to pray.

Lifting holy hands. The posture is the ordinary one of the ancient world: standing, hands raised and open, palms up. Jews prayed like this (1 Kings 8:22; Psalm 28:2; 141:2), and so did early Christians; it is the natural attitude of someone asking. Nothing here forbids kneeling or bowing, which the Bible also describes. The adjective is where the weight falls: holy (hosios, pure, devout). Hands lifted to God must be clean from sin. God told Israel that when they spread out their hands he would hide his eyes, because their hands were full of blood (Isaiah 1:15).

Without anger or quarreling. What makes the hands unholy is not ritual impurity or scandalous sin. Anger (orgē) is settled wrath, resentment. Quarrelling (dialogismos) is disputing, argument, or the internal churn of a man rehearsing his case. The hands are disqualified by the state of the man’s relationships. The false teaching had stirred up controversy (1:4; 6:4–5), and men in Ephesus were apparently carrying that into worship. Raised hands do not make up for grievances carried against a brother.

The same track. This is the consistent biblical order and it never changes. Leave your gift at the altar and go; first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift (Matthew 5:23–24). Whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone (Mark 11:25). Husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, so that your prayers may not be hindered (1 Peter 3:7). Worship does not run on a separate track from how you treat people; it runs on the same track, and a blockage in one is a blockage in the other. If a man’s praying feels obstructed, the first place to look is not his technique or his discipline, but whether there is somebody he is angry with.

The one who can ascend the hill. Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? asks Psalm 24, and answers: he who has clean hands and a pure heart (Psalm 24:3–4). Only one man has ever fully answered that description. Our high priest is holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners (Hebrews 7:26), and he has gone into the true sanctuary on our behalf. That is why men can lift their hands in every place, as Malachi foresaw: not because they have qualified themselves, but because the one mediator has opened the way and they come in his name. Holy hands are not hands that never sinned. They are hands that have been cleansed by him and are no longer clenched against a brother.

May women pray aloud in church? Yes. Paul assumes that women pray and prophesy in the gatherings at Corinth (1 Corinthians 11:5), and in Acts the women were praying with the apostles before Pentecost (Acts 1:14). What this verse does is lay a particular duty on the men: to lead in prayer, and to do it with clean hands. A church where only women pray has not obeyed this verse, and a church where women are silenced from praying has misread it.

What if I want to be reconciled and the other person refuses? Then do what lies with you, and leave the rest with God. Paul’s own limit is realistic: as far as it depends on you, be at peace (Romans 12:18). Go to them, admit your part honestly without excusing it, forgive them from the heart whether or not they ask, and refuse to nurse the grievance or talk about it to others. If they still will not be reconciled, your hands can be holy even though the relationship is broken, because what defiles them is your anger, not their refusal. Keep praying for them. And if the conflict involves abuse or danger, reconciliation does not mean putting yourself back in harm’s way; forgiveness and safety can go together.

On a Tuesday. Is there resentment in your heart toward someone in your church, or your home? Christ has made your peace with God, and his Spirit is at work to make peace through you, so deal with it before you next lead or join in prayer: a phone call, a message, an apology, or at the very least an honest prayer of forgiveness.
verseByVerse.note: Standing with raised hands was a common posture for prayer.

parallels.desc: the lifting up of my hands

verseByVerse.quote: likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire, but with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Women should adorn themselves. Likewise (hōsautōs) ties this to verse 8: as the men have their besetting problem in the assembly, anger, so the women have theirs, display. Both address what was actually going wrong in that room. Adorn (kosmeō, from which comes cosmetic) is to arrange, to make beautiful. Paul is not against beauty; he directs it.

Respectable apparel. Respectable (kosmios) is orderly, decent, from the same root as adorn: let your adornment be adorned.

With modesty and self-control. Modesty (aidōs) is a sense of shame in the good sense, reserve, the instinct not to draw improper attention. Self-control (sōphrosynē) is soundness of mind, good sense, the settled self-mastery that was among the most prized virtues in Greek moral thought. Both are inner qualities expressed outwardly, in vocabulary Paul’s readers admired.

Braided hair and gold. The specifics tell us what the problem was. In the first century, elaborately braided hair threaded with gold and pearls was a recognised display: it required slaves and hours to produce, and it existed to announce wealth and rank. Peter makes a similar point (1 Peter 3:3–4).

Ranking in the assembly. So the issue is not vanity in the abstract but the importation of social ranking into the assembly. A poor woman, perhaps a slave, entering a room where wealth was being advertised knew exactly where she stood. James addresses the same problem when a man with gold rings gets the good seat (James 2:1–4), and the same problem at Corinth, where the Lord’s Supper had become a display of who had more (1 Corinthians 11:21–22).

With good works. This is the point of the whole paragraph. Profess (epangellomai) is to claim, to make a public declaration; godliness (theosebeia) is reverence for God. A woman who claims to worship God should be known not for her outward display but for her good works: kindness, hospitality, service, like Dorcas, who was full of good works and acts of charity, and whose widows showed Peter the garments she had made (Acts 9:36–39; 1 Timothy 5:10). Paul does not tell them to look poor but to change what they are adorned with. The ornament of a Christian woman is her good works, and that is a genuinely levelling standard: a wealthy woman can outspend a poor one on pearls, but nobody can outspend anybody on kindness. Paul has taken the currency of the room and replaced it with one everybody can trade in.

Adorning the Saviour’s teaching. Paul uses this same verb in Titus, where Christian slaves are to adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in everything (Titus 2:10). A woman’s good works do not merely decorate her; they decorate the gospel, making the beauty of Christ visible in a city that knew only the beauty of money. And the works themselves are his gift: we are his workmanship, Paul told the Ephesians, created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10). The Saviour who came without outward splendour, with no form or majesty that we should look at him (Isaiah 53:2), is still shown to the world in the plain kindnesses of his people.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid all braiding, jewellery, or nice clothes. Rebekah received gold jewellery from Abraham’s servant as a sign of God’s blessing (Genesis 24:22), and the bride in the Song of Songs is adorned. The issue is extravagant display, status-seeking, and immodesty, and character matters far more than appearance.

How do I decide what is modest and appropriate? Ask three questions, of any outfit. What is it saying? If the honest answer is look how wealthy I am, or look at my body, it is saying the wrong thing in the house of God. Whom does it serve? Clothing that makes a poorer sister feel shabby, or that pulls attention away from worship, does not serve the church. And what does it cost, in money and in time? If your appearance absorbs more of both than your good works do, the balance is wrong. Within those questions there is freedom, and cultures differ. Do not judge other women by your own preferences, and do not make rules Scripture has not made.

Does this make women responsible for men’s lust? No. Every man is responsible for his own eyes and his own heart; Jesus put the guilt of the lustful look on the man who looks (Matthew 5:28), and Job made a covenant with his eyes (Job 31:1). A woman is never to blame for a man’s sin against her, and no one may ever excuse harassment or abuse by pointing at what a woman wore. Paul’s concern here is different: that a Christian woman’s aim should not be to draw attention to herself, whether by wealth or by immodesty, but to adorn the gospel with a godly life. Modesty is a woman’s gift to God and to the church, not a fence she must build around men.

For worship. God himself is the great adorner. He clothed Adam and Eve with garments of skin after their shame, he clothes the lilies more splendidly than Solomon, and he has clothed his people with the robe of Christ’s righteousness. The church is being made ready as a bride adorned for her husband, and her fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints (Revelation 19:8). A woman adorned with good works is wearing, already, the clothes of the wedding.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness. I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two contested verses. These two verses are among the most contested in the New Testament, and they should be read carefully, with the actual words in front of us, and with care for the many Christian women who read them with a lump in the throat.

In the flow. Verses 11–12 belong with verses 8–10. Paul is still setting the gathered church in order: the men are to pray without quarrelling, the women are to adorn themselves with good works, and now he says who learns and who teaches when the church meets. Verses 13–14 give his reasons, from creation and the fall, and chapter 3 goes straight on to describe the men who are to hold the teaching and governing office (3:1–7). The whole section serves the purpose Paul names at 3:15: that the church may know how to behave in the household of God.

Let a woman learn. Begin with what is easily missed. Learn (manthanō, be a disciple, study) is an imperative: a command, not a grudging permission. In the first century it was a generous one. Formal religious education for women was not assumed in either Jewish or Greek settings. In first-century Judaism, women were often not taught the law at all, and some rabbis spoke with contempt of teaching it to a woman. Paul requires it. Whatever else this passage does, it puts women in the class rather than outside the door. Christianity received women as full disciples, as Jesus did when Mary sat at his feet and he said she had chosen the good portion (Luke 10:38–42).

Quietly. The phrase (en hēsychia) is in quietness, a settled spirit, the same root as the quiet life of verse 2 that Paul wants for the whole church. It does not mean absolute silence, as if women could never speak, but a receptive, peaceable attitude, not disruptive or contentious.

With all submissiveness. Submissiveness (hypotagē) is ordering oneself under. It describes the posture of any learner under teaching, which is how a disciple sits: submission to the teaching and to the church’s order, under the elders who teach. Not submission of every woman to every man, but a recognition of God’s order for the church.

I do not permit a woman to teach. Permit (epitrepō, allow) is present tense: I am not permitting, as my settled practice. Teach (didaskō) in the Pastoral Letters refers to the authoritative teaching of doctrine in the church, the work of elders (3:2; 4:11; 5:17; 2 Timothy 2:2). Paul is forbidding women to hold the teaching office in the gathered church.

To exercise authority. The crux is authenteō, have authority, take authority, a rare word found only here in the New Testament. Some argue it carries a negative shade, to domineer or usurp, so that Paul forbids only overbearing authority rather than a woman’s teaching as such. That is a serious reading held by serious Christians, and it should not be caricatured. But two things weigh against it. Much of the wider evidence for the word in that period, on many scholars’ reading, points to plain authority without built-in negative force, though the evidence is debated. And the grammar of the sentence tells: in sentences built like this one, the two activities joined by or normally carry the same value, and didaskein, to teach, is a good thing throughout these letters. If teaching is good, then having authority is good too, and Paul is not forbidding an abuse of a thing but restricting the thing itself. Man (andros) here means the adult males in the congregation. The two activities together describe the eldership: teaching and governing (3:2, 5; 5:17).

To remain quiet. Again in quietness: she is to have a quiet, receptive disposition, not taking the place of public teacher over men.

Where Christians differ: may women be pastors and elders? Egalitarians (Christians who hold that every church office is open to women and men alike) argue that this verse addressed a temporary situation in Ephesus (uneducated women spreading false teaching), so that once women are educated, they may teach and lead equally. They also point to Galatians 3:28, to the women who prophesied and laboured beside Paul, and to the debated meaning of authenteō, and many hold their view precisely because they want to honour both Scripture and the gifts God gives to women. Verdict: The complementarian view is the natural reading. Paul grounds the restriction not in local culture or women’s lack of education but in the order of creation (v. 13) and the account of the fall (v. 14), which apply to all times and places. The same principle appears elsewhere (1 Corinthians 11:3; 14:33–35; Ephesians 5:22–33), and the qualifications for elders assume men (3:2; Titus 1:6). This does not mean women are inferior: men and women are equally made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27), equally heirs of grace (1 Peter 3:7), and equally gifted for ministry. Women may teach other women (Titus 2:3–5) and children (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15), share the gospel, explain Scripture privately (Acts 18:26), serve as deaconesses or in a diaconal role, and exercise a vast range of gifts. The restriction concerns the office of elder: authoritative teaching and governing of the whole church. Egalitarian brothers and sisters are not enemies of the Bible; this commentary simply judges that Paul’s appeal to creation reaches beyond Ephesus.

The scope. The scope is narrower than it is often made. Paul is addressing the gathered assembly (in every place, v. 8) and two functions: authoritative teaching and governing authority. He is not saying women may not speak, since they pray and prophesy (1 Corinthians 11:5), nor that they may not teach anyone at all. He is not saying women are more easily deceived by nature, or that every woman must submit to every man.

Every disciple sits at one Teacher’s feet. Whatever the order of the assembly, it is ordered under Christ. Jesus told his disciples not to be called rabbi, for they have one teacher, and they are all brothers (Matthew 23:8). An elder does not teach his own word but Christ’s, as an under-shepherd answerable to the chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:1–4). So the woman who learns in quietness and the man who teaches are both, first and last, disciples of the same Lord. The authority Paul restricts was never a man’s possession to boast of; it is a stewardship of Christ’s word, and teacher and hearer alike will give account to him.

So may women be pastors or elders? The more likely reading is no. Paul grounds the restriction in creation, Adam was formed first, then Eve (v. 13), not in the culture of Ephesus, and in the next chapter an overseer must be the husband of one wife (3:2). The office of elder, with its authoritative teaching and governing of the church, belongs to qualified men. Egalitarian Christians read the verse as a temporary restriction on uneducated women in Ephesus; but Paul does not argue from their lack of education.

What of a woman teaching a Sunday school class, leading a Bible study or reporting on mission? Complementarians draw the line at the authoritative teaching of the gathered church and the office of elder, and churches apply it with some differences. Women may teach women and children (Titus 2:3–4), share their testimony, and explain the faith in many settings, as Priscilla did privately with her husband (Acts 18:26). Many churches also welcome women to teach mixed groups under the elders’ oversight, as long as they are not exercising the elder’s authority. The aim is to honour both the gifts God gives women and the order he has set.

Doesn’t this make women second-class Christians? No, and a church where it feels that way has misunderstood it. A restriction on a function is not a verdict on a person. In the work of salvation the Son willingly submits to the Father, and he is not less God, equal with the Father in nature and glory (1 Corinthians 11:3; 15:28; Philippians 2:6); within the church, the members submit to their elders, and they are not lesser Christians (Hebrews 13:17). The New Testament is full of women honoured for their faith and service: the women who stayed at the cross when most of the men fled, and were first at the empty tomb; Lydia, whose home became the church at Philippi; Phoebe, servant of the church at Cenchreae and bearer of the letter to the Romans; Priscilla, often named before her husband; the women who laboured side by side with Paul in the gospel (Philippians 4:3). Eldership is one calling. The church depends on a thousand others, and on the women who fill them.

What about Deborah, Phoebe and Junia? Deborah was a prophetess and judge in Israel at a time when, as the story itself notes, the men were failing to lead (Judges 4:4–9); she is honoured, but the priesthood of Israel remained male, and her story is not about the office of elder in the church. Phoebe was a servant (diakonos) of her church, likely a deaconess, and Paul commends her warmly (Romans 16:1–2); serving in that way is not the teaching and governing office of elder. Junia (Romans 16:7) is described as well known to the apostles, or well known among them; even if she is called an apostle, the word is used there in the broader sense of a sent messenger or missionary, not one of the Twelve or Paul. None of them overturns the reason Paul gives, which is rooted in creation.

What if a man uses these verses to control or abuse? Then he is defying them. Paul has just told men to lift holy hands without anger; he will require elders to be gentle, not violent and not quarrelsome (3:3); he tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). Headship in Scripture is self-giving love and responsibility, never domination. This passage concerns the office of elder in the church; it does not put every woman under every man. Abuse is never tolerated: a woman being harmed should seek safety and tell the authorities and her church leaders, and a church that protects an abuser or tells his victim to submit to him has betrayed Christ.

On a Tuesday. If you are a woman, use your gifts in every way Scripture opens to you, and there are many. If you are a man in leadership, train women to serve, ask their counsel, and honour them publicly. If your church has never thanked the women who keep it running, start.

verseByVerse.quote: For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Adam was formed first, then Eve. The word to watch is the first one: for. Paul is giving his grounds for verse 12, and they determine how far the instruction reaches. He does not appeal to Ephesian culture, the education available to women, or the false teaching in that city. He goes to Genesis. Formed (plassō) is moulded, shaped, as a potter shapes clay, the verb used in the Greek translation of Genesis 2:7. Paul’s first reason is the order of creation: God made Adam first and then made Eve from him and for him as his helper (Genesis 2:18–23; 1 Corinthians 11:8–9). In the Old Testament the firstborn usually carried the responsibility of leading the family. This reason comes from before the fall: it is part of God’s good design, not a result of sin or culture.

Order, not worth. It is the logic of 1 Corinthians 11, and it is about ordering, not worth. Genesis is emphatic that both are made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), and Paul is emphatic that in Christ there is neither male nor female (Galatians 3:28). Whatever verse 13 establishes, it cannot mean women are lesser, because the same apostle denies it. And the word helper, which Genesis uses of Eve, is used most often in the Old Testament of God himself, the helper of Israel (Psalm 33:20; 121:1–2). It is not the title of a servant but of one who brings what is lacking.

Adam was not deceived. Deceived (apataō) is tricked, misled, intensified in the second case as exapataō, thoroughly deceived. Paul’s second reason comes from the fall (Genesis 3:1–6, 13). This is harder, and it should not be read as a claim that women are more gullible. Paul nowhere says that, and men are deceived all the time (2 Timothy 3:13; Titus 1:10). Elsewhere he lays the fall squarely at Adam’s door, twice, in the passages where he is assigning responsibility (Romans 5:12–19; 1 Corinthians 15:22).

What happened in the garden. What the verse observes is what happened there. The serpent went around the order God had established, approaching Eve and bypassing Adam’s headship, and she was deceived. Adam, who was not deceived, went along with it anyway: he sinned with his eyes open, which made his sin, if anything, worse. He was with her (Genesis 3:6), and the text records no word from him. In the fall, God’s order was reversed: the woman took the lead, and the man followed and failed to protect. Paul’s point is about what occurs when the given order is bypassed, and both parties in Genesis failed in it. The church should not repeat that reversal.

The man who did not stand by. Paul himself calls Adam a type of the one who was to come (Romans 5:14), and this garden scene shows why a second Adam was needed. The first man stood silent while his wife listened to the serpent; the last Adam stepped between his bride and the enemy and took the blow himself. He loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). The first man hid among the trees; the second was lifted up on a tree in her place. That is headship done perfectly: not passivity and not domination, but a husband who protects at the cost of his life. The order broken in a garden was restored at a cross.

And became a transgressor. The phrase (en parabasei gegonen) is came to be in transgression: stepping over the line God had drawn.

Isn’t the appeal to creation just Paul’s culture talking? That is exactly what Paul rules out by going to Genesis. When Jesus was asked about divorce, he did the same thing: from the beginning it was not so (Matthew 19:4–8). Going back to creation is the Bible’s way of saying, this is not a custom of our time, but how God made things. If Paul had argued from Ephesian conditions, we could set his instruction aside when the conditions changed. He did not. He argued from the way God made the first man and the first woman, and that has not changed.

How can there be order without inferiority? Look at the Trinity, and at Christ. The Son is equal with the Father in every way, God from God, and yet he delights to do the Father’s will: I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29). He is not less for obeying. On earth he submitted to Joseph and Mary as a boy (Luke 2:51), and he was not less than them. Order is the way love arranges itself in a family. The world assumes that whoever leads is worth more, and whoever follows is worth less; the gospel has abolished that arithmetic. The greatest among you shall be your servant.

On a Tuesday. Men, see in Genesis 3 where Adam was standing while his wife was being deceived. Godly headship is not control; it is the courage to protect, to speak and to take responsibility. Ask where in your home or church you have been silent when you should have spoken, or passive when you should have served. Where you have failed, the last Adam did not: his perfect obedience is counted as yours, and his Spirit gives the courage you lack.

For worship. The Son of God met the same serpent, not in a garden but in a wilderness, and was not deceived. Where Eve was talked out of trusting God’s word, he answered every lie with what is written; where Adam said nothing, he spoke the truth and kept it. The serpent’s first lie was that God was holding back something good. At the cross God held back nothing, not even his own Son (Romans 8:32), and the transgression that began with a lie believed was carried away by the one who is the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet she will be saved. This is one of the genuinely difficult verses in the New Testament, and the first duty is to say what it cannot mean. It cannot mean that women are saved by having babies. Paul has just said, in this very letter, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners and that there is one mediator between God and men (1:15; 2:5). Whatever verse 15 means, it does not add a second route. After Eve’s transgression, Paul gives hope, and saved is the normal word for salvation in Paul. She at first refers to Eve, and through her to women generally; the change to they in the next clause shows he means Christian women.

Through childbearing. Childbearing (teknogonia) is bearing children. It is one of the hardest phrases in Paul. Main readings: (1) women will be kept safe physically through childbirth, which killed a great many women in that world, though Paul’s word saved is normally spiritual, and many godly women have died in childbirth, which no reading of this verse may treat as a sign of God’s displeasure; (2) women will be saved through the childbearing, that is, the birth of the Messiah, the offspring of the woman promised in Genesis 3:15, which reads beautifully against verses 13–14, which have just been in the garden, though the article is not clearly emphatic; (3) women will be saved, that is, will work out their salvation and show its genuineness, by embracing their God-given role, of which motherhood is a central example, rather than seeking the role of elder. The third reading fits the context best: the curse on Eve touched childbearing (Genesis 3:16), and the false teachers were apparently forbidding marriage (4:3). Paul is dismantling a teaching that despised ordinary life, and against it he insists that a woman is not saved by escaping her circumstances but within them. Women need not take on men’s roles to be saved; they will persevere to final salvation in the path of godly womanhood, typified by motherhood, if they continue in faith, love and holiness. Reading 2 is also attractive, and the two can be combined: the Child born of a woman reversed the curse, and in him women’s ordinary calling is redeemed. Either way, the work of bearing and raising children, which the curse made painful (Genesis 3:16), is not outside God’s favour; it can be offered to Christ as service, like every ordinary task done for him (Colossians 3:23).

If they continue. The condition itself is the sentence’s real anchor. Not if they bear children; if they continue in faith. Continue (menō) is abide, remain. Salvation is by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8–9), not by childbearing as a work; the conditions are spiritual: faith (trust in Christ), love, holiness (hagiasmos, sanctification), and self-control (sōphrosynē, the same word as v. 9). Perseverance in these is the evidence of genuine salvation (Colossians 1:22–23). Sanctification here means the Spirit’s slow remaking of someone already forgiven, so that year by year the believer grows more like Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:3; 2 Corinthians 3:18). Whatever weight the first half carries, the evidence Paul asks for is exactly what he has asked for from everybody in this letter.

What is clear. It is honest to say that this verse is not fully clear and that good readers differ. What is clear is enough: no woman is saved by anything other than the one mediator, and the life that proves salvation is the same for her as for anyone: continuing in faith, love and holiness.

Where does this leave me if I am single or cannot have children? Exactly where it leaves every believer: saved by Christ, and called to continue in faith, love and holiness. Motherhood is a central example of a woman’s calling, not a condition of salvation. Some of the most fruitful women in the church’s history were unmarried, and Paul himself commended singleness as a gift that frees a person for undivided devotion to the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:32–35). Many childless women are spiritual mothers to dozens. If your childlessness is a grief, it is a real one, and Scripture does not dismiss it: Hannah wept before the Lord, and he heard her. But you are not less in his eyes, and your calling is just as real.

Does if they continue mean I could lose my salvation? No. The condition describes what true faith does, not a test it might fail. Those whom God has justified he will also glorify (Romans 8:30), and he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). But he brings it to completion through our continuing, and warnings like this are one of the means he uses to keep us. The person who is anxious to continue in faith is the person God is keeping. The one who should fear is the one who has stopped caring.

On a Tuesday. If you are a mother, see your work as holy service to God, not a lesser calling: the nappies, the meals, the patient answers to the same question, the prayers at the bedside are where your faith is being worked out, and where God is at work. And whoever you are, thank a mother in your church this week, especially one who is weary.

For worship. The woman who was deceived was given a promise in the same breath as her sentence: her offspring would crush the serpent’s head. Through childbearing, in the long line of mothers that ran from Eve to Mary, the Saviour came. He was born of a woman, carried and nursed and raised by a woman, and on the cross he made sure his mother was cared for. He has redeemed the curse at its root, and every woman who trusts him will be brought safely home, not through her own labour but through his.
verseByVerse.note: One of the harder verses in Paul. Suggested readings include: kept safe through childbirth; saved through the Childbirth, the birth of Christ; or saved while fulfilling her calling. It cannot mean earning salvation.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people,<sup>2</sup>for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way.<sup>3</sup>This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior,<sup>4</sup>who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.<sup>5</sup>For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,<sup>6</sup>who gave himself as a ransom for all, which is the testimony given at the proper time.<sup>7</sup>For this I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth, I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.<sup>8</sup>I desire then that in every place the men should pray, lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling;<sup>9</sup>likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire,<sup>10</sup>but with what is proper for women who profess godliness—with good works.<sup>11</sup>Let a woman learn quietly with all submissiveness.<sup>12</sup>I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; rather, she is to remain quiet.<sup>13</sup>For Adam was formed first, then Eve;<sup>14</sup>and Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.<sup>15</sup>Yet she will be saved through childbearing—if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with self-control.

3.title: The Household of God
3.overview:
Paul sets out who may lead God’s household. Overseers (elders) must be men of proven character: faithful in marriage, self-controlled, hospitable, gentle, not lovers of money, managing their homes well, mature in faith and respected by outsiders. Only one requirement is a skill: “able to teach”. Deacons, who serve rather than teach, must meet the same standard of character and be tested first.

Then Paul says why it matters. The church is the household of the living God, the pillar that holds up the truth for the world to see. And the truth it holds up is Christ himself, sung in an early hymn: “manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit … taken up in glory.” The rules about wine and money exist so that the pillar stands straight.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wanting to be an overseer, or elder, is a good aim, and Paul lists what such a man must be: almost all of it character, tested at home, over time, and in the eyes of outsiders.
verseByVerse.theology:
Character, Not Competence

Of some fifteen requirements only one, ‘able to teach’, is a skill; everything else concerns what a man is, and the vices named are the kind a congregation cannot see for years.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: ‘Overseer’ and ‘elder’ name one office (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5–7).

Now: Verse 7 gives outsiders a say: what would your neighbours say about you if the subject came up?

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Timothy 3 sets out who may lead the church, at a time when false teachers had arisen, probably including some of the elders themselves (Acts 20:30). Paul describes two offices. The overseer or elder (vv. 1–7) does a noble work but needs proven character: above reproach, faithful in marriage, self-controlled, hospitable, able to teach, gentle rather than violent or quarrelsome, free from love of money, a good manager of his household, not a new convert, and well regarded by outsiders. Deacons (vv. 8–13) serve the church’s practical needs and must likewise be serious, honest, sober, free from greed, sound in the faith and tested first; the women associated with them (either their wives or women deacons) must be similarly trustworthy. Then Paul says why this matters (vv. 14–16): the church is God’s household, the pillar and support of the truth, and that truth is the mystery of godliness, sung in an early hymn about Christ. The chapter that begins with job descriptions ends with a song, because the ordinary machinery of a church exists to hold up one glorious person where the world can see him.

The setting. In the New Testament, overseer (episkopos, from which come bishop and episcopal) and elder (presbyteros, from which come presbyter and Presbyterian) appear to be two names for the same office. Paul summons the elders of Ephesus and tells them the Holy Spirit has made them overseers (Acts 20:17, 28), and Titus 1:5–7 moves between the two words in consecutive verses. One office, two words: elder stresses maturity and dignity; overseer stresses the function of watching over the flock. Churches were led by a plurality of elders, not a single ruler (Acts 14:23; Philippians 1:1; James 5:14). The later system of one bishop over several churches developed in the second century.

The saying is trustworthy. The second of the five trustworthy sayings in these letters (1:15; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8). It most likely introduces what follows, the nobility of the office, though some take it back to 2:15.

If anyone aspires. Two different verbs, and both are positive. The first, aspires (oregō), means to reach out for, to stretch toward something. Paul does not treat wanting this as suspicious, as though the only safe candidate were the man who has to be dragged to it. It is right to desire this work, and it is not pride to want to serve as an elder, provided the motive is to serve Christ and his people.

A noble task. The second verb, desires (epithymeō), is to set one’s heart on, to long for. The task is a work, not a title or a rank. Eldership is hard labour (5:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:12), not honour for its own sake. Everything that follows in this chapter is about character rather than ability precisely because the job is not a platform but a labour. And in a culture where church leadership could bring danger rather than prestige, the desire was a mark of devotion: when persecution came, leaders were often the first to suffer, as James was in Jerusalem (Acts 12:1–2).

A flock bought with blood. Why is the work noble? Because of whose flock it is. Paul told the elders of this very church to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood (Acts 20:28). The overseer watches over people for whom Christ died, and that makes the job both splendid and frightening. The office itself is a gift of the risen Lord: when he ascended on high, he gave shepherds and teachers to equip his people (Ephesians 4:8, 11). A man who desires to be an overseer is asking to become one of Christ’s gifts to his church, which is a noble thing to want, and a humbling one.

Keeping the office. Paul still calls it an office. Ephesus had just been described as full of men who wanted the standing of a teacher (1:7). Paul does not respond by abolishing the position or treating leadership as inherently corrupting. He keeps the office, affirms the desire, and raises the bar, which is a better answer to the abuse of authority than pretending authority should not exist.

Where Christians differ: how should the church be governed? Episcopal churches have bishops over priests and deacons (three orders); congregational churches vest final authority in the members; presbyterian churches govern through elders in local sessions and wider courts. Each reads the New Testament honestly, and each has produced faithful churches. Verdict: The New Testament knows two ongoing offices in the local church: elders (overseers), who shepherd, teach and govern, and deacons, who serve practical needs (Philippians 1:1). Each church should be led by a plurality of qualified elders, men who meet these qualifications (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5). Apostles were a unique, foundational office that has ceased. Within this, churches differ charitably on how much authority the congregation holds and how churches relate to one another.

What does an elder actually do? He shepherds the flock: knowing the people, praying for them, visiting the sick, warning the wandering, comforting the grieving (Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2–3). He teaches, in public and in private, and guards the church from error (Titus 1:9). He leads, with his fellow elders, in the decisions that shape the church’s life (5:17). And he will give an account for the souls in his care (Hebrews 13:17). That is why the work is noble and why it is heavy. An elder is not a board member who attends meetings; he is an under-shepherd of Christ’s sheep.

How do I know whether I should aspire to this? Begin with the desire, and examine it: do you want to care for people and feed them God’s Word, or do you want to be recognised? Then hold your life up against the list that follows, honestly, and ask others who know you well to do the same. Look at what you already do. Men who will make good elders are usually already doing elders’ work without the title: opening their homes, teaching a group, visiting the lonely, praying for the flock. Tell your elders of the desire, ask them to watch and test you, and be content to wait. The call is confirmed by the church, not by the man alone.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your elders by name today. Their work is noble and hard, and much of it is invisible: the hospital visit at night, the conversation with a couple in crisis, the hours over a passage that you will hear in forty minutes on Sunday. Send one of them a note this week to say you are praying for him, and name one specific thing he has done that has helped you.
verseByVerse.note: “Overseer” and “elder” appear to be two names for the same office.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above reproach. The list begins with the heading that governs everything after it. Must (dei, it is necessary): these are requirements, not ideals. Above reproach (anepilēmptos) means not able to be taken hold of: there is nothing to grab, no handle by which he can be seized. Not sinless, which would empty every pulpit, but with no glaring, ongoing pattern of sin that could be fairly charged against him. The rest of the list explains it.

Character, not performance. Very little of the list concerns gifts; nearly all of it concerns character. The single item that is a skill rather than a character trait is able to teach. Any church selecting leaders by gifting, competence or platform has inverted the proportions Paul set, and given what chapter 1 says about men who wanted to teach without understanding, the emphasis is deliberate.

A life the flock can follow. The reason for the proportions lies in what an elder is for. He shepherds Christ’s flock as an example to it (1 Peter 5:3), and the sheep learn their Shepherd partly by watching his under-shepherds. Paul could say, Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). An elder’s marriage, his table, his temper and his teaching are meant to show the congregation, in small and imperfect measure, what Christ is like: faithful, self-governed, open-handed, truthful. A gifted man of poor character teaches one thing with his mouth and another with his life, and the flock usually believes the life.

The husband of one wife. Literally a one-woman man (mias gynaikos andra), and this is the most argued-over phrase in the list. Several meanings have been proposed: (1) he must not be a polygamist; (2) he must not have remarried after divorce or the death of his wife; (3) he must be married; (4) he must be sexually faithful to his wife, devoted to one woman. The fourth best fits the wording and the context. Polygamy was rare in the Greek world; Paul encourages remarriage of younger widows (5:14), which sits badly with a ban on any second marriage; and he himself was apparently unmarried and commends singleness (1 Corinthians 7:8), so he cannot mean must be married. The phrase stresses marital and sexual faithfulness: a man of one woman in heart and conduct. It fits the tenor of the whole list, which is about present character rather than an audit of a man’s history. What the phrase requires is a marriage nobody can point at. And the qualifications assume that elders are men, which agrees with 2:12, where Paul argues from creation, not custom.

Where Christians differ: may a divorced and remarried man be an elder? Some churches forbid it absolutely; others ignore the question. Verdict: The phrase concerns present faithfulness and character, not merely marital history. A man who was divorced on biblical grounds (adultery or desertion by the other spouse, Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15) and has since lived faithfully may be considered. But a man whose divorce was sinful, especially recent, or whose marriage history brings reproach, would not be above reproach. Each case requires wise judgment by the church.

A widower and the past. A widower who remarried is plainly not excluded. And a man divorced long ago, before he came to Christ, may qualify if his life now is above reproach and his past is not a present scandal; the church must judge each case carefully, and must not pretend that a man’s history is irrelevant or that it is unforgivable.

Sober-minded. The word (nēphalios) means temperate, clear-headed: alert, balanced, not given to excess. A shepherd who is not awake cannot see the wolf.

Self-controlled. Sensible, of sound judgment, the soundness of mind Paul commended in the women of 2:9 (also 2:15; Titus 1:8; 2:2, 5): a man in possession of his own judgment, not driven by his moods or appetites.

Respectable. Orderly, the same word as 2:9: a life that is not chaotic. His days, his finances and his commitments are in order, and people can rely on him to do what he said.

Hospitable. Literally a lover of strangers (philoxenos), and in the first century it was a serious matter. Inns had a bad name, and many were little better than brothels; travelling Christians and itinerant preachers depended on households opening to them. An elder’s home was to be one of them (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2; 1 Peter 4:9), which means his family bore the cost of his office. An elder whose home is closed cannot shepherd a flock, because the flock is mostly shepherded around tables.

Able to teach. It is the one gift-based qualification, and it distinguishes elders from deacons. Elders must be able to hold firm to the trustworthy word, to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it (Titus 1:9). Not every elder must be a gifted preacher, but every elder must be able to teach sound doctrine, whether to a congregation, a small group or a troubled man across a kitchen table.

What it does not mean. It does not require that elders be married or have children; it describes how they behave if they are. And these qualities are expected of every Christian; elders must model them.

Does a terrible past before conversion disqualify a man? Not in itself. Paul, a former persecutor, wrote these words, and he had been the foremost of sinners. Above reproach describes the man’s present life and reputation, not a record with nothing in it. What matters is whether he has been changed, whether that change has been tested over time, and whether his past still brings reproach on the church: some offences, such as the abuse of children, rightly bar a man from office permanently, because the trust the office needs cannot be restored and the vulnerable must be protected. The church must judge with both grace and wisdom.

Does this list mean the church is to be led by the respectable? No. It describes a man in whom grace has done visible work, not a man who never needed grace. The respectable man who trusts his own record is not what Paul means, because a heart proud of its goodness is rarely gentle, teachable or safe with other people’s failures (vv. 3, 6). The man who wrote this list called himself the foremost of sinners (1:15). And the list is for office, not for belonging: no one is welcomed into the church by meeting it, because everyone enters the same way, as a sinner received through Christ. Elders must show what that grace produces, so that the flock can see it is real.

On a Tuesday. Use this list as a mirror for your own life. You will not meet it perfectly; Christ has, in your place, and the Spirit who joins you to him is growing these qualities in you. Which of them is he growing now? If it is hospitality, invite someone to eat with you this week whom you would not normally invite; if self-control, name the appetite that is ruling you and take one concrete step against it.

verseByVerse.quote: not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not a drunkard. Four more, and they come in two pairs that describe how a man behaves when things are difficult. Drunkard (paroinos) is literally beside wine: one who lingers over wine, addicted to it. Drinking wine was normal in the ancient world, and the Bible does not forbid it; this letter will shortly tell Timothy to take a little for his stomach (5:23). What is in view is the man whose relationship with drink has become the governing fact about his evenings. Drunkenness disqualifies.

Not violent but gentle. Violent (plēktēs) means a striker, a bully, a man quick to use his fists. Against it he sets epieikēs, that hard-to-translate word from Philippians 4:5: gracious, reasonable, forbearing, yielding; the man who does not insist on the last inch of what he is owed, who knows when the strict letter would do an injustice. An elder deals with people patiently, not harshly, not domineering over those in his charge (2 Timothy 2:24–25; 1 Peter 5:3).

The gentleness of Christ. Paul chose this word knowing whose it was. When he appealed to the stubborn Corinthians, he did it by the meekness and gentleness of Christ (2 Corinthians 10:1), using the noun of this same word. Gentleness is not a temperament Paul happened to prefer in leaders; it is the character of the Lord they serve. The one who has the right to judge everyone did not insist on it among us: he would not quench a smouldering wick (Matthew 12:20), and he restored Peter with questions by a charcoal fire rather than a rebuke (John 21:15–17). An elder is to be gentle because the church already has a Shepherd who is.

Not quarrelsome. Literally not a fighter, and here with words rather than fists. Given chapter 1, this is pointed. Ephesus was full of vain discussion and confident assertion (6:4–5), and it would be easy to conclude that what the church needed was a leader who could out-argue them. Paul says the opposite. A man who enjoys the fight is disqualified from the office, however right he happens to be. That does not stop an elder contending for the truth; he must refute error (Titus 1:9). The difference is between a contentious spirit and a faithful defence.

Not a lover of money. Literally without love of silver.
