Money runs through this letter: the false teachers imagining that godliness is a means of gain (6:5), the love of money as a root of all kinds of evils (6:10), the rich charged not to be haughty (6:17). Greed was a mark of the false teachers (Titus 1:11). Elders may be paid (5:17–18), but they must not be in it for money. A man who loves money will eventually be bought, and everyone will find out what the price was.

What they have in common. Drink, violence, arguing, money: each is a way of handling pressure or appetite badly, and each is invisible to a congregation until it is far too late. That is why the qualifications are for character rather than performance. You can assess a man’s preaching in twenty minutes; these take years to see. Ask his wife, his children, his employees and the people who have disagreed with him.

What if my pastor is harsh, controlling or a bully? Then he is failing one of the plainest requirements of his office, and it should not be excused as strong leadership. Elders are not to domineer over the flock (1 Peter 5:3), and a man who manipulates, intimidates, shames people from the pulpit or punishes disagreement is not gentle. If it is a single incident, speak to him privately and humbly. If it is a pattern, take it to the other elders, or to whatever wider body your church answers to. If you have been harmed, you are not being disloyal by speaking up, and abuse of any kind, spiritual, emotional or physical, must never be covered up to protect a leader’s reputation. The flock belongs to Christ, not to the shepherd.

Should Christians drink alcohol at all? Scripture permits it and warns against its abuse. Jesus made wine at a wedding, and the Psalms praise wine that gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15). But drunkenness is sin (Ephesians 5:18), and wisdom may call for abstinence: if you have a history of addiction, if drink runs in your family as a destroyer, if you are with someone who is struggling, or simply for the sake of a weaker brother (Romans 14:21). Many godly Christians choose not to drink, and many godly Christians drink moderately. Neither should judge the other, and both should watch that the thing never becomes their master.

On a Tuesday. Are you known as gentle? Ask someone close to you, and listen to the answer without defending yourself. If it stings, take it to Christ, who is gentle with you, before you take it anywhere else.

For worship. The Lord of glory came gentle and lowly in heart. Every honour in heaven was his by right, and he laid it aside. He would not quarrel or cry aloud in the streets; when he was reviled he did not revile in return. And the one man who never loved silver was sold for thirty pieces of it by a man who did. His gentleness is not weakness. It is the strength of a King who has nothing to prove, and it is how he shepherds us still.

verseByVerse.quote: He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive, for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must manage his own household well. Manage (proistēmi) is to lead, to preside over, to care for, the same word used of elders who rule well (5:17). The household in the ancient world included family, servants and property. A man’s leadership at home is a testing ground for leadership in the church.

With all dignity. Submissive (hypotagē) is under order, obedient. With all dignity (meta pasēs semnotētos) could describe the father’s manner (he leads with dignity, not harshness) or the children’s behaviour (they are respectful). Probably the father: he maintains order in a dignified way, not by shouting or force. A house kept in line by fear would meet the letter of this requirement and fail its spirit entirely, and Paul has already ruled out the violent man in verse 3. This concerns children still at home and under his authority.

For if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God’s church? Then the reason, put as a question that answers itself. The argument runs from lesser to greater, and it assumes something the modern church often does not: that home and congregation are the same kind of thing. Both are households, and Paul will call the church the household of God ten verses later (v. 15). If a man cannot lead his small family well, he will not lead God’s family well.

Care for. The verb Paul chooses for the church changes at the crucial moment. He does not ask how a man will manage God’s church. He asks how he will care for it (epimeleomai, take care of, look after), the same word used of the Good Samaritan taking charge of the wounded man at the inn (Luke 10:34–35). Church leadership is not corporate management but tender care. Managing a household qualifies a man for something warmer than management.

The Son over the house. Hebrews draws the comparison plainly: Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son, and we are his house (Hebrews 3:5–6). An elder is never the master of the church, only a steward in a house that belongs to the Son, caring for brothers and sisters whom the Son is not ashamed to call his brothers (Hebrews 2:11). That is why the qualification looks at a man’s home. The church is to be cared for by someone who answers to its true Head, and he must first have learned at his own table what faithful, gentle care looks like.

What it does not mean. It does not mean an elder must have perfect children who never sin, or that he is disqualified because an adult child has chosen to rebel. Children have their own wills. It is not a guarantee that a good father’s children will all believe; Scripture nowhere promises that. It means his household should show a pattern of godly, loving leadership, and his children at home should generally be respectful and orderly.

The place where character is known. And the principle reaches past elders to everyone. The place where a person’s real character is known is the house he lives in. Public competence is easy to manufacture for a few hours a week; nobody sustains a performance in front of the people who see him tired. If you want to know what a man is like, ask how his children speak of him when he is not in the room.

Have I failed if my child has walked away from the faith? Not necessarily, and you must not assume it. Every parent fails in many ways, and it is right to confess those failures to God and, where it helps, to your child. But a child’s faith is not manufactured by parenting; it is the gift of God, who calls whom he wills. Adam and Eve had a perfect Father and walked away. Keep loving your child, keep the door open, keep praying without ceasing, and do not turn every conversation into a sermon. Many prodigals have come home years later, remembering a father or mother who never stopped loving them. Leave the outcome with God, who loves your child more than you do.

On a Tuesday. Fathers: is your leadership at home marked by dignity and care, or by harshness or neglect? Lead out of the Father’s patience with you, not fear of failing; his Spirit gives what you lack. This week, apologise to one of your children for something you got wrong. Children learn what God the Father is like by watching their fathers.

For worship. God is the Father from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named. He rules his household with perfect dignity and perfect tenderness, never harsh, never neglectful, disciplining his children for their good and running to meet the prodigal on the road. The church is his household, and he has never once mismanaged it. Every earthly father, and every elder, is learning to do in small what he does perfectly.

verseByVerse.quote: He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil. Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must not be a recent convert. Two final requirements, and each is guarded by a warning about the devil: the only two places in the list where Paul explains what happens if you get it wrong. Recent convert (neophytos) is newly planted, our neophyte. A young believer, however gifted, has not yet been tested or matured. The church at Ephesus was about ten years old, so it had mature believers available. (In Crete, a younger church, Paul omits this requirement, Titus 1:5–9.)

Puffed up with conceit. The danger is named exactly. Puffed up (typhoō, related to a word for smoke or mist) means conceited, blinded by pride, swollen larger than the substance warrants. Quick promotion can go to the head. Give a new believer standing and authority quickly, and you may not be honouring him. You may be endangering him.

The condemnation of the devil. Two possible meanings: the condemnation the devil received (pride was the devil’s sin, which brought his downfall), or the condemnation the devil brings (accusation by the devil). Most take it as the first: the new convert, swollen with pride, might fall under the same judgment as the devil (Isaiah 14:12–15 and Ezekiel 28:17 are often applied to Satan’s fall, though their primary reference is to earthly kings). The sin that ruined the devil was pride, and a man promoted before he is ready is being walked along the same road.

A church in a hurry. This is a hard rule for a young or growing church that needs leaders now, but a shortage is no reason to promote early, because the cost falls on the man himself.

Thirty quiet years. The church has a better example of patience than any rule. The Son of God, sinless from the cradle, spent some thirty years in a carpenter’s home before he began his public ministry (Luke 3:23), increasing in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man (Luke 2:52). Even then, the Spirit first led him into the wilderness, where the devil offered him every shortcut to glory and he refused them all (Luke 4:1–13). If the Lord of the church was content to wait for his Father’s hour, his under-shepherds can wait for theirs.

Well thought of by outsiders. The most surprising qualification in the chapter. The church does not get to assess its leaders on its own. Paul makes the opinion of non-Christians, neighbours, tradesmen, employers, the people who see the man when he is not being religious, a formal qualification for office. Not that they must approve of his beliefs; the gospel will always offend. But they must not be able to say he is dishonest, or cruel, or unreliable.

A snare of the devil. Snare (pagis) is the word for a bird-snare. The devil sets traps for leaders, and a poor reputation can be one: accusations, scandal, ruined witness (2 Timothy 2:26). A leader with a bad reputation outside the church is already caught: everything he says about Christ is discounted by the people who know what he is like, and he cannot free himself by arguing.

In the flow. The overseer’s list closes on a warning (vv. 6–7), and the warning has a history in this letter. The enemy has already appeared: Hymenaeus and Alexander were handed over to Satan (1:20), and the serpent deceived Eve (2:14). He will be named again in 4:1, behind the deceitful spirits and teachings of demons. So the qualifications are not a job description drawn up in calm conditions. They are part of the good warfare of 1:18, and an unready or disreputable leader is a gap in the wall.

How long is a recent convert? Scripture gives no number of years, and wisely, because people mature at different speeds. The question is whether a man’s faith has been tested by time and trouble, whether his character has been seen under pressure, and whether he has shown humility when corrected. In an established church that will usually mean years, not months. Paul himself, after his conversion, spent years in relative obscurity before his great missionary work began (Galatians 1:17–18; 2:1).

Should a famous convert be put on the platform straight away? No, and churches do great harm when they do it. A celebrity, an athlete or a public figure who comes to Christ is a cause for joy, and his testimony may be told. But to give him a pulpit, a book contract or a leadership role before his roots have grown is to do exactly what this verse forbids, and many such men have fallen publicly, to the gospel’s shame and their own harm. Love him by letting him be an ordinary church member for a good long while: learning, serving, being known.

On a Tuesday. What would your neighbours and colleagues say about you if the subject came up? Be the one who pays on time, keeps his word, does not gossip about the boss, and treats the cleaner with the same respect as the director, so that they think well of the Christ you follow.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deacons serve rather than teach, but their character is held to the same standard and tested first; so is that of the women of verse 11, whether deacons’ wives or women deacons. Those who serve well gain great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
Wives, or Women Deacons?

The gynaikas of verse 11 may be deacons’ wives (so the ESV) or women serving as deacons (compare Phoebe, Romans 16:1). The passage does not settle it; the standard of character is the same either way.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Missing from the deacons’ list is ‘able to teach’: they serve rather than teach, under standards just as demanding.

Now: Test first, then appoint (v. 10): the order churches reverse to their cost.

verseByVerse.quote: Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain. They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deacons likewise. The word ties the second office to the first: same seriousness, different function. Deacons (diakonoi) are servants, ministers. The roots of the office are often traced to Acts 6:1–6, where seven men were chosen to handle the daily distribution to widows so that the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and the word. Deacons care for the practical and material needs of the church, freeing elders to shepherd and teach.

What is missing. One thing is missing from this list: there is no able to teach. That single skill separated the overseer, and its absence here defines the deacon’s work: he serves rather than teaches. Everything else, the character, the testing, the blamelessness, is just as demanding.

Dignified. Serious, worthy of respect, the same root as the dignity of the overseer’s household manner (v. 4).

Not double-tongued. Literally two-worded (dilogos): saying one thing to one person and another thing to another. It is a precise hazard for men who move between households collecting and distributing, hearing everybody’s business. A deacon who repeats in one house what he heard in another destroys the trust the job runs on.

Not addicted to much wine. The same concern as for the elder, and for the same reason: a servant who cannot master his appetite cannot be trusted with other people’s needs.

Not greedy for dishonest gain. The word (aischrokerdēs) means fond of shameful profit, eager for it, and it is exact for the office. Since deacons handled the church’s money and gifts to the poor, they must be scrupulously honest. The temptation is obvious: funds passing through your hands with no ledger anybody checks. The disciples had a treasurer once who helped himself to what was put into the bag (John 12:6).

The mystery of the faith. This is the positive at the centre. Mystery (mystērion) is a truth once hidden, now revealed by God; the faith is the body of Christian truth. Deacons are not required to expound the faith, but they must hold it, firmly, and hold it with a conscience that is clean. Conscience has already appeared twice in the letter, as a good conscience (1:5, 19), and it is the letter’s steady concern, linking belief and behaviour. A man may distribute bread faultlessly while carrying something unresolved, and Paul will not have it.

The mystery is a person. What exactly do deacons hold? Paul answers at the end of this chapter, when he names the mystery of godliness and it turns out to be a hymn about Christ: he was manifested in the flesh, and taken up in glory (3:16). The mystery of the faith is not a secret doctrine for insiders but the open secret of the Son of God made man, crucified, raised and reigning. So a deacon carrying bread to a widow is not doing something less theological than preaching. He is holding Christ while he does it, and his clean conscience is the evidence that his grip is real.

Tested first. Tested (dokimazō) is examined, proved, the assayer’s word for testing metal. Not tested by an examination necessarily, nor a formal probation, but by time: an observed track record. The church should know a person’s character before appointing them.

Blameless. Blameless (anenklētos) is unaccused, without charge, similar to above reproach for elders. Paul’s order is: observe the man, then appoint him. The reverse order, appoint him and find out afterwards, has brought many churches to grief.

What do deacons do in a church today? Whatever practical service frees the elders to pray, teach and shepherd. In many churches deacons care for the poor and those in need, manage the church’s finances and buildings, organise care for the sick and the elderly, welcome newcomers, run the practical side of the Lord’s Supper and baptisms, and coordinate the many volunteers who keep a church running. The details vary, and Scripture leaves room for that. What does not vary is the spirit: deacons serve, and they serve so that the Word can run and no one in need is forgotten, as in Acts 6, where the widows were being overlooked.

Is serving less spiritual than teaching? No. The word deacon means servant, and the Lord of the church took that title for himself: I am among you as the one who serves (Luke 22:27). The seven in Acts 6 were required to be full of the Spirit and of wisdom, to wait on tables. Carrying meals to a widow, fixing a leaking roof, counting the offering honestly and driving an old man to church are as much the work of Christ as preaching, and they are often how the gospel becomes visible to a watching world.

On a Tuesday. Deacons serve quietly. Look for one practical need in your church that nobody has noticed, and meet it without telling anyone.
verseByVerse.note: Deacons (“servants”) cared for the church’s practical needs.

verseByVerse.quote: Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things. Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well. For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their wives likewise. The Greek simply says women (gynaikas), which can mean either wives or women; the language does not distinguish, and there is no possessive their in the text. So the verse is genuinely ambiguous, and the choice matters. Two readings are held by serious Christians: (1) the wives of deacons, who would assist their husbands in ministry; or (2) women deacons, often called deaconesses. In favour of the second: likewise introduces a new group, as with deacons in verse 8, as though a third category is being named; the qualities listed match the deacons’ own point for point; no qualifications are given for elders’ wives, which would be odd if deacons’ wives needed them; and Phoebe is called a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae (Romans 16:1). In favour of the first: the verse sits inside the deacon paragraph, and verse 12 returns to male deacons as husbands of one wife, suggesting the women of verse 11 belong to them. The ESV reads their wives, with a note that the word can mean women. Both views are held by faithful complementarians, since the diaconate is not an office of teaching or governing authority over men.

Not slanderers. Slanderers (diaboloi) are accusers, malicious gossips, and the same word is used of the devil, whose name means accuser. Careless talk about people is given the devil’s own title, which should sober anyone who has ever enjoyed passing something on. Women who visit homes hear a great deal, and must not spread it.

Faithful in all things. Trustworthy in every respect: the woman to whom you could give the keys, the money and the secret, and sleep well. The qualities are the ones this letter keeps returning to, and the same standard of character is required whichever reading of the verse is right.

Husband of one wife. The same requirements as elders (vv. 2, 4): faithful in marriage, a good leader at home. The one who serves the household of God must first serve his own well.

A good standing. This is a promise rather than a requirement. Good standing (bathmon kalon) is a good step, a good rank, good ground to stand on. Faithful deacons gain respect in the church, and perhaps a good standing before God.

Great confidence. Confidence (parrēsia) is boldness, freedom of speech, the word used of Peter and John before the council (Acts 4:13). Faithful service grows assurance and boldness in faith, toward God and in speaking to others. Paul does not promise deacons promotion; he promises them assurance. A man or woman who has carried food to widows for years, quietly and honestly, ends up with a settledness in the faith that no amount of study produces on its own.

Boldness that rests on Christ. Paul is careful to say where the confidence lies: in the faith that is in Christ Jesus. Writing to this same church, he used the same word: in Christ we have boldness and access with confidence through our faith in him (Ephesians 3:12). A faithful deacon does not grow bold by admiring his record of service. He grows bold because, year after year, he has watched Christ keep his promises in the homes of the poor and the sick, and his confidence has moved off himself and onto the Lord he was serving.

Where Christians differ: may women serve as deacons? Some say the diaconate is for men only; others allow women deacons. Verdict: Either reading of verse 11 is within faithful bounds. Since deacons do not hold the authority to teach and govern the church (2:12), women may serve in a diaconal capacity, as Phoebe did. Churches should decide wisely and charitably, without treating the question as a test of orthodoxy.

So may my church have women deacons? It may, and many faithful churches do; others keep the office for men and have women serve alongside in diaconal work without the title. Paul calls Phoebe a servant of the church and asks the Romans to help her in whatever she needs, for she has been a patron of many (Romans 16:1–2). Whatever your church decides, the work matters more than the title. Within a few generations the church had women formally serving in this way, caring for women in need, visiting the sick and assisting at the baptism of women. If your church is divided on the question, do not let it become a cause of quarrelling; Paul has just said that a quarrelsome man is unfit to lead.

How do I share a prayer need without gossiping? Ask three questions before you speak. Is it mine to tell? If it was told you in confidence, it is not, and asking for prayer does not change that. Would they be glad to hear me telling it? If not, keep it between you and God. And what is my aim: that this person be helped, or that I be the one who knows? Often the best prayer request is the vaguest: please pray for a friend going through a hard time. Gossip disguised as concern is still gossip, and the devil’s name is on it.

On a Tuesday. Christ has covered your secrets rather than exposing them, so guard your tongue this week. When a conversation turns to someone who is not there, change the subject, or say something kind about them.

For worship. The accuser’s name is slanderer, and his work is to spread what will wound. Christ’s name is Advocate, and his work is to speak for us before the Father, covering our sins rather than exposing them. He knows every secret of every household in his church, and he has never once betrayed a confidence or brought up again a sin he has forgiven. He is faithful in all things, and the accuser’s whispers fall silent before the one who has answered every charge against his people with his own blood.
verseByVerse.note: “Their wives” may also be translated “women,” that is, women deacons; the Greek can mean either.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter’s statement of purpose: how to behave in the household of God, the church that holds up the truth. And the truth it holds up is Christ, in an early hymn that runs from his coming in the flesh to his being taken up in glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
Pillar and Buttress

The church does not create the truth; it holds it up where it can be seen (v. 15). And the hymn of verse 16 is six passive lines, God doing all of it, from ‘manifested in the flesh’ to ‘taken up in glory’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In a city proud of Artemis’s hundred-odd columns, house churches are called the pillar of the truth.

Now: The question to ask of a church is not whether it is impressive but whether it is holding up Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that, if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am writing these things. Here is the letter’s own statement of purpose, and the honesty of it should be noted. Paul intends to come, but he may not. The letter stands in for his presence, and now stands in for it for the whole church in every generation.

The household of God. This verse is the key to the whole letter. Everything in chapter 3 has been building here. The overseer must manage his own household because the church is one; the deacons serve in it; and now the whole is named. A household in that world was not a nuclear family but an extended body, kin, servants, dependants, with an order to it and a head. The church is that, and it is God’s: God as Father, believers as brothers and sisters, elders as stewards (Titus 1:7).

The church of the living God. Of the living God: the adjective has teeth in Ephesus, whose great temple housed an image that could not move, and whose craftsmen made a living selling silver shrines of it (Acts 19:23–41). The Ephesians boasted that their image had fallen from the sky (Acts 19:35). The true God is alive and present among his people, and the Thessalonians turned to him from idols, to serve the living and true God (1 Thessalonians 1:9). And a living God is a holy one. It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (Hebrews 10:31), which is why Paul cares so much how people behave in his house: it is not a club with rules but the dwelling of the Holy One.

A pillar and buttress of the truth. Pillar (stylos) is a column, which holds up and displays. Buttress (hedraiōma) is a foundation, support, bulwark, which keeps it from shifting. The temple of Artemis, according to Pliny, had 127 enormous columns, each sixty feet high, and was counted one of the seven wonders of the world. Paul takes the architectural vocabulary of the most famous building in Asia and applies it to a congregation meeting in houses. The church holds up the truth for the world to see and holds it firm against attack.

The right way round. The relation is often inverted. The church does not create the truth or authenticate it. A pillar does not make the roof; it holds it up where people can see it. The truth stands on its own, and the church’s task is to hold it visibly in place, which is exactly what the false teachers of chapter 1 were failing to do.

A temple with a cornerstone. Paul had already told the Ephesians what this temple stands on: the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure grows into a holy temple in the Lord (Ephesians 2:20–22). The living God of this verse does not live in a marble shrine; he lives among a people joined to his Son. And the truth the pillar holds up is not finally a system but that same Son, who said, I am the way, and the truth, and the life (John 14:6). A congregation is not primarily a service provider, a campaign or a community centre. It is a pillar of the truth to the degree that it lifts Christ up where the town can see him.

Where Christians differ: does the church stand above Scripture? Roman Catholic teaching uses this verse to argue that the church, through its teaching office, is the infallible guardian and interpreter of truth, and that Scripture and tradition together form the rule of faith. Verdict: The church supports the truth; it does not create it or stand over it. The truth is God’s Word, which the church receives, guards, and proclaims (2 Timothy 1:13–14; Jude 3). When a church departs from Scripture, it ceases to be a pillar of truth, as the false teachers in Ephesus showed. Scripture alone is the final authority over the church (sola Scriptura, by Scripture alone). Roman Catholic Christians who see it otherwise often love the church’s long history deeply, and that love is right; the question is only whether the church is the roof or the pillar.

Why do I need to belong to a local church? Because this is what God has made for you to live in. You cannot be a member of a household by yourself. The New Testament knows nothing of Christians who believe privately and belong nowhere: every letter is written to a gathered church or its leaders, and every command about loving one another, bearing burdens, submitting to elders, using gifts and sharing the Lord’s Supper assumes you are in one. Online sermons can feed you, but they cannot know you, visit you when you are ill, correct you when you wander or need your gifts. Find a church where the Bible is taught faithfully, join it, and commit yourself to its people.

What if my church is a poor pillar? Every church is imperfect, and Timothy’s church was troubled by false teachers when Paul wrote this. Do not leave over preferences, disappointments or ordinary weakness; pray, serve, and be part of the remedy. But if a church has abandoned the gospel itself, denying the truths about Christ that the church has always confessed, or refusing to submit to Scripture, it has stopped being a pillar of the truth, and you should find one that still is. The question is not whether the church is impressive but whether it is holding up Christ.

On a Tuesday. Think of your local church as it really is, with its weak points and its awkward people, and ask what it is holding up in your town. Christ has built you into this house; are you bearing weight in it, or watching from the forecourt?

For worship. The living God has a house, and it is not made of marble. It is made of forgiven people, gathered in his Son’s name, and he lives among them by his Spirit. The temple of Artemis lies in ruins, a single reconstructed column standing in a marsh; the household of the living God still stands in every nation on earth, in rented halls and village chapels and crowded flats, holding up the truth about Jesus. Empires have fallen around it, and its foundation has never moved, because the one it rests on is alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness. We confess (homologoumenōs) means by common confession, undeniably, as all agree. Paul introduces what the whole church confesses. Mystery (mystērion) is a truth hidden in the past and now revealed. Of godliness (tēs eusebeias) is the truth that produces godliness, the revealed secret at the heart of true religion. And the opening may be a deliberate contrast with the cry that filled the theatre at Ephesus for two hours: Great is Artemis of the Ephesians! (Acts 19:28, 34). The mob shouted the greatness of a goddess who could not hear them. The church confesses the greatness of a Saviour who came.

A hymn. What follows is rhythmic, balanced, and almost certainly an early Christian hymn or creed the churches sang, and Paul quotes it whole. It has six lines, each beginning with a verb in the same form, arranged perhaps in three pairs that contrast earth and heaven: flesh and Spirit, angels and nations, world and glory. The movement is from the incarnation to the exaltation. And every verb is passive: he was manifested, vindicated, seen, proclaimed, believed on, taken up. Christ is the subject throughout, and God is doing all of it.

He was manifested in the flesh. The truth at the centre of godliness is not a principle but a person: Christ. He (hos) is literally who. Manifested (phaneroō) is made visible, revealed, which means he existed before he appeared. And in the flesh: in true human nature, not a semblance, not a costume, but the real thing. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). The first line rules out the two errors the early church had to fight: that he was not truly divine, and that he was not truly human.

Vindicated by the Spirit. Vindicated (dikaioō) is declared righteous, justified, shown to be in the right. He had been condemned by a Jewish council and a Roman court and executed as a criminal; the resurrection by the Spirit was the higher court overturning the verdict. He was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4; 1 Peter 3:18). Or it may mean in the spirit, in the realm of the Spirit, the new life of resurrection.

Seen by angels. The unseen world watched. Angels appear at every hinge of his life: the announcement, the birth, the wilderness, Gethsemane, the empty tomb, the ascension (Matthew 28:2–7; Acts 1:10–11), and perhaps the whole of his triumphant entry into heaven, with angels and authorities and powers made subject to him (Ephesians 1:20–21; 1 Peter 3:22). The salvation they watched unfold, Peter says, is something they long to look into even now (1 Peter 1:12).

Proclaimed among the nations. The message went to the whole world; Paul himself had been appointed its herald to the Gentiles (2:7).

Believed on in the world. Not merely proclaimed but believed, and this is the least likely thing on the list. The other lines are about him; these two are about what happened next. A crucified provincial was announced to the empire, and people believed it. Nothing in the world’s self-interest explains that. There was no army, no money and no prestige behind the message, only witnesses who said they had seen him alive and held to it under threat of death (1 Corinthians 15:3–8), and the Spirit opening hearts to believe them. Paul is writing to a church in Ephesus that exists because that line came true, and every believer reading it today is more evidence of the same.

Taken up in glory. Taken up (analambanō) is the word used of the ascension (Acts 1:2, 11, 22). The hymn ends where he now is. He reigns in glory at the Father’s right hand.

Textual note. Many later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) read God was manifest in the flesh (theos) instead of He who was manifested (hos). In ancient manuscripts, the abbreviation for God (ΘΣ) looked very like who (ΟΣ) with a small line added. The earliest and best manuscripts read who, and this is the more likely original. The deity of Christ does not depend on this verse; it is clearly taught elsewhere (John 1:1; Romans 9:5; Titus 2:13; Hebrews 1:8), and the hymn itself assumes his pre-existence.

What it is all for. Paul has spent a chapter on overseers, deacons, wine, money, household management and reputation: the unglamorous machinery of a working church. Then he says: and this is what it is all for. The rules about drink and quarrelling are not religious housekeeping. They exist so that the pillar stands straight and this can be seen from the street.

What is godliness, and how does a hymn about Christ produce it? Godliness (eusebeia) is a life turned toward God in reverence, love and obedience: the whole person living before his face. Paul calls this hymn the mystery of godliness because godliness grows from it and from nothing else. You do not become godly by trying harder to be religious, as the false teachers taught; you become godly by beholding Christ. As we see the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). The incarnate, risen, ascended Christ is not only the object of your faith but the pattern and the power of your new life.

On a Tuesday. When you are weary of the ordinary business of church life, the meetings, the rotas, the disagreements about small things, come back to this verse. Read the six lines aloud slowly. Take one line a day this week into your prayers, and go back to the rota with them in your heart.
verseByVerse.note: Probably an early Christian hymn or creed, with six lines in three pairs. “He” is literally “Who” in Greek; some manuscripts read “God,” others “Which” (ESV note).

3.text: <sup>1</sup>The saying is trustworthy: If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task.<sup>2</sup>Therefore an overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, sober-minded, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach,<sup>3</sup>not a drunkard, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money.<sup>4</sup>He must manage his own household well, with all dignity keeping his children submissive,<sup>5</sup>for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how will he care for God's church?<sup>6</sup>He must not be a recent convert, or he may become puffed up with conceit and fall into the condemnation of the devil.<sup>7</sup>Moreover, he must be well thought of by outsiders, so that he may not fall into disgrace, into a snare of the devil.<sup>8</sup>Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for dishonest gain.<sup>9</sup>They must hold the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience.<sup>10</sup>And let them also be tested first; then let them serve as deacons if they prove themselves blameless.<sup>11</sup>Their wives likewise must be dignified, not slanderers, but sober-minded, faithful in all things.<sup>12</sup>Let deacons each be the husband of one wife, managing their children and their own households well.<sup>13</sup>For those who serve well as deacons gain a good standing for themselves and also great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus.<sup>14</sup>I hope to come to you soon, but I am writing these things to you so that,<sup>15</sup>if I delay, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of the truth.<sup>16</sup>Great indeed, we confess, is the mystery of godliness: He was manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory.

4.title: A Good Servant of Christ Jesus
4.overview:
The Spirit has warned that some will abandon the faith, following teachers whose consciences are seared and who forbid marriage and certain foods. Paul answers with creation: everything God made is good and to be received with thanks, made holy by God’s word and prayer.

Then he turns to Timothy: the kind of minister who trains for godliness, sets an example, puts the reading of Scripture first, and watches his life and his doctrine, the means by which God will bring him and his hearers safely home.

verseByVerse.ref: 4:1–5 – Some Will Depart from the Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lie behind the Ephesian error, and the answer to it: what God made is good, and is to be received with thanks.
verseByVerse.theology:
False Teaching That Restricts Rather Than Permits

The Ephesian error was ascetic, impressive for what it gave up, and Paul answers it not by negotiating but with Genesis 1: everything God made is good, created to be received with thanksgiving (vv. 3–4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Seared consciences are made one over-ruling at a time, through ordinary men saying what they know to be untrue (v. 2).

Now: Grace at the table sets a common meal apart (v. 5): neither refuse the gift nor grab it, but take it and say thank you.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Spirit expressly says that in later times some will depart from the faith by devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the insincerity of liars whose consciences are seared,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Timothy 4 moves from the truth the church upholds (3:15–16) to the lies that attack it, and then to the kind of minister Timothy must be. Chapter 3 ended with a hymn to Christ: manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, taken up in glory. Chapter 4 opens with the opposite sound, the voice of spirits that deceive. First, the danger (vv. 1–5): the Spirit has warned that some will abandon the faith, led by demonic teaching passed on by hypocritical liars who forbid marriage and demand abstinence from foods. Paul answers that everything God created is good, made holy by God’s word and prayer. Second, Timothy’s own ministry (vv. 6–16): he is to feed on sound doctrine, refuse silly myths and train himself for godliness, which has promise for this life and the next, because his hope is in the living God, the Saviour of all people, especially of believers. He must be an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity, devote himself to reading Scripture publicly, to exhorting and teaching, use the gift given at his ordination, and watch his life and doctrine closely, for so he will save both himself and his hearers. The chapter that begins with demons ends with a young man reading the Bible aloud to a congregation, and that is the whole strategy of God against the lie.

The setting. The false teaching had an ascetic strand: it treated the material world, marriage and certain foods as spiritually dangerous. This may have mixed Jewish food laws with early Greek ideas that matter is inferior to spirit, ideas that later grew into Gnosticism. The teachers may also have believed that the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:18), so that believers should already live like angels, who do not marry (Luke 20:35–36).

The Spirit expressly says. The word is rhētōs: in so many words, explicitly, in plain terms. Paul is reporting something the Holy Spirit has stated, through Jesus himself (Matthew 24:10–12; Mark 13:22), through Paul’s own earlier warnings (Acts 20:29–30; 2 Thessalonians 2:3), and through the prophets of the early church. And the tense is present: the warning still speaks to every congregation that reads it, and there is comfort in that. The church has never been taken by surprise by apostasy. Its Lord saw it coming, named it, and told his people in advance, which means that when it happens it is not evidence that he has lost control but evidence that he spoke the truth.

That in later times. The phrase (hysterois kairois, subsequent seasons) does not mean some distant final period at the edge of history. The New Testament treats the whole stretch between Christ’s first and second comings as the last days (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2; 1 John 2:18). The later times began when Christ came, and the prophecy was being fulfilled in the room where the letter was read, as it has been in some room in every generation since.

Depart from the faith. The verb (aphistēmi) gives us the word apostasy: a standing away, a defection. The faith is the body of revealed truth, once for all delivered to the saints. These are not pagans who never believed, but people who had professed it, sat in the meetings, perhaps taught in them, and then walked away from it.

Deceitful spirits. These are spirits that lead astray, and the teachings of demons are doctrines whose real source is demonic. Paul does not treat false teaching as merely a human mistake, a clever man reasoning badly. He treats it as having a source behind the visible one. The men in Ephesus were not, so far as anyone could see, occultists. They were church people with opinions about genealogies and diet. Paul says there is something else in the room (2 Corinthians 11:13–15; 1 John 4:1–3). Satan’s great weapon has always been the lie, from the garden onward: he is a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44).

The insincerity of liars. The demonic works through entirely ordinary channels: no possession, no spectacle, no darkened room. Insincerity (hypokrisis) is play-acting, the word for an actor behind a mask. Men saying things they know to be untrue, in a normal voice, in a meeting, wearing the face of piety. The devil rarely appears with horns. He far prefers a pulpit.

Consciences are seared. The verb (kaustēriazō) is the one used of a hot iron, and there are two pictures in it, both true. A slave or a criminal was branded, marked as belonging to someone: these consciences carry the owner’s mark. And a wound was cauterised, burned until the flesh no longer felt: scar tissue does not feel. These men have not lost their consciences; they have anaesthetised them, by the ordinary process of going against them repeatedly until the nerve dies. It is the same sequence as 1:19, where the conscience was rejected first and the faith went down after it. Nobody arrives at a seared conscience suddenly. It is done one small overruling at a time, and the frightening part is that by the end it does not hurt.

The same Spirit who vindicated him. The chapter break hides a link. A few lines earlier Paul sang of Christ manifested in the flesh and vindicated by the Spirit (3:16); now the same Spirit speaks again, this time to warn. And what he warns against is a teaching that despises the flesh: it bans marriage and food as if the body were the enemy. That lie strikes at the heart of the hymn. If matter were unclean, the Son of God could not have taken a body, eaten at tables, or been raised bodily from the tomb. Teaching that despises the body is, at bottom, teaching that is embarrassed by the incarnation. The Spirit’s hymn and the Spirit’s warning defend the same Christ.

Can a genuine Christian be deceived like this? A true believer can be confused, misled for a season, and drawn into error on secondary matters; the Galatians were bewitched for a while (Galatians 3:1), and Peter himself had to be corrected (Galatians 2:11–14). What Christ promises is that his sheep will not finally be snatched from his hand (John 10:27–29). The elect cannot be finally deceived (Mark 13:22): the false Christs would lead them astray if that were possible, and it is not. So the right response to this verse is not anxiety about whether you will fall, but watchfulness: stay close to Scripture, stay in a faithful church, and keep your conscience soft. Those are the very means by which God keeps his own.

How can I tell if a teaching comes from deceitful spirits? Not by how spiritual it sounds or how sincere the teacher seems, because hypocrisy is exactly the disguise Paul names. Ask three questions. What does it say about Jesus Christ: does it confess him come in the flesh, truly God and truly man, the only Saviour (1 John 4:2–3)? What does it do with Scripture: does it submit to the Bible, or add to it, subtract from it, or claim a secret key to it? And what does it do to grace: does it rest everything on what Christ has done, or quietly move the weight onto what you must do or avoid? Teaching that makes Christ smaller, the Bible thinner, or grace conditional is not from the Spirit of truth.

Is talk of demons not just an old way of describing bad ideas? No, though the question is understandable. Jesus himself spoke of the devil as a real person who lies and murders (John 8:44), and he cast out demons as a sign that the kingdom of God had come (Luke 11:20). Paul is not being superstitious here; notice how undramatic his demons are. They work through sermons, opinions and diets, not through séances. That is the claim: behind ordinary persuasion there can be a will set against God. If we wave the idea away, we have not become wiser than Jesus; we have only made ourselves easier to deceive. And the remedy is not fear but Christ, who disarmed the powers at the cross (Colossians 2:15).

On a Tuesday. Keep your conscience tender by confessing sin quickly. Pay attention this week to the small things you have learned to overrule: the remark you know was unkind, the figure you rounded in your favour, the thing you watch that you would not watch with your pastor in the room. Nobody sears a conscience in one act. Go to God about the small overrulings while they still sting, because the sting is a mercy.

For worship. Against the father of lies stands the God who cannot lie, and against every seared conscience stands the blood of Christ, which purifies the conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). The hot iron leaves scar tissue that no human hand can soften; his blood does what no surgeon can, and makes a dead conscience feel again. Teachers wear masks; he did not hide his face even from those who spat on it (Isaiah 50:6).

verseByVerse.quote: who forbid marriage and require abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who forbid marriage. The content of the false teaching is not what a modern reader would predict: not licence, but restriction, a religion of renunciation, marked by what it refused. We assume false teaching will be permissive; this kind impresses by how much it gives up. These men taught that marriage and sexual union were unspiritual, which flatly contradicts God’s design. It was God who said it is not good for the man to be alone, God who made the woman and brought her to him (Genesis 2:18–24), and God who calls marriage honourable and the marriage bed undefiled (Hebrews 13:4). Paul will soon tell younger widows to marry (5:14).

Abstinence from foods. Probably specific foods, such as meat or wine, were treated as impure. Jewish food laws may have been part of it, but the attitude went further: treating material things as defiling in themselves. Behind it lay an old and durable idea, that the material world is the problem and that spirituality means getting free of the body. Marriage and food are the two most bodily things there are, so both had to go. The same instinct produced the teaching Paul attacks in Colossians, do not handle, do not taste, do not touch (Colossians 2:21). And it has a pull on the heart that is easy to miss. A religion of rules you can keep gives you something to measure and something to be proud of: it puts holiness within your own control. That is why it impresses, and why it is a do-it-yourself salvation, with an appearance of wisdom and no power against the flesh (Colossians 2:23).

Received with thanksgiving. Paul’s answer is not a compromise about how much asceticism is appropriate. He goes straight to the doctrine of creation. God made food (ktizō, created; Genesis 1:29–31; 9:3), and that single clause dismantles the whole system. If the world is God’s and he made these things deliberately, then refusing them is not superior spirituality; it is an insult to the Giver. And note the purpose he names: God created them to be received (metalēmpsis, a sharing, a partaking). They were made for the taking. Declining a gift is not humility when the gift was made on purpose for you. The proper response to God’s gifts is gratitude, meta eucharistias, with thanksgiving: the same root as the Eucharist, as though every meal were meant to be a small thanksgiving service.

Those who know the truth. Believers who understand the gospel know that Christ has declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:15) and that the food laws were a shadow fulfilled in him (Colossians 2:16–17). And there is something deeper here. The capacity to enjoy created things rightly belongs to people who know where they came from. An unbeliever can eat and marry, and often does both with great pleasure; what he cannot do is receive them as gifts, because he does not know there is anyone to thank. The Christian alone can taste the bread and see the hand that gave it.

What marriage and bread were made to show. The false teachers banned the two things God has used most plainly to picture his Son. Marriage was made from the beginning with Christ in view: Paul says the union of husband and wife is a profound mystery that refers to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). And bread is the sign Christ chose for his own body given for us (Luke 22:19). To forbid marriage and food as unspiritual is to tear down the pictures God set up of his Son’s love and his Son’s sacrifice. The Lord himself came eating and drinking (Luke 7:34), and he gave his church a meal to remember him by. A religion of refusal cannot follow a Saviour who gives.

Where Christians differ: is celibacy holier than marriage? Some traditions require celibacy of clergy, or have treated virginity as a higher spiritual state. Verdict: Celibacy is a gift for some, and can free a person for undistracted service (1 Corinthians 7:7, 32–35; Matthew 19:12). But marriage is equally honourable and holy (Hebrews 13:4). Forbidding marriage to ministers contradicts both this passage and 3:2, where an elder may plainly be a married man. Neither state is more meritorious before God. The Reformers applied this verse directly to compulsory clerical celibacy, and they were right to: a calling to singleness freely chosen for the kingdom is good; a rule forbidding ministers to marry is not.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid voluntary fasting or personal abstinence for good reasons, such as health, conscience, or love for a weaker brother (Romans 14:21; Matthew 6:16–18). The error is making abstinence a rule that defines holiness.

I am single, and not by choice. Is this verse saying I am missing out on God’s best? No. Paul is attacking teachers who forbade marriage as unholy; he is not saying every Christian must marry or that the unmarried are second class. Your singleness is not a spiritual failure, and neither is your longing for marriage, which is the desire for a good thing God made. Jesus was unmarried, and so, at least in his ministry, was Paul. Bring the longing to God honestly; it is not unspiritual. Meanwhile your life is not on hold: the single believer has real freedom to serve (1 Corinthians 7:32–35), a family in the church (Mark 10:29–30), and the same full inheritance in Christ as any married saint. God’s best for you is himself, and that is not rationed by marital status.

Are there modern versions of this error? Yes, and they rarely use religious language. Any teaching that makes a diet, a regime of abstinence, or a renunciation the mark of the truly spiritual is walking this road: the Christian circle where what you do not eat, drink or own becomes the badge of seriousness; the subtle suggestion that married people are less devoted; the wellness gospel that treats certain foods as defiling rather than merely unhelpful. Self-denial for love of Christ and neighbour is good. Self-denial as a ladder to holiness, or a way to look down on others, is the Ephesian error in modern dress (Colossians 2:20–23).

On a Tuesday. Watch for where you are tempted to measure spirituality by renunciation, your own or someone else’s. If you are fasting, keep it secret (Matthew 6:17–18); if someone else eats or drinks what you would not, do not file them lower.

For worship. Here is the generosity of the Creator against the stinginess of every false religion. The demons forbid; God gives. The lie says the world is dirty; the Maker says it is good. He set a man and a woman in a garden and gave them each other and every tree but one, and when they took the one, he did not withdraw the rest. He still opens his hand and satisfies the desire of every living thing (Psalm 145:16). And on the night he was betrayed, the Son through whom every grain of wheat was made took bread into his own hands and gave thanks for it, and then gave himself, so that the hungry might eat and live for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For everything created by God is good. Paul is echoing Genesis 1, where God looks at what he has made and pronounces it good, six times, and then, at the end, very good (Genesis 1:31). Good (kalos) is beautiful, fine, fit for purpose, and that verdict has never been withdrawn. The fall corrupted human beings and brought a curse on creation (Genesis 3:17; Romans 8:20), but it damaged the world’s use, not its origin. Matter is not the problem, and a religion that treats the physical as inherently unspiritual is at odds with the first page of the Bible, and with the last, where the new creation has rivers and fruit and a city, and with the middle, where the Son of God took a body and kept it.

Nothing is to be rejected. The scope is total. No food is unclean in itself (Romans 14:14). But the condition matters and is not a formality: if it is received with thanksgiving. Thanksgiving is what turns consumption into worship. The same meal eaten with gratitude and eaten greedily are two different acts, and Paul’s line is not between the things but between the receivings.

Made holy. Sanctified, set apart for God’s use, by two instruments, and both are ordinary. The word of God is God’s declaration that creation is good and that foods are clean, quite possibly the Genesis verdict just cited, and perhaps also Scripture used in prayers at meals. Prayer (the same word as 2:1) means thanks before eating. Saying grace over a plate of food sets it apart. The most routine act of Christian domestic piety, the one children learn first and adults do on autopilot, is here given a genuinely priestly weight. A common meal becomes a holy thing when it is received consciously from God’s hand, and is eaten to his glory (1 Corinthians 10:31).

The harder way. That is the practical answer to asceticism, and it is harder to live than it sounds. The ascetic refuses the gift and feels holy. Paul’s alternative is not to refuse and not to grab, but to take it and say thank you, which requires you to think about God at the very moment you are most likely to forget him: the moment you are enjoying something. It is easy to remember God in a hospital. It takes grace to remember him at a feast.

Good because it is his. The New Testament tells us whose hands made the world Paul calls good: all things were created through the Son and for him (Colossians 1:16; John 1:3). The goodness of bread, wine, marriage and morning light is the goodness of Christ’s own workmanship, which is why despising it is never a harmless opinion. And the same Son came into the world he had made and blessed its ordinary things. Before he fed the five thousand he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over five loaves (Mark 6:41). Every Christian grace at a table follows him: thanks given over bread the Son made, by people the Son redeemed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anything is acceptable if we say grace over it. Paul speaks of what God created, like food and marriage; sin cannot be sanctified by prayer. Nor does it override love: a believer may choose not to eat something to avoid harming another’s conscience (1 Corinthians 8:13).

Does this cover things like alcohol, or food I struggle with? It covers what God made, received rightly. Wine is among God’s gifts (Psalm 104:15; John 2:1–11), so total abstinence cannot be made a test of holiness. But receiving it with thanksgiving rules out drunkenness, which Scripture forbids (Ephesians 5:18), and the same goes for gluttony with food. If something has become a master to you, it is not being received as a gift, and the loving and wise thing may be to put it down altogether (1 Corinthians 6:12). That is not asceticism; it is freedom. A believer who abstains for that reason, or for a weaker brother, is obeying this passage, as long as he does not turn his choice into a rule for everyone else.

Is saying grace just a habit, or does it really matter? It really matters, and this verse is the reason. Thanksgiving at a meal is not a superstition that makes food safe, and God does not need the words. But by it you confess before him, and before whoever is at the table, that this came from his hand and not merely from the shop or your wages. You are setting apart an ordinary act as worship. If grace has become mechanical, do not stop; change it. Name one thing on the table, or one mercy of the day. Let children hear you thank God for specific gifts, and they will learn that the whole world is his.

On a Tuesday. Take one ordinary pleasure today, the first cup of coffee, a walk in the light, an evening with your wife or husband, and receive it deliberately from God, out loud if you can. A gift received tastes different from a thing merely taken.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A good servant of Christ Jesus: fed on sound doctrine, training for godliness in hope of the living God, an example to the believers, given to the reading and teaching of Scripture, and watching both his life and his teaching to the end.
verseByVerse.theology:
Godliness Is Trained For

Godliness is trained for like a body, by repetition (v. 7), and unlike bodily training its results survive the body, with value for this life as well as the next (v. 8). God is Saviour of all as their preserver, and especially of believers (v. 10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Public reading of Scripture came first (v. 13) in a church where few could read: read, explain, apply.

Now: A young leader earns respect by being an example where nobody is watching (v. 12), and a minister whose progress is visible (v. 15) teaches his people that growth does not stop.

verseByVerse.quote: If you put these things before the brothers, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, being trained in the words of the faith and of the good doctrine that you have followed. Have nothing to do with irreverent, silly myths. Rather train yourself for godliness;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put before the brothers. The verb (hypotithēmi) is a gentle word: to lay down, suggest, point out. Not barking orders, but setting the truth before people, as a guide points out the path or a host sets food on the table. These things are the truths of verses 1–5: the goodness of creation, the danger of the lie, the gift received with thanks. Timothy’s task is not to innovate, but to serve up what he has been given.

A good servant. Servant (diakonos) is the same word as deacon, here used in the general sense of minister, and Paul uses it of Timothy the way he uses it of himself. What makes a servant good in this verse is not brilliance, not originality, not a large following, but faithfulness in setting the truth before God’s people. It is a standard any minister can meet and none can exceed.

Being trained. The word (entrephomenos) is a feeding word: nourished, nurtured, brought up on. And it is present and continuous: Timothy is to be constantly feeding on the truth while he feeds others. A minister who has stopped being fed will shortly have nothing to serve. Good doctrine is fine, beautiful teaching, the same word used of God’s creation in verse 4.

That you have followed. The verb (parakoloutheō) means followed closely, investigated carefully, the word Luke uses of his own research (Luke 1:3). Timothy had kept close to sound doctrine since childhood, taught the Scriptures by his mother and grandmother (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:14–15). He was not chasing novelty; he was continuing in what he had learned.

Irreverent, silly myths. Irreverent (bebēlos) is profane, common, without any sense of the holy. And the adjective translated silly (graōdeis) is literally old-womanish: the sort of tale told by the fire to keep children quiet. Paul is denying these teachings the dignity of a refutation. Some error should be answered carefully; some should be declined. To argue is to concede that the thing is worth arguing about, and there are teachings whose only power is the seriousness with which opponents treat them. Timothy is not told to defeat the myths. He is told to walk past them. That is the deepest thing wrong with them. They may be clever, but they treat holy things as common, and they leave a person less in awe of God than they found him.

Train yourself for godliness. The verb is gymnaze, the gymnasium word, and it means the disciplined, repetitive, unglamorous work of an athlete in training. Paul does not merely tell Timothy to avoid a distraction; he gives him somewhere to spend the effort. The false teachers had their own rigorous training, the training of abstinence; Paul calls Timothy to the right kind: Scripture, prayer, worship, fellowship and obedience. Godliness, on this account, is not a temperament some people are born with. It is trained for, the way a body is, by doing the same unremarkable things repeatedly, long past the point where they feel interesting. What, then, is godliness? It is reverence for God that reaches into everything: a life that takes God seriously at the breakfast table and at work as much as in church, because it knows he is there (Proverbs 3:6).

The mystery of godliness has a name. Timothy is told to train for godliness, and the word must be read with what Paul wrote a few lines earlier: great indeed is the mystery of godliness, and the next words are about Christ, manifested in the flesh and taken up in glory (3:16). Godliness in this letter is not a technique or a temperament. Its secret is a person. The athlete trains towards a standard; the Christian trains towards a Saviour, learning to fear, trust and love the God who has shown himself in Jesus. That is why the myths must go. They offer spiritual exercise with Christ left out, and exercise without him builds nothing that lasts.

If grace trains me, why do I have to train myself? Because God’s grace does not bypass your will; it works through it. The athlete’s strength is a gift: he did not create his muscles or his lungs. But he still has to run. In the same way, it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure, and that is exactly why you are told to work out your salvation (Philippians 2:12–13). Effort is not the opposite of grace; earning is. You do not train in order to be accepted by God; you train because you already are, and because the Spirit has given you the desire. A Christian who waits to feel holy before he prays will wait a long time. One who prays in obedience finds, slowly, that the Spirit meets him there.

What does training for godliness actually look like? Ordinary things, done regularly. Reading the Bible daily, even briefly, with a plan rather than at random. Praying at a set time and place, using the Lord’s Prayer or the Psalms when your own words dry up. Being in church every Lord’s Day, under the preached Word and at the Lord’s Table, not when convenient but as a fixed point. Memorising Scripture. Keeping close company with other believers who will ask how you are really doing. Practising obedience in the small things: the honest word, the kind act, the temptation refused. None of it is dramatic. That is the point. Athletes do not train by waiting for big races; they train on wet Tuesdays.

On a Tuesday. What is your training plan for godliness? Choose one discipline (daily Scripture, prayer, memorising a verse) and practise it this week. Make it small enough to keep and specific enough to check: ten minutes in the Gospel of Mark before breakfast, not a vague intention to read more.

verseByVerse.quote: for while bodily training is of some value, godliness is of value in every way, as it holds promise for the present life and also for the life to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bodily training. Paul continues the gymnasium image and makes a comparison, but read it carefully, because it is not the dismissal it is often taken for. Bodily training is physical exercise, highly prized in Ephesus with its great gymnasium and athletic games. He does not say it is worthless. He says it is of some value (pros oligon ōphelimos, profitable for a little, or for a little while), which is a genuine concession, and one you would not expect from a man supposedly hostile to the body. He has just spent five verses defending food and marriage against people who despised the physical. He is not about to turn round and despise it himself. It may also be a glance at the false teachers’ ascetic regimen, which was its own kind of bodily training, and just as limited.

Of value in every way. The comparison is one of scope. Bodily training profits a little, for a while, in one department of life. Godliness is profitable for everything. It benefits the whole person, in every sphere and for all time.

Promise for both lives. Holds promise means it has a promise attached, like a deed. Every athlete knows that whatever he builds will eventually be taken from him; the strongest body on earth is on a schedule. Training for godliness is the only regime whose results survive the body it was performed in. But do not miss the first half: godliness holds promise for the present life, not only the next. A life ordered toward God is better now: peace with God, contentment (6:6), wisdom, love and purpose, in the plain sense that self-control beats being ruled by appetite, that a clear conscience sleeps better, that love makes richer company than resentment. And it holds promise for eternity: the life to come, the inheritance, the crown (2 Timothy 4:8). Not that godliness earns eternal life, but that eternal life is promised to those whom grace makes godly.

Progress without inspiration. Nobody expects a body to change through good intentions or a single decision. It changes through repetition, when you do not feel like it, over years. The soul works the same way, which is more encouraging than it sounds: progress does not depend on inspiration.

The promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus. Paul uses that very phrase at the start of his next letter to Timothy (2 Timothy 1:1). The promise attached to godliness is not a separate reward that piety earns. It is life in Christ, already begun and not yet complete. For the present life, he is the vine and we are branches drawing everything from him (John 15:5). For the life to come, he has gone ahead to prepare a place and will come again to take his people to himself (John 14:2–3). All the promises of God find their Yes in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). That is why godliness profits in every way: it is the life of people joined to the risen Lord.

What it does not mean. It does not mean godliness guarantees health, wealth and comfort in this life. Paul himself suffered greatly (2 Timothy 3:12). The promise for this life is real spiritual blessing, not freedom from trials. Paul will guard this promise against the false teachers who imagined godliness was a means of financial gain (6:5), but he does not withdraw it.

Should a Christian exercise, then? Yes, and with a good conscience. Your body is God’s creation and the Spirit’s temple, and caring for it is stewardship, not vanity. Exercise can give you energy to serve, clarity to think, and years to love your family and your church. What Paul guards against is the inversion: when fitness, appearance or performance becomes the thing you are really living for, and the hours at the gym are guarded jealously while prayer and worship are fitted around them. The question is not whether to train the body but which training is getting the best of you. Keep the body in its place: valued, cared for, and second.

On a Tuesday. Read your diary for a normal week as a training log, and see which part of you gets the best hours. The soul, like the body, answers to small and steady change: one block of time moved, and kept for a month, will tell.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance. For to this end we toil and strive, because we have our hope set on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying is trustworthy. The third of the five trustworthy sayings in the Pastoral Letters (1:15; 3:1). It most likely points back to verse 8, the value of godliness for this life and the next, though some think it refers to verse 10. Either way it is a seal stamped on the truth: this is not a pious hope or an inspiring slogan; it can bear your whole weight.

We toil and strive. Two hard words. Toil (kopiaō) is labour to the point of weariness; strive (agōnizomai) is the athletic word for contending in the arena, from which comes agonise. The gymnasium image from verse 7 is still running, and Paul puts himself in it with a plural we. He is not prescribing a discipline he watches other people perform. To this end means for the sake of godliness and the life it promises. Some manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read suffer reproach (oneidizometha); the earliest read strive, and most modern Bibles follow them. Christian ministry and Christian life both require exhausting effort.

Hope set on the living God. There is the fuel, and it is hope rather than duty. Hope set (ēlpikamen) is perfect tense: we fixed our hope, and it remains fixed. The reason a man will work himself to exhaustion for godliness is that he expects something, and the God he expects it from is alive (zōnti), unlike the one in the great temple of Artemis down the road, whose image could neither see nor hear nor save. The living God acts, sees, hears and rescues.

The Savior of all people. A phrase that has caused genuine difficulty. Saviour and especially (malista, most of all, or perhaps that is, namely) must be read together. It cannot mean everyone is finally saved; this chapter has just spoken of men departing from the faith, and the New Testament everywhere assumes a real division. Nor is especially a way of saying believers simply get a better version of the same thing. There are two main explanations. First, God is the preserver and benefactor of all people, giving life, breath, rain and food to all (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17; 17:25), and he is the Saviour in the full, eternal sense of believers. The word saviour in Scripture covers rescue and preservation as well as eternal salvation, and every breath any human being draws is his gift. Second, malista may mean namely, defining which people God saves: all people, that is, all who believe. Read the first way, the verse fits its context exactly. Paul has been defending the goodness of creation against men who despised it. The God who feeds and sustains everybody is the same God who saves believers, and it is one generosity running at two depths.

The living God has shown his face. Paul’s hope is set on the living God, and this letter has already said how that God saves: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1:15), and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (2:5). The Saviour of verse 10 is not a vague kindness above the clouds. He is the God who sent his Son and raised him from the dead, and that resurrection is the decisive proof that he is alive. This is why the toil is not wasted. Paul labours towards a Saviour who has already done the saving work and walked out of the grave, and the One who rose keeps those who believe.

Where Christians differ: does this verse teach universal salvation? Universalists cite this verse to argue that God will finally save everyone. Verdict: The verse itself distinguishes between all people and those who believe, which would make no sense if all were saved in the same way. Scripture plainly teaches that unbelievers will face eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46; John 3:36; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). God is the Saviour of all in that he preserves all, shows kindness to all, and offers the gospel freely to all; he is the Saviour of believers in that he actually rescues them from sin and death forever.

How does this fit with God choosing his people? Comfortably. Scripture teaches both that God chose a people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4) and that he is truly kind to all and sincerely offers Christ to all (Matthew 11:28; 2 Peter 3:9). He gives sun and rain to his enemies; he commands all people everywhere to repent; and he effectually draws those he has chosen, so that they believe (John 6:37, 44). The general goodness is real goodness, not a trick, and it is meant to lead people to repentance (Romans 2:4). Election does not shrink God’s kindness to the world. It guarantees that his saving purpose will not fail, and it is why Paul could toil so hard: he knew the living God would certainly save those who believe. Election is God’s choosing, before time began, of particular people to be saved in Christ, out of his own love and not for anything in them (Ephesians 1:4–5).

On a Tuesday. If your effort is running on duty alone, it will run out; lift your eyes to the living God and to what he has promised, and let hope do what willpower cannot. And look at your unbelieving neighbour with new eyes: every good thing in his life, his health, his children, his harvest, is the kindness of the God who also offers him eternal life in Christ. Tell him whose kindness it is.

For worship. He feeds the sparrows and the ungrateful, the farmer who curses him and the child who has never heard his name, because it is his nature to give. Every loaf on an unbeliever’s table is a kindness from his hand. And to those who believe he gives what no harvest can grow: forgiveness, adoption, a living hope and an inheritance that cannot fade, bought with the blood of his Son. The God who sends rain on the fields of his enemies sent his Son to die for enemies, and made them his friends (Romans 5:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Command and teach these things. Let no one despise you for your youth, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Command and teach these things. The first verb (parangellō) is stronger than we expect for a young man in a difficult post: to give orders with authority. Both are present imperatives: keep on commanding and keep on teaching. Timothy is not merely to suggest or commend. He is to command, because, as chapter 1 established, the instructions were never his in the first place. He speaks as Paul’s delegate, and Paul speaks as Christ’s apostle.

Let no one despise you. To despise (kataphroneō) is to look at someone and mentally file him lower. Youth is relative: in the ancient world a man under forty could be called young. Timothy was probably in his thirties, which in a culture that gave authority to age was young for the job he had, and the congregation contained older men, some of whom he had to correct, and some of whom fancied themselves teachers of the law (1:7). Paul does not tell Timothy to assert himself, or to remind people of his commission, or to be tougher. Nor does he tell the church to respect him. He tells Timothy to be so obviously worth following that contempt has nothing to feed on.
