An example. The word is typos, the stamp or die that leaves its impression, the pattern or model (2 Thessalonians 3:9). Authority in this letter is not claimed; it is displayed. Timothy’s life would win the authority his age could not. It is the same logic as Paul’s own night-and-day work at Thessalonica, and the same word he used of it.

Five areas. Their order repays attention. Speech: what comes out of his mouth and how it is said, the most public thing about him (Ephesians 4:29; Colossians 4:6). Conduct: the whole visible manner of life. Love: the goal of all instruction named back at 1:5. Faith: his actual trust in God, and with it his trustworthiness. And purity (hagneia): chastity, moral and sexual purity, especially important for a young man ministering to women (5:2). Purity is the private one, and the last, and the foundation of the other four. They run from the most visible to the least, and the least visible is where it is actually decided. A young minister cannot make a congregation respect him. What he can do is give them nothing to point at, and Paul’s counsel to a man being looked down on is not to fight for standing but to earn it where nobody is watching.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) add “in spirit” after “in love.” The earliest manuscripts lack it.

A copy of the true pattern. Paul has already used this kind of word of himself. He received mercy, he says, so that in him Jesus Christ might display his perfect patience as an example to those who were to believe (1:16). The example Paul set was not first his own virtue but Christ’s mercy on show in a forgiven man. Timothy’s example is to be the same kind of thing. What the believers in Ephesus are meant to see in his speech and his purity is not a young man’s achievement but the work of the Saviour who has laid hold of him. That is what makes the standard bearable: the example is Christ’s work before it is Timothy’s.

In the flow. Verse 11 looks back over verses 6–10; verse 12 turns from Timothy’s message to Timothy himself, and the rest of the chapter stays there: his example, his reading of Scripture, his gift, his progress. That is the order of the whole letter. Paul wrote it so that people would know how to behave in the household of God (3:15), and in that household the truth is never carried apart from a life that matches it.

Is this only for pastors? It was written to a pastor, but the pattern is for every believer. Every Christian is watched by someone: children watch parents, colleagues watch the one they know goes to church, younger believers watch older ones. And the five areas are the same for all of us. The particular word to the young applies widely: a teenager can be an example to his parents’ friends, a new Christian to someone who has been in church for decades. You do not need a title to be a typos. You need a life that has been stamped by Christ, so that it leaves his impression on others.

What if people still look down on me, however I live? Then you are in good company. Some despised Jesus, who was without sin. Paul’s instruction is not a technique guaranteeing respect; it is a way of making sure that if you are despised, it is not for good reason (1 Peter 2:12; 3:16). Keep living faithfully, do not retaliate, and do not try to win standing by louder claims or harsher words. Leave your reputation with God. Over time, a consistent life usually earns trust, but even when it does not, it pleases the One whose opinion finally matters.

On a Tuesday. Take purity seriously where only God sees: the screen at midnight, the private thought life, the friendship that is drifting somewhere it should not. That is where an example is actually made.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy was probably in his thirties — young for a church leader in that culture.

verseByVerse.quote: Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching. Do not neglect the gift you have, which was given you by prophecy when the council of elders laid their hands on you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Until I come. Timothy’s commission was until Paul returned (3:14). Paul expected to come, but in the meantime the church was not left without what it needed: it had the Scriptures and a man to read them.

The public reading of Scripture. Devote yourself (prosechō) is the same word used of the false teachers absorbed in myths (1:4) and devoted to deceitful spirits (4:1). Everyone is absorbed in something; Timothy is to be absorbed in Scripture instead. Public reading (anagnōsis) is reading aloud, and it tells us something easily lost. Many, perhaps most, Christians could not read, and copies of the Scriptures were expensive and scarce. For a congregation, hearing the Bible meant one literate person standing up and reading it aloud to everybody, and that is what Paul puts first. Before explanation, before application: the text itself, read out. This is the synagogue pattern carried into the church: Scripture read aloud and then explained (Acts 13:15). Early churches read the Old Testament and the apostles’ letters (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27). A church’s primary act of teaching is letting the Bible be heard.

Exhortation and teaching. Exhortation (paraklēsis) is the coming-alongside word: urging, encouraging, applying, calling the hearers to respond to what was read. Teaching is instruction in doctrine, explaining what the Scripture means. Read, explain, apply. It is the shape of Christian ministry in three words, and it has not changed in two thousand years.

Do not neglect the gift. Neglect (ameleō) is to let something lie unused. The gift (charisma) is a gift of grace: Timothy’s gift for ministry, especially for preaching and teaching and leading. And the warning tells us that a gift can be possessed and wasted. Paul does not say Timothy might lose it, but that he might leave it in a drawer. Gifts must be used and developed; elsewhere he says to fan it into flame (2 Timothy 1:6).

The council of elders. Two things had happened at that commissioning: something was spoken over him (dia prophēteias, through or accompanied by prophecy; the prophecies of 1:18 had identified his gift and calling), and a group of men put their hands on him. The council of elders (presbyterion, the body of elders, the presbytery) did it together, with Paul (2 Timothy 1:6). The laying on of hands was the Old Testament gesture of commissioning, identification and blessing (Numbers 27:18–23; Acts 6:6; 13:3), and here it is the church’s public act of setting a man apart. The gift came from God; the laying on of hands publicly recognised and confirmed it. And note who did it: a council of elders, plural. Timothy’s ministry was not self-generated and not conferred by one man alone. A body of men had publicly identified themselves with him, which is exactly the thing to remember when the job is going badly and a man wonders whether he was ever meant to be doing it.

The reader in the synagogue at Nazareth. The pattern Paul commands has a famous scene behind it. Jesus stood up in the synagogue at Nazareth, was handed the scroll of Isaiah, read it aloud, sat down, and said that this Scripture had been fulfilled that day in their hearing (Luke 4:16–21). The sermon on that public reading was preached by the One the reading was about. After his resurrection he opened all the Scriptures to his disciples, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, and showed them the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27). So when Timothy stands up to read, he is not reciting religious literature. He is reading the book whose subject is Christ, and the reading, the exhortation and the teaching all exist to set him before the church.

Where Christians differ: does ordination convey grace? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches regard ordination as a sacrament that confers an indelible spiritual character and power, and they treat it with a reverence that is right in itself. Verdict: Ordination is the church’s solemn recognition of a man’s gifts and calling, and its commissioning of him to office, with prayer. The gift is from God; the church recognises it. The laying on of hands is a fitting sign, not a channel that transmits grace by the act itself. Scripture names only two sacraments: baptism and the Lord’s Supper.

What it does not mean. The role of prophecy here mean new revelation continues today; prophecy belonged to the foundational era of the church (Ephesians 2:20). Many Pentecostal and charismatic believers expect prophecy now, and they are brothers and sisters to be heard with respect; this commentary holds that revelation of that kind ended because the foundation has been laid and Scripture is complete.

How do I know what my gift is, and am I neglecting it? Look for where three things meet: what you are able to do that builds others up, what you find yourself drawn to serve in, and what mature believers around you recognise and confirm. That last is the lesson of this verse: Timothy’s gift was recognised by the elders, not merely self-diagnosed. Gifts are discovered mostly by serving, not by questionnaires: say yes to needs in your church and see where God blesses the work. You are neglecting a gift if you know you have been given something useful to others and have quietly stopped using it, through fear, busyness or resentment. Ask an elder or a trusted friend where they see God using you, and start there.

Why does public Bible reading matter if everyone has a Bible now? Because hearing God’s Word together is different from reading it alone. In public reading the whole church sits under the same word at the same moment, the young and the old, the scholar and the child, and God addresses his people as a people. It also guards the church: when Scripture is read at length, the sermon is held accountable to the text everyone has just heard. Many churches now read only a few verses before a long sermon. Paul put the reading first. Listen to it as God speaking, not as a preliminary, and read it well if you are asked to.

On a Tuesday. Before Sunday, read the passage that will be read in church, and pray for the one who will read and the one who will preach. And if there is a gift the ascended Christ gave you that you have let slide, pick it up again this week, even in a small way.

verseByVerse.quote: Practice these things, immerse yourself in them, so that all may see your progress. Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Practice these things. Practise (meletaō) is take pains with, cultivate. Immerse yourself is literally be in these things: be found inside them, live there, given over to them. Ministry is not a part-time hobby, and godliness is not a weekend interest.

Your progress. The word is prokopē, progress, advance, sometimes explained by the picture of pioneers cutting a road ahead of an army, though in Paul’s day it simply meant progress. And Paul expects it to be visible. The congregation should be able to see that he is a better man than he was five years ago. Timothy is a man still under construction, and Paul wants the building work on public view. A minister does not need to appear perfect; he needs to be visibly growing. A leader who cannot be seen to be growing is teaching his people that growth stops somewhere.

Watch yourself and the teaching. Two objects, in that order, and the order is the point. His own life first, his character and walk with God; then his doctrine, what he teaches. A man may guard his theology with great care while his character quietly comes apart, and this letter has already shown where that ends: the conscience goes, and the doctrine follows it down (1:19). But Paul will not let it collapse into one either. A sound teacher with an unholy life will destroy his message; a holy man with false doctrine will mislead. Both must be watched closely, and for good. Paul said the same to the Ephesian elders at Miletus: pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock (Acts 20:28).

Persist in this. Not a one-time effort but lifelong faithfulness. Many begin well. The crown is for those who finish.

Save yourself and your hearers. The last clause sounds startling and needs stating carefully, because save is the full word. No minister saves anybody; Paul has said there is one mediator between God and men (2:5). What he means is what Scripture regularly means by such language: Timothy’s perseverance in godliness and sound doctrine is the means by which God will bring him and his hearers safely through to final salvation. God saves through means: the faithful preaching of the Word and the believer’s persevering faith. Those whom God has chosen will persevere, because he preserves them through these means (Philippians 1:6; 2:12–13). Timothy is not the Saviour. He is one of the instruments, and the instruction is to stay usable.

Progress towards a person. The progress Paul wants the church to see is not general self-improvement. Elsewhere he names its goal: that we grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ (Ephesians 4:15), and he labours until Christ is formed in his converts (Galatians 4:19). A minister’s visible growth is Christ becoming more visible in him: more of the Lord’s patience in his answers, more of his humility in his authority, more of his compassion for the flock. And the doctrine Timothy watches is not a set of private opinions but the truth about that same Christ. He watches his life so that it looks like Christ, and his teaching so that it tells of Christ.

In the flow. Verses 15–16 close the chapter by gathering it up. The chapter began with men who departed from the faith because they devoted themselves to deceitful spirits (4:1); it ends with a man told to give himself wholly to the right things and persist in them. Watch yourself and the teaching is the cure for both diseases this letter has diagnosed, the shipwrecked conscience and the false doctrine (1:19). And it prepares chapter 5: only a man who watches himself first can safely correct anyone else.

If God guarantees that his people persevere, why warn them to persist? Because the warning is one of the ways he guarantees it. God does not keep his people like parcels in a vault, but like a father keeping a child on a mountain path: he holds the hand, and he also says watch your step. The promise and the command are not rivals. The elect will certainly persevere (John 10:28–29), and they will do so by heeding exactly these exhortations. So if you hear the warning and it makes you watch yourself more closely, that is not a sign you are unsafe. It is the Shepherd’s voice doing what it is meant to do in you.

What does watching my life and doctrine look like for someone who is not a pastor? For your life: a regular, honest look at yourself before God, asking where you are drifting, what you are hiding and whom you are not loving, and confessing it quickly. For your doctrine: knowing what you believe and why, from Scripture, and not absorbing every idea that comes through a feed or a friend. Read a good catechism or confession. Ask questions of your pastor. Belong to a church where both are taught. And do it with others: watching yourself is hard alone, because the log is in your own eye. Give one or two mature believers permission to tell you the truth.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself the progress question: what can people see in me now that they could not see five years ago? If the answer is nothing, do not despair: your standing rests on Christ’s perfect watch, not yours, and his Spirit has not stopped working. Go back to the training of verse 7 and begin again, today, with the Word and prayer.

For worship. The God who saves is the God who uses means, and that is itself a mercy. He could have saved us by lightning; he chose to do it through a Book read aloud, a man who keeps watch over himself, and a people who keep listening. And behind every faithful pastor stands the Chief Shepherd, who kept perfect watch over his life and his teaching, persisted to the end, and by so doing saved, not himself, for he would not come down from the cross, but all his hearers who believe. He who began a good work in us will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6).

5.title: Honour and Order in the Family of God
5.overview:
The church is a family, and Paul tells Timothy how to treat its members: older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity. Then two practical matters. Widows: the church must support those truly alone, but families must first care for their own, and a Christian who neglects his relatives “has denied the faith”. Younger widows should remarry rather than take a vow they may not keep.

Elders: those who lead well, especially in preaching, should be paid generously, and Paul quotes a saying of Jesus as Scripture. Accusations against elders need two or three witnesses, but elders who persist in sin are rebuked publicly. Appoint slowly, judge without favouritism, and remember that both hidden sins and hidden goodness will come to light.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The church is God’s household, so Timothy is to treat its members as family, in all purity.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as Household, in Practice

This is 3:15 turned into method: treat people as what they actually are, fathers, brothers, mothers, sisters, which rules out both harshness and a deference that never says anything.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A young leader not taken seriously is tempted to be harsher than the case requires (4:12).

Now: ‘As sisters, in all purity’ gives a relationship rather than a rulebook as the safeguard.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Timothy 5 applies the truth that the church is God’s household (3:15) to its ordinary relationships and practical problems. It opens with a principle (vv. 1–2): treat the church as family, older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity. Then it turns to widows (vv. 3–16), the most vulnerable people in ancient society. The church must support widows who are truly alone and devoted to God, but families must care for their own, and anyone who refuses is worse than an unbeliever. There seems to have been an enrolled list of widows, aged sixty or more and with a record of good works, who were supported by the church and served it; younger widows should rather remarry and avoid idleness and gossip. Finally, elders (vv. 17–25): those who lead well, especially in preaching and teaching, deserve double honour, including pay; accusations need two or three witnesses; those who persist in sin are rebuked publicly; Timothy must act without favouritism and must not appoint elders hastily. A word about Timothy’s health interrupts (v. 23), and the chapter closes by noting that sins and good works alike come to light. It is a chapter about welfare lists, salaries and procedure, and it is full of God: the protector of widows, the Lord who sees in secret, the Judge before whom the angels stand. Church administration, in Paul’s hands, is theology with its sleeves rolled up.

Do not rebuke an older man. The verb (epiplēssō) means to strike at, to rebuke sharply, to upbraid harshly; it is a strong word, found only here in the New Testament. Paul does not say older men never need correcting; he says this is not how it is done. Timothy is young (4:12), in a church where some wanted to be teachers of the law without understanding it (1:7), and where the trouble was entrenched. The temptation for a young man in authority who is not being taken seriously is to compensate: to assert himself sharply, to be harder than the case requires. Paul takes the option away. Respect for age is a biblical principle: you shall stand up before the grey head and honour the face of an old man (Leviticus 19:32).

Encourage him as a father. The word implies coming alongside with a gentle appeal. The correction is real, but the manner is respectful, as a son would speak to his father. You do correct your father, but carefully, and never in public.

Brothers and mothers. The frame governing all four categories is the family. This is 3:15 in practice: the church is the household of God, so treat people as what they actually are. Younger men as brothers: as equals, with frankness and affection, not as a superior lording it over them. You are frank with a brother in a way you are not with a stranger. Older women as mothers: with honour, gentleness and respect. And it cuts against the two failures available to a young leader at once: the harshness that treats the congregation as subordinates, and the deference that never says anything at all. Neither is how families work.

In all purity. The phrase is added to one category only, and purity is the same word as 4:12. Paul is a realist. A young minister, possibly unmarried, doing pastoral work with young women is in a situation that has destroyed a great many ministries, and he says so without fuss or embarrassment. His dealings with younger women must be utterly free of any impropriety, in thought, word and action, and of anything that could give rise to suspicion. The safeguard he gives is not distance but a relationship: as sisters, which is better than a rulebook. A man does not have to invent boundaries with his sister; he already knows what is and is not thinkable. Paul asks Timothy to import that instinct, with protective, brotherly love, which protects the women, protects him, and does not require him to treat half his congregation as a hazard.

The family Jesus named. These words, mothers, brothers and sisters, were first given to the church by Jesus. When his relatives came to take him home, he looked at those sitting around him and said that whoever does the will of God is his brother and sister and mother (Mark 3:31–35). Paul’s instruction is that saying put into practice in Ephesus. The church is a family because it gathers round him, and every relationship in it is shaped by his: no believer is a stranger to another, because each has been made a brother or sister of the Son. That is also why purity is not negotiable. No one may treat a sister of Christ as anything less than his.

What practical safeguards does purity call for? The family instinct comes first, but wisdom adds sensible habits, especially for anyone in pastoral care. Avoid situations that would be private and unaccountable: meet in an open office or a public place, keep a door ajar, let someone else know where you are. Do not let pastoral conversations drift into emotional dependence; if they do, involve a wise older woman or your wife and step back. Never send messages you would not want read aloud. These are not signs of suspicion but of love: they protect the vulnerable from harm and the church from scandal, and they make sure that a sister is always treated as a sister.

What if an older person in the church really is in the wrong? Then he must be told, but as a son would tell his father. Go privately, not in front of others. Speak with respect: begin by honouring what is good in him, and put the matter as a concern rather than a verdict. Appeal rather than command: ask him to consider it before God. Be ready to listen, because age often sees what youth misses. Respect for age never means silence about sin, and it never means tolerating harm to others; if the wrong is serious, or the person is unwilling to listen, involve the elders (Matthew 18:15–17). The gentleness is in the manner, not in the content.

On a Tuesday. Picture your church as the family it is: the widower is your father, the teenager your younger brother, the woman who has been missing for weeks your mother. Phone her. The church is the only family on earth that includes every age, and it only works if we cross the generations deliberately.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Widows: families care for their own first, the church supports those who have no one, and Paul sets out who may be enrolled and why younger widows should rather remarry.
verseByVerse.theology:
Family First, and Why

To neglect one’s own relatives is to deny the faith and fall below the decency of unbelievers (v. 8); caring for an ageing parent is not a lesser duty but where godliness is practised (v. 4).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The enrolled widows were intercessors (v. 5), and their credentials were a lifetime of unrecorded service (v. 10).

Now: Paul’s remedy for the dangers of verses 11–13 is not more restriction but ordinary life (v. 14).

verseByVerse.quote: Honor widows who are truly widows. But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The setting. In the ancient world, widows were often destitute. There were no pensions; a woman typically depended on her husband, then on her sons, and had few respectable ways to earn. A widow without family could face starvation or be forced into prostitution. The Old Testament repeatedly commands care for widows and orphans (Exodus 22:22–24; Deuteronomy 14:28–29; 24:17–21). God himself is the one who executes justice for the fatherless and the widow (Deuteronomy 10:18), a father of the fatherless and protector of widows (Psalm 68:5). The early church continued this (Acts 6:1; James 1:27); indeed its first recorded administrative crisis was about widows being overlooked in the daily distribution. But resources were limited, and some were abusing the system, so Paul gives guidelines. He is not inventing a policy. He is protecting one.

Truly widows. Honour (timaō) means respect and value, and here it clearly includes financial support, as in 5:17 and Matthew 15:4–6, where honouring parents includes supporting them. The same word lies behind the double honour of verse 17, which Paul immediately supports with two texts about paying workers. This is a paragraph about the church’s welfare roll. Truly widows are those who are genuinely alone and without family support (v. 5). The phrase is doing the work: the church has limited resources and must direct them where they are most needed.

Godliness at home. The family, not the church, is the first line of support, and Paul puts the piety of the children and grandchildren in a surprising place. Caring for an ageing mother is not a lesser, secular duty that keeps a person from spiritual things. It is where godliness is practised; it is the fifth commandment in practice (Exodus 20:12). Godliness begins at home. That is the opposite of the arrangement Jesus condemned, where a man declared his resources Corban, a gift devoted to God, and left his parents unsupported (Mark 7:9–13).

Make some return. This is the language of repaying a debt or recompense. Paul is not appealing to sentiment but to obligation. Parents cared for us when we were helpless; we should care for them when they are. This was a widely recognised duty even in the pagan world.

Pleasing to God. The word is the same as 2:3, where prayer for all people was pleasing to God our Saviour. Caring for elderly parents is not merely a social duty but worship. The changed sheets and the hospital visits and the patient repetition of the same conversation are seen, and welcomed, in heaven.

Godliness at the foot of the cross. The Son of God kept this command himself. As a boy he went down to Nazareth and was submissive to Mary and Joseph (Luke 2:51). And when he hung on the cross, bearing the sins of the world, he looked down at his mother and gave her into the care of the beloved disciple, who took her to his own home from that hour (John 19:26–27). In the hour of his agony he did what Paul asks of every child and grandchild: he made some return to his mother. The One who fulfilled all righteousness fulfilled the fifth commandment too, and his obedience is counted to believers who have often failed in it. Caring for an ageing parent is walking where he walked.

In the flow. The long section on widows (vv. 3–16) is the family principle of verses 1–2 tested at its most practical point. In a letter written so that people know how to behave in God’s household (3:15), this is where the household’s love has to be paid for.

Does this mean I must have my elderly parent live with me? Not necessarily. The command is to honour and provide, and what that requires depends on the parent’s needs, your own circumstances, and other responsibilities God has given you, including to your spouse and children. For some families, a parent moving in is the loving choice. For others, good professional care is the wise and loving choice, especially where medical needs are beyond what a family can safely give. What Scripture forbids is not using a care home; it is abandonment: leaving a parent unvisited, unfunded, unknown. Whatever the arrangement, stay involved, contribute what you can, visit often, and make sure they know they are loved.

What if my parent was abusive or neglectful? Honour does not require you to put yourself back under harm, to pretend the past did not happen, or to submit to further abuse. You may need distance and boundaries for your own safety and your family’s, and that is not sin. But even then, the gospel may call you, in ways that are wise and safe, to make sure your parent’s basic needs are met, perhaps through others, and to pray for them. Seek counsel from a wise pastor. God sees the debt you never received, and he is a Father who does not fail (Psalm 27:10). Honouring a parent who did not honour you is costly, and it is one of the places where the grace of Christ shows most clearly.

On a Tuesday. Ask your parents or grandparents what they need this week, and listen to the answer. If they have died, honour them by caring for someone else’s parent in your church who has no one nearby.

For worship. The God of this paragraph is the God who notices widows. He hears the cry of the bereaved woman whom the world has forgotten; he made laws in Israel so that she would find grain left at the edges of the fields; he sent Elijah to a widow of Zarephath; and he sent his Son to the gate of Nain, where he had compassion on a widow and gave her only son back to her (Luke 7:11–15).

verseByVerse.quote: She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day, but she who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Left all alone. Now Paul describes the two kinds of widow, and the contrast is stark. The verb (memonōmenē) is perfect tense: left alone and remaining alone, isolated. The word is from the same root as our monastery and monk: solitary, without anyone. That is the qualifying condition: not merely bereaved but without husband or family, with nobody to turn to.

Set her hope on God. Perfect tense again, the same form Paul used of himself in 4:10: she has fixed her hope and keeps it fixed. With no human support, she trusts God alone. Her loss has driven her to depend on him, and that is not a sad consolation but the best thing that could have happened to her. Every human prop was taken away, and she found she was standing on the Rock.

Night and day. Supplications and prayers are the words of 2:1. Night and day is exactly what Paul says of his own prayers elsewhere (2 Timothy 1:3), and what Luke says of Anna in the temple (Luke 2:37). This reframes the whole arrangement. The church is not merely dispensing charity to the helpless. It is supporting women who are doing something for the church: a body of intercessors, praying through the night hours while everyone else sleeps. A true widow is a woman of prayer, and her prayers are a ministry to the church. A congregation that keeps its widows is buying prayer it could not otherwise afford.

Dead even while she lives. The word (spatalōsa) is strong: living luxuriously, pleasure-seeking, given over to indulgence, with a note of wantonness. Some widows may have been living for pleasure, and some commentators think a few were even selling their bodies to support themselves. Paul is describing a widow with freedom and no dependants who has turned her freedom into indulgence, and the church should not support such a lifestyle. Dead even while she lives is one of the most arresting phrases in the letter. Not dying, not spiritually endangered: dead, present tense, while the body carries on. It is the same verdict Jesus passes on the church at Sardis: you have the reputation of being alive, and you are dead (Revelation 3:1). Her diary is full, but toward God there is no prayer, no hunger for him, no love: like cut flowers in a vase, still bright for a while, but already severed from the root.

Two widows. Set the two women side by side and you have the whole point. Both are widows; both have lost a husband; both have time on their hands. One spends it praying and is alive. The other spends it on herself and is a corpse that has not noticed. What a person does with unstructured freedom is revealing, and it is worth asking of every retirement, every empty evening, every free Saturday.

What Anna’s prayers were waiting for. The widow Paul describes has a portrait in Luke. Anna had been a widow for many years and did not depart from the temple, worshipping with fasting and prayer night and day, and her hope was answered in a person. When the infant Jesus was carried into the temple, she came up at that very hour, gave thanks to God and spoke of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (Luke 2:36–38). That is what a hope set on God looks like in the New Testament: it is fixed on the God who has kept his word in Christ. And the woman who is dead while she lives has the remedy every sinner has: God, rich in mercy, makes the dead alive together with Christ (Ephesians 2:4–5).

I am widowed and lonely. How can I set my hope on God when it hurts this much? Grief is not a lack of faith. The widow in this verse is not someone who has stopped feeling her loss; she is someone who has taken her loss to God, again and again, night and day. Setting your hope on him does not mean pretending; it means telling him the truth and asking him for help, as the psalmists do. Begin there, even with a few words. Let the church carry you: accept the meals, the visits, the invitations, even when it is hard. And know that your prayers matter. A widow who prays is not on the edge of the church’s life but at the centre of it.

On a Tuesday. If you know a widow in your church, ask her what you can pray for, and then ask her to pray for you.

verseByVerse.quote: Command these things as well, so that they may be without reproach. But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without reproach. These are commands, not suggestions, issued with the authority already established (1:3; 4:11), and without reproach is the word used of overseers in 3:2. The same standard applied to leaders is here applied to widows and to families caring for their own: no one should be able to accuse them, whether of neglect or of self-indulgence. Paul is not merely arranging finances; he is protecting the reputation of Christian households in a watching city.

Provide for his relatives. One of the fiercest sentences Paul ever wrote. Provide (pronoeō) means think ahead for, plan for: not crisis rescue but forethought. Relatives are his own people, the extended family, and members of his household the immediate family; the closer the relationship, the greater the duty.

He has denied the faith. To fail here is not a lapse in a secondary duty. Denied (arneomai) means disowned, renounced, the same verb used of Peter in the courtyard (Mark 14:68). It is a denial not in words but in deeds. Practice can deny what the lips confess (Titus 1:16). A man may recite the creed accurately and, by leaving his mother destitute, have denied every word of it.

Worse than an unbeliever. That is the sharper edge. Pagans looked after their own; family obligation was a recognised virtue across the ancient world, no gospel required. So a Christian who neglects his relatives has not merely fallen below a Christian standard. He has fallen below the ordinary decency of people with no faith at all, and brings shame on the name of Christ. Spirituality here is not measured by devotion, insight or ministry activity. It is measured by whether the people related to you have what they need.

The Provider of his own household. Neglect denies the faith because the faith is about a Saviour who provides. Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, and he nourishes and cherishes her as a man does his own body (Ephesians 5:25, 29). He has never received his people and then left them to fend for themselves. A believer who leaves his own family in want is telling a story about Christ that is not true. A believer who plans and provides for them is preaching without a word the faithfulness of the Son, who is faithful over God’s house (Hebrews 3:6). The family table is one of the places where the gospel is either confirmed or contradicted.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a person who is unable to provide, through illness, poverty or circumstance, has denied the faith. The point is unwillingness, a refusal to take responsibility. Nor does it mean only men provide; verse 16 applies the same duty to believing women. It does not settle every hard case; some families are estranged for grave reasons, some relatives cannot be helped by any amount of money, and some carers are already at the end of their strength. Paul is not writing about those situations. He is writing about people who could and do not, and who have arranged their religion so as not to notice.

Does this apply to a husband who will not work or support his family? Yes, directly. A man who is able to work and support his wife and children and refuses, or who spends on himself what his family needs, is the person this verse describes. Scripture expects able-bodied people to work (2 Thessalonians 3:10). A wife and children left in want by such a man are not obliged to pretend all is well, and the church should not pretend either: the elders should lovingly confront him and, if he persists, treat it as a matter of discipline, while making sure his family is cared for. Financial neglect can also be part of a pattern of control or abuse; where it is, the church must protect the vulnerable, not the abuser.

How do I balance providing for my family with giving to the church and the poor? Begin with the order Paul gives: your own household is your first earthly responsibility, and neglecting it is not generosity but disobedience. But provision is not the same as luxury, and the Bible also commands generous giving to God’s work and to the poor (2 Corinthians 9:6–8; Galatians 6:10). Most of us have more room for both than we think, once wants are separated from needs. Plan ahead, as the word provide implies: budget, save for your family’s future, and give first rather than from what is left. Then trust the God who feeds the sparrows to keep his promises to those who honour him.

On a Tuesday. Christ has never left you to fend for yourself. Look ahead as well as around: is there an ageing parent whose needs you have not planned for, a sibling who is quietly struggling, a will you have not written? Provision is forethought. Do one piece of it today.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years of age, having been the wife of one husband, and having a reputation for good works: if she has brought up children, has shown hospitality, has washed the feet of the saints, has cared for the afflicted, and has devoted herself to every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let a widow be enrolled. Now the criteria for the official list, an actual roll of names receiving regular support. There seems to have been an official list of widows supported by the church, who in return devoted themselves to prayer and service (v. 5), perhaps caring for orphans, visiting the sick, and ministering to women. It was something like an order of widows, which is attested in the early church.

Not less than sixty. Sixty was considered the beginning of old age. A practical threshold: past the age of likely remarriage, and past the age of earning a living. Paul is not being arbitrary; he is drawing the line where genuine long-term dependence begins. It also meant she would probably not want to leave the role to remarry (vv. 11–12).

The wife of one husband. Literally a one-man woman (henos andros gynē), the mirror of the phrase used of overseers in 3:2, and best read the same way: faithful in her marriage. It is not a rule against having remarried after widowhood, since Paul tells younger widows to marry in verse 14, and he would hardly command something that disqualifies them later.

A reputation for good works. Literally well attested: a track record of faithful service, known to all. Then the reputation is spelled out, and it is a list of unglamorous things.

Children and hospitality. Bringing up children is the ordinary work of years, her own children or perhaps orphans she took in. Hospitality is welcoming strangers, opening her house, as the overseer must (3:2).

Washed the feet of the saints. The lowest job in the household, given to the least slave, and the one Jesus did in the upper room. Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, he rose from supper, tied a towel round himself and washed his disciples’ feet, and then told them that they also ought to wash one another’s feet (John 13:3–5, 14; compare Luke 7:44). The widow on Paul’s list has simply done what her Lord said. Her credentials are his: the Lord of glory set the pattern with a basin, and she has spent a lifetime following him to it. The phrase stands for every kind of humble service, and it is the plainest proof that a woman has learned Christ.

Cared for the afflicted. The afflicted are those under pressure, in distress: perhaps the sick, the poor, the persecuted. And it says something about a woman now dependent herself. Before she needed help she gave it, which is precisely why the church now owes her.

Every good work. The list is summarised in that phrase, and the whole shape of it should be weighed. Not one item is public, spectacular or recorded anywhere. Raising children, feeding guests, washing feet, sitting with the sick: these are the credentials Paul asks the church to verify. A woman is put on the roll because of a lifetime of things nobody wrote down.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church should refuse all help to widows under sixty or without this record. Paul is describing the criteria for the enrolled list with its lifelong commitment, not for emergency help. Any person in genuine need may receive help (Galatians 6:10).

Should churches keep a list of widows today? Churches today rarely keep a formal roll, and nothing here requires one. Much of what the list did is now partly met by pensions and state provision. But the principle remains: real need, met first by family and then by the church, with care to support those who are genuinely alone, and wisdom to make support a blessing rather than a trap. Many churches meet this through deacons, who know the widows and the needy by name and make sure no one is overlooked (Acts 6:1–6). And the honour remains: older women who have given a lifetime of quiet service should be valued, visited and drawn on for their wisdom and prayer, not left at the edge.

On a Tuesday. The Lord who knelt with a basin for you is at work in you by his Spirit; begin now the kind of record this list describes, not the kind that gets a mention in the notices: a meal taken round, a guest welcomed, a sick friend sat with. Do one of them this week, and tell no one.

For worship. Heaven’s list of honour is not the world’s. God does not record the speeches and the titles; he records the cup of cold water, the guest made welcome, the night by a sickbed. Nothing done for his people is forgotten by him (Hebrews 6:10). On the last day the King himself will read the list aloud, and to women whose names were never written anywhere but in his book he will say that what they did for the least of his brothers they did for him (Matthew 25:40). The Lord who served will honour those who served, and their reward will be himself.
verseByVerse.note: There seems to have been an official list of widows supported by the church, who in turn served it.

verseByVerse.quote: But refuse to enroll younger widows, for when their passions draw them away from Christ, they desire to marry and so incur condemnation for having abandoned their former faith. Besides that, they learn to be idlers, going about from house to house, and not only idlers, but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Refuse younger widows. These three verses are the difficult ones. Refuse is the verb used of the silly myths in 4:7. Not because younger widows are less worthy, but for their own good.

Passions draw them away. The verb (katastrēniasōsin) means to grow restless or wanton against something, to feel desires that pull away. Natural desire for marriage and companionship is not wrong (v. 14), but here it pulls them away from a commitment they had made to Christ.

Their former faith. That sounds at first like a condemnation of remarriage, until verse 14, where Paul tells these same younger widows to marry. So he plainly is not against it. Something else is going on, and the phrase former faith (tēn prōtēn pistin, their first pledge) is the clue. Most likely, enrolled widows made a pledge to devote themselves to Christ and the church’s service for the rest of their lives, without remarrying. A young woman who makes that commitment and later finds she cannot keep it has broken a promise, and the problem is the broken pledge, not the marriage. Breaking it would bring condemnation (judgement, censure) because it broke a vow made to God (Numbers 30:2; Ecclesiastes 5:4–5). A vow is spoken to the holy God, who is in heaven while we are on earth (Ecclesiastes 5:2), and he does not treat our words as lightly as we do. This is pastoral realism rather than severity. His judgement is that a woman in her twenties or thirties should not be asked to bind herself for life, because many will not manage it and the failure will damage them. The kindest policy is not to let them make the vow.

They learn to be idlers. The second danger is entirely practical. The verb is learn: this is not a character flaw these women arrive with. It is something the arrangement teaches them. Put a young woman on a stipend with no dependants, no work and no structure, and she will fill the days somehow.

Going about from house to house. The houses of a congregation are open to her, and the traffic in other people’s business begins: visiting homes, perhaps under the guise of ministry, but actually spreading gossip. The false teachers also worked through house visits (2 Timothy 3:6).

Gossips and busybodies. Gossips are babblers; busybodies (periergoi) are meddlers, busy with other people’s affairs, the same root as 2 Thessalonians 3:11, where Paul saw the same thing among idle men at Thessalonica: not busy, but busybodies. Saying what they should not may mean spreading the false teaching, or revealing private matters learned in visiting homes. The diagnosis is not really about women or widows: idleness is never neutral. Remove a person’s proper work and the energy does not evaporate; it goes into other people’s affairs. Paul’s remedy in the next verse is correspondingly practical: give them something real to do.

The pledge Christ never breaks. Paul’s worry is a broken pledge to Christ, and it throws light on the One to whom the pledge was made. Our promises to him are fragile; his to us are not. Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end (John 13:1), and he set his face to go to Jerusalem knowing what waited for him there (Luke 9:51). If we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself (2 Timothy 2:13). That is why a woman who had broken her first pledge was not beyond hope. The censure Paul mentions is real, but the Lord she failed is the Lord who restored Peter after three denials, and his faithfulness is the ground on which she could return.

What it does not mean. It does not mean younger widows are worse people; Paul is giving practical wisdom based on observed patterns. Nor does condemnation mean eternal damnation or loss of salvation; it is the censure due to a broken vow.

How do I know if I am gossiping? Ask three questions before you speak about someone who is not present. Is it true, and do I actually know it, or am I passing on what I heard? Is it mine to tell, or was it shared in confidence, or is it simply none of my business? And would I say it the same way if the person were standing here? Gossip often wears the clothes of concern: let me tell you so you can pray. If you genuinely need help with a situation, go to someone who can help, such as an elder, not to someone who will merely enjoy knowing. And when someone brings gossip to you, you can kindly stop it: ask whether they have spoken to the person directly.

Does this teach that Christians should not make lifelong vows? No. Marriage is a lifelong vow, and so is the covenant made in church membership. What Paul warns against is binding people, especially the young, to vows they are unlikely to keep and that Scripture does not require, such as lifelong celibacy. He is wary of the very thing the false teachers promoted in 4:3. Vows to God are serious and must be kept (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5), which is exactly why they should not be made lightly. Jesus warns against rash oaths (Matthew 5:33–37). Make the promises God asks of you, keep them by his grace, and do not add others that he has not asked for.

On a Tuesday. If you have unstructured time, give it somewhere good to go before it finds somewhere bad: a person to serve, a skill to learn, a task to finish.

verseByVerse.quote: So I would have younger widows marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no occasion for slander. For some have already strayed after Satan. If any believing woman has relatives who are widows, let her care for them. Let the church not be burdened, so that it may care for those who are truly widows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Younger widows marry. I would have is the same word of direction as 2:8. Paul does not merely permit remarriage; he prefers it. Set that against chapter 4, where the false teachers were forbidding marriage. Paul’s answer to a genuine pastoral risk is not more restriction but ordinary life: a husband, children, a household to run. He is sending these women into the very things the ascetics despised, and calling it the safer road. Remarriage after a spouse’s death is entirely lawful (Romans 7:2–3; 1 Corinthians 7:39), provided it is only in the Lord, which means to a fellow believer, someone who also belongs to Christ (2 Corinthians 6:14).

Bear children, manage their households. Manage their households (oikodespotein) is a strong word: to rule the house, to be mistress of the home. The wife has real authority and responsibility in running the home (Proverbs 31:10–31). A modern reader may hear this as small. Paul does not: the ascetics despised home and children as unspiritual, and he answers that running a household is a calling from God with real authority in it, and a far better use of a life than drifting from house to house.

No occasion for slander. The adversary is either a human enemy of the church who would seize on scandal, or Satan himself. Occasion (aphormē) began as a military word for a base of operations, and came to mean any opening or opportunity. The church is being watched, and its arrangements can hand ammunition to people looking for it, as the overseer’s reputation with outsiders showed (3:7).

Strayed after Satan. This is not hypothetical. Strayed means turned aside, gone off the road, as in 1:6. Some younger widows had already fallen into sin, perhaps immorality, perhaps following the false teachers. Following false teaching is following Satan (4:1). Whatever the arrangement had been doing to young widows in Ephesus, it had already cost some of them.

A believing woman. Verse 16 closes the argument, and the believing woman is addressed directly: the duty of verse 8 is not the men’s alone. Perhaps a well-off woman who has widows in her extended family, or in her household. Care for is the same word as verse 10, where the widow cared for the afflicted. What she once did, others now do for her.

Let the church not be burdened. The principle is stated as plainly as it can be. Every family that supports its own frees the church’s limited resources for the women who have nobody. This is not meanness; it is the arithmetic of love. A congregation that carries people whose families could carry them will run out before it reaches the destitute, and the destitute are the ones the whole chapter exists to protect.

Homes that carry the Saviour’s name. Paul gives Titus the same concern about young wives: that the word of God may not be reviled, and that believers may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in everything (Titus 2:5, 10). A Christian household is a public sign of what the gospel does. The street that never reads Paul can read a home: a widow given a new start, children raised in love, a house run with order and kindness. When such homes collapse into idleness and scandal, it is Christ’s name that is mocked. When they flourish, the watching city sees in ordinary kitchens what the Saviour does with lives he has taken in hand.

What it does not mean. It does not command every younger widow to remarry; it is Paul’s counsel in general, and singleness remains honourable (1 Corinthians 7:8, 40). Nor does it limit women to the home; it describes a good and worthy calling, not the only one.

How does this apply today? The church still has a duty to care for members in real need who have no family to help, and families may not pass their own duty to the church or the state (v. 8). Churches today may not keep a formal roll of widows, but the order still stands: families first, then the church, for those in real need.

Is it disloyal to my late husband or wife to remarry? No. Marriage is for this life; death ends the bond (Romans 7:2), and Jesus taught that in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matthew 22:30). Paul here actively encourages remarriage for younger widows, and it was God who said it is not good for the man to be alone. Love for a spouse who has died is not betrayed by a new marriage; many find that a good first marriage prepared them to love again. Take time, grieve honestly, seek counsel, and marry only in the Lord. And be patient with children or friends who find it hard; their grief may move at a different pace.

On a Tuesday. Is there a widow in your family or church you could help this week? Ask her what would actually help: a lift to the shops, help with paperwork, an evening of company. And ask whether the way your household lives gives the watching street any reason to speak badly of Christ, or any reason to wonder at him.

For worship. God is the great Householder who sets the lonely in families (Psalm 68:6). He gives husbands to widows and children to the barren, homes to the homeless and a family to the friendless. He does not despise ordinary life; he fills it with his presence, so that a kitchen and a nursery can be as holy as a temple. And over every widow stands the Bridegroom whose own Bride the church will never be widowed, because he died and rose, and lives for ever, and is coming back for her.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elders: how to pay them, protect them from accusation, rebuke them when they persist in sin, and appoint them slowly, with a personal word to Timothy about his health in the middle, and the assurance that neither sins nor good works stay hidden.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Gospel Quoted as Scripture

Verse 18 introduces both Deuteronomy 25:4 and a saying of Jesus recorded at Luke 10:7 with ‘the Scripture says’; on the most natural reading, this is among the earliest signs that the written words of Jesus were already counted as Scripture.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Elders are hard to accuse (v. 19) and hard to hide behind (v. 20); a church needs both verses.

Now: Verse 23 shows Paul correcting a good man’s over-scrupulous mistake, and verse 25 promises that unrecorded goodness cannot stay hidden.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching. For the Scripture says, "You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain," and, "The laborer deserves his wages."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elders who rule well. Elders hold the same office as the overseers of 3:1–7. Rule (proistēmi) is the word used of managing a household (3:4), a word with a father’s care in it rather than a manager’s distance. Not all elders lead equally well; those who do deserve recognition.

Double honor. Honour is the same word as in verse 3, where it plainly included money, and the two Scripture quotations Paul immediately produces are both about paying workers, which settles it. This is about the church’s obligation to support its elders financially. Double probably means ample, generous honour rather than literally twice a figure, or perhaps honour in two forms: respect and remuneration. The point is that the support should be ample and not grudging.

Preaching and teaching. The word for labour is kopiaō: work to exhaustion, the word for a man at the end of a long day. Paul chose it for preaching and teaching deliberately. Whatever else pulpit work looks like from a pew, it is not restful. All elders must be able to teach (3:2), but the especially implies that some devote themselves particularly to the ministry of the word, and these particularly deserve support, since their work takes their whole time and strength.

Do not muzzle an ox. Paul gives two quotations under the single heading Scripture says. The first is from the law of Moses (Deuteronomy 25:4). Oxen walked over the harvested grain on the threshing floor to separate it from the husk, and the law said they must be free to eat as they worked. Paul reads the law’s kindness to animals as establishing a principle about people, as he does at length in 1 Corinthians 9:9–11: if God cares that an ox is fed from its labour, how much more those who labour in the gospel.

The laborer deserves his wages. The second is not from the Old Testament at all. These are the words of Jesus as recorded in Luke 10:7 (compare Matthew 10:10). On the most natural reading, Scripture says covers both quotations, so Paul places a saying of Jesus, apparently in its written form in Luke, alongside Deuteronomy and calls both Scripture. Some scholars take the second line as a well-known saying simply added on, and those who date the letter after Paul’s death read it differently; but if Paul wrote it, as this commentary holds, it is one of the earliest signs that the words of Jesus were already received as Scripture alongside the Old Testament, stated without argument, as something his readers would accept. Peter does the same with Paul’s letters (2 Peter 3:16).

The Lord of the harvest pays his workers. The saying Paul quotes was spoken as Jesus sent out the seventy-two (seventy in some manuscripts and the KJV) ahead of him. He told them to pray to the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers, and then to eat what the houses that received them provided, for the labourer deserves his wages (Luke 10:2, 7). The workers were his, the harvest was his, and their bread was to come from the people they served. So a church that supports its preachers is not hiring staff or doing them a kindness. The risen Lord is feeding the men he sent, through the people he sent them to, and he himself called it wages.

In the flow. Verse 17 begins the last section of the chapter, on elders (vv. 17–25), and the word honour joins it to the widows of verse 3. Chapter 3 told Timothy what an elder must be; this passage tells the church how to treat one, so that God’s household is led by men who are both supported and accountable.

Where does the idea of teaching and ruling elders come from? From the especially of this verse, which implies that some elders laboured in preaching and teaching and some did not, or not to the same degree. Presbyterian churches speak of teaching elders (ministers) and ruling elders; many Baptist and independent churches speak simply of elders, some of whom are set apart and paid to preach. Both read this verse honestly, and both agree on the essentials: there is one office of elder, all must be able to teach, and some give themselves especially to the ministry of the word and should be supported to do it. Faithful churches differ on the details of government, and this text does not settle them all.

How much should a church pay its pastor? Scripture gives no figure, but it gives a spirit: double honour, ample and not grudging. A good test is whether the pastor can live without distraction at a level comparable to the people he serves, provide for his family (5:8), offer hospitality (3:2) and buy books, without either luxury or anxiety. A church that keeps its minister poor to keep him humble has misread this verse, and so has a minister who demands more than his people can bear. Many churches set the salary in relation to the average income of the congregation. And remember that honour includes more than money: respect, prayer, encouragement and a willingness to be taught.

On a Tuesday. Write your pastor a note naming one specific way God has used his preaching in your life. A single sentence of specific thanks can carry a tired man for a month.
verseByVerse.note: The two sayings come from Deuteronomy and from Jesus’ words as recorded in Luke — a sign that the Gospels were already being received as Scripture.

parallels.desc: You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain

verseByVerse.quote: Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses. As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A charge against an elder. Elders are especially vulnerable to accusations, from disgruntled members, false teachers, or simple misunderstanding. A man in public office is a target. Accusations cost the accuser nothing and can end a ministry before anything is established. Timothy must not take every complaint seriously, and is not to open proceedings at all on the word of one person.

Two or three witnesses. The rule comes straight from the law, the standard for any legal charge in Israel (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15), applied by Jesus to church discipline (Matthew 18:16) and by Paul himself (2 Corinthians 13:1). It protects leaders from malicious or careless accusations and ensures justice. That is not indifference to wrongdoing; it is the ordinary requirement of justice, and a church that ignores it will destroy good men on rumour.

Those who persist in sin. But the protection is not a shield, and verse 20 is the other half. The participle is present tense: those who keep on sinning, continuing, going on with it after being dealt with. Most likely these are elders who, after the charge is established, continue in their sin without repentance. It could also refer more generally to any church member, but the context suggests elders. This is not a first response.

In the presence of all. Rebuke (elenchō) means expose, convict, reprove. In the presence of all means publicly, before the church, or possibly before the other elders. Leaders sin publicly in the sense that their sin affects the whole church; the correction must be equally public. That reverses a common instinct, which is to protect the institution: settle it quietly, move the man on, tell nobody. Paul’s instruction is that an elder who persists in sin is rebuked in front of everyone, precisely because his position was public. Is that not humiliating? It is meant to be sobering, not cruel. It comes only after private warnings have been refused, and its aim is the man’s repentance and the flock’s safety, not his ruin (Galatians 6:1).

That the rest may stand in fear. The rest may be other elders or the whole church, and the fear is a healthy fear of sinning, a sobering reminder that leaders are accountable (James 3:1). Hold the two verses together and you have a workable and demanding standard. Hard to accuse, and hard to hide behind. A church that keeps only verse 19 becomes a place where leaders are untouchable; one that keeps only verse 20 becomes a place where any grievance can ruin a man. Keep both, or neither will work.

The trial where the rule was broken. The law Paul cites was broken once in a way that changed history. At the trial of Jesus the chief priests sought testimony against him and found none; many bore false witness against him, and their testimony did not agree (Mark 14:55–59). No two witnesses could be found to agree, and the one wholly innocent man was condemned in the end for his own confession that he is the Christ (Mark 14:61–64). So a church that refuses to condemn on rumour is honouring its Lord, who knows from the inside what a false accusation is. And a church that openly rebukes persistent sin honours him too, because he is the holy Head of the church, and its leaders carry his name.

What it does not mean. It does not mean elders are above correction; the opposite. Nor does it mean that a victim’s report of abuse should be dismissed for lack of witnesses; corroborating evidence, patterns of behaviour and the testimony of multiple victims can serve as witnesses, and civil authorities must be involved in criminal matters (Romans 13:1–4). The principle is careful justice, protecting both the accused and the vulnerable.

I have been harmed by a church leader and there were no other witnesses. Will I be believed? You should be heard, carefully and seriously, and this verse must never be used to silence you. The two or three witnesses rule concerns what is needed to establish a charge, not whether a report may be made or investigated. Abuse usually happens in private, and Scripture’s own standard allows for evidence beyond eyewitnesses: patterns of behaviour, other people who come forward, messages, records. If the matter involves a crime, report it to the police; the church must not handle criminal abuse internally, and should help you do so. Speak to another elder or a trusted leader outside the situation. God is the defender of the oppressed, and a church that protects an abuser to protect its reputation has abandoned this very passage.

What should I do if I hear an accusation against my pastor? Do not repeat it. If someone brings it to you, ask whether they have spoken to the person directly or to the other elders, and encourage them to do so, or to go to the authorities if it is criminal. If you yourself have a concern, take it to the elders, not to the congregation or social media. Then pray, and wait for a fair process. Being slow to believe an accusation is not the same as refusing to believe it; it means letting the truth be established before you act on it, as you would want done for yourself.

On a Tuesday. Be slow to believe or spread an accusation against a leader. Pray by name this week for each of your elders: for their purity, their marriages, their humility, and for the courage to deal with sin in their own number when it appears.

For worship. God is perfectly just. He never condemns the innocent and never clears the guilty, and his courtroom has no favourites and no cover-ups. He hears the cry of the wronged when no human witness stood with them. And the Son who was falsely accused was also openly shamed: stripped, mocked and lifted up in the presence of all, as if he were the one who had persisted in sin. He bore that public rebuke for the hidden and the open sins of his people, so that those who come to him may stand before God without fear, and need never hide again.
