verseByVerse.quote: In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels I charge you to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the presence of God. This is one of the two most solemn sentences in the letter (the other is 6:13), and the solemnity is the point. It is an oath-like formula (2 Timothy 4:1). Paul swears Timothy in, as a witness is sworn before testifying, and he names three parties watching: God, Christ Jesus, and the elect angels. The angels are the surprising item. The elect angels are the angels who did not fall with Satan, kept by God’s choice (contrast 2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). Paul mentions them elsewhere as observers of church life (1 Corinthians 4:9; 11:10; Ephesians 3:10), and they will accompany Christ at the judgement (Matthew 25:31). The picture is of a courtroom with an unseen gallery: what Timothy does about a difficult elder is done in front of a congregation that includes more than he can see.

Keep these rules. Charge (diamartyromai) means solemnly testify, adjure. These rules are the instructions about elders and discipline (vv. 17–20), perhaps the whole chapter. Why such weight for what is, after all, church administration? Because of what Paul is guarding against, and he names it twice.

Without prejudging. Prejudging (prokrima) is having decided in advance; partiality (prosklisis) is literally leaning toward, favouritism. Do not favour friends, the wealthy, the influential, or those you like. God shows no partiality (Romans 2:11; James 2:1–9; Deuteronomy 1:17). Timothy will like some of these elders and find others difficult. When a charge comes in, he will know before he hears it which way he wants it to go, and that is exactly what Paul puts him under oath about. Rules for discipline are easy to write and easy to keep when the accused is a stranger. The test is the case where you already know whose side you are on, and Paul’s answer is not a better procedure but a reminder of who is watching.

Before Christ Jesus, the Judge without favourites. Paul uses the same oath in his last letter, and there he adds who Christ Jesus is: the one who is to judge the living and the dead (2 Timothy 4:1). Timothy must judge without partiality because the Lord watching him has none. Even his enemies admitted it. Meaning to trap him, they told him that he was true, did not care about anyone’s opinion, and was not swayed by appearances (Mark 12:14). It was flattery, and it was exactly right. He welcomed a despised tax collector and let a rich man walk away sorrowful, and in each case he looked at the heart. A church leader who refuses favouritism is copying his Lord.

What does it mean that angels are elect? It means God chose and kept some angels so that they did not fall when Satan and others rebelled. Their standing, like ours, rests on God’s sovereign choice, not on their own strength. That is a quiet confirmation of the doctrine of election: even in heaven, those who stand, stand by grace. But there is a difference. The elect angels never fell and so needed no Saviour; elect sinners fell and were redeemed by Christ, who became man, not angel, to save us. That is why the angels look on with wonder at the church (Ephesians 3:10; 1 Peter 1:12). They have seen God’s power and holiness from the beginning; in us they see his mercy.

How do I avoid partiality when someone I love is involved? Admit the bias first; you cannot correct what you will not name. Then put distance between your feelings and the decision: hear both sides fully before you form a view, ask what you would conclude if the names were reversed, and involve others who do not share your attachment. In church matters, a leader with a close relationship to someone involved should often step back from the decision altogether. And remember, as Paul tells Timothy, who is watching. Fairness is not coldness; it is loving everyone involved, including the person who is not your friend, enough to give them the same justice.

On a Tuesday. Look today for where you have already decided before you have heard: about a colleague, a family member, someone in church you find difficult. Go and hear the other side. And in the small judgements of the day, the email you answer, the child whose account you believe, act as one who knows the gallery is full.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands, nor take part in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be hasty. The laying on of hands is, in context, ordination: the public act by which the church sets a man apart, as the elders did over Timothy himself (4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6). Some have thought it refers to restoring repentant sinners, but the context of elders favours ordination. This picks up 3:6, where a recent convert must not be made an overseer lest he be puffed up and fall, and 3:10, where deacons must first be tested. Take time to observe a man’s life before appointing him. Ephesus needed leaders; the church was under pressure and its existing teachers were part of the problem. The temptation to fill posts fast would have been considerable, and Paul says no. The pressure is usually a matter of the heart before it is a practical one. A church that wants to look successful, or a leader who wants to be rid of a burden quickly, will see gifts and overlook character, because gifts can be put to work at once.

The sins of others. Then the reason, and it is startling. Take part (koinōneō) means share, participate in, be a partner. Paul is saying that a man who ordains hastily shares in what the ordained man subsequently does. Not that he commits the sin, but that he is implicated in it, because he put him there. Endorsing someone makes you a partner in their conduct (2 John 11). Whoever recommends, appoints or installs is not a neutral party who can later say he could not have known. Paul’s assumption is that with proper testing (3:10) he could often have known, and that haste is itself the fault.

Keep yourself pure. Pure (hagnos) means clean, chaste, free from moral defilement: free from complicity in others’ sins, and personally holy. It follows naturally rather than changing the subject. A man who appoints carelessly does not stay clean; the compromises attach to him. The purity in view is the same thing Paul told him to model in 4:12, and here it is defended by an administrative discipline, which is a useful reminder that a great deal of personal holiness is protected or lost in decisions that look purely procedural.

The Lord who chose after a night of prayer. The church’s caution copies its Lord. Before he chose the twelve, Jesus went out to the mountain and spent the whole night in prayer to God, and only when day came did he call them (Luke 6:12–13). He knew all hearts, and still he did not appoint in a hurry; the church, which knows far less, has far more reason to wait. And the laying on of hands is not finally the church’s own gift to bestow. The ascended Christ gives shepherds to his church (Ephesians 4:11), and elders who ordain act as his servants, recognising men he has prepared. Haste presumes to know his choice before he has shown it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that a church that ordained a man who later fell is guilty of his sin, if it acted with care. The point is not to act carelessly. Nor does it mean we may never be associated with sinners; Jesus ate with them (Luke 15:1–2).

How long should a church take before appointing someone? Scripture sets no fixed period, but it sets a principle: long enough for the man’s character to be genuinely known (3:2–7, 10). That usually means years of observed faithfulness, not months of enthusiasm. A gifted speaker can impress quickly; the qualities Paul lists, self-control, a well-ordered home, a good reputation with outsiders, gentleness, can only be seen over time. Talk to his wife, his colleagues, those he has served under. Watch how he handles disappointment and correction. The greater the responsibility, the longer the testing. And the same applies, in proportion, to youth leaders, small group leaders and anyone entrusted with the vulnerable.

On a Tuesday. Before you recommend someone, for a church post, a job or a reference, take time to know them well: your endorsement is a responsibility. And ask where your own purity is being quietly lost in decisions that seem merely practical: the corner you let someone else cut, the thing you signed off without reading.

verseByVerse.quote: No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Drink only water. It is one of the strangest verses in the New Testament: a piece of medical advice dropped into a passage about elders and discipline, and it is a small window into a friendship. The word (hydropotei) means be a water-drinker. Timothy apparently abstained from wine entirely. Probably he did it on principle. Paul has just told him to keep himself pure (v. 22), and this letter’s opponents were ascetics who forbade marriage and food (4:3). A conscientious young minister in that environment, wanting to be above reproach and not a drunkard like the men excluded in 3:3, might well have gone teetotal to be safe, at some cost to a body that was already often unwell. Paul’s next words show that purity does not require asceticism.

A little wine. A little means moderation, not excess. In the ancient world, water was often contaminated, and wine was used medicinally (Luke 10:34). Wine mixed with water could help prevent illness and settle the stomach. Paul’s correction is gentle and entirely practical. He does not say your theology of wine is mistaken; he says take a little, for your stomach. And note the restraint on both sides: a little, and for your stomach. This is not a licence any more than it is a prohibition, and it does not mean those who abstain are wrong (Romans 14:21).

Frequent ailments. Recurring weaknesses, illnesses. Timothy was often sick; this was not a single episode, and Paul answers it with an ordinary remedy (compare Philippians 2:25–27).

A window into a friendship. The verse also says something about the man who wrote it. Paul has been dictating solemn instructions about elders, witnesses and the elect angels, and in the middle of it he remembers that his friend is unwell and stops to say so. It is the same apostle who asked for his cloak and his parchments (2 Timothy 4:13). Great theology and ordinary care for a person’s body sit in the same paragraph without embarrassment. And there is a lesson for the scrupulous. Timothy’s mistake was a good man’s mistake: trying to be blameless and overshooting into something that damaged him. Paul does not praise the rigour. He tells him to stop.

A high priest who knows weakness. Paul’s care for his friend’s body reflects the Saviour they both served. The Son of God had a body that grew hungry in the wilderness (Matthew 4:2), slept exhausted in a boat (Mark 4:38) and thirsted on the cross (John 19:28). He does not look on our frailty with suspicion, as the ascetics did. We have a high priest who is able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), and the word Hebrews uses there is the word Paul uses here for Timothy’s ailments. Timothy’s stomach was not beneath Christ’s notice, and neither was the humble remedy: wine that gladdens the heart is his gift too (Psalm 104:15).

Why did Paul not simply heal Timothy? Even the apostle who had done extraordinary miracles (Acts 19:11–12) did not heal at will, and here he prescribes a remedy for his closest friend. He left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). God does not always heal miraculously, illness is not always a sign of sin or weak faith, and using medicine is no lack of trust. The miracles of the apostles were signs confirming the message in the founding era (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Christians differ on whether gifts of healing like the apostles’ continue; this commentary holds that those signs belonged to the founding era, while honouring brothers who expect them now. Today we pray for the sick, and God often answers, sometimes beyond what doctors expect (James 5:14–15); but we also take the medicine, and both are ways of looking to him.

I am often unwell, like Timothy. Does it mean God is displeased with me, or that I am less useful? No. Timothy was one of the most trusted men in the apostolic church, and he was frequently ill. Paul himself served with a thorn in the flesh that God would not remove, because his power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:7–10). Illness can limit what you do, and that is a real grief, but it does not lower your standing before God or your worth to his church. Use the means: rest, see the doctor, take what helps. Bring the weakness to God honestly. And serve in the ways your strength allows; prayer offered from a sickbed is not second-class ministry.

On a Tuesday. If you have been putting off a doctor’s appointment out of a sense that it is unspiritual to worry about yourself, make it. And if you have taken on a rule for yourself that is quietly harming you, ask a wise friend whether it is godliness or scrupulosity.

For worship. The God of all glory cares about a young man’s stomach. The Spirit who inspired the mystery of godliness also inspired a sentence about indigestion, so that we would never imagine our bodies are beneath his notice. The Lord who touched lepers and took a fevered woman by the hand has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows, and one day he will raise these weak and ailing bodies in power, with no more frequent ailments, no more pain, and no more death.

verseByVerse.quote: The sins of some people are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later. So also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sins that are conspicuous. These verses return to the subject of choosing elders (v. 22), and they are the realistic postscript to it. Conspicuous (prodēlos) means openly evident, obvious beforehand. Some people’s sins are obvious; they disqualify themselves at once, and no examination is needed.

Going before them to judgment. The image is of sins walking ahead like heralds, reaching the court before the accused does, announcing their guilt before they arrive. Everyone already knows. In the church’s evaluation, and ultimately at God’s judgement, these sins are already known.

Sins that appear later. Other people’s sins follow along behind and catch up eventually: hidden at first, they come to light only over time, sometimes long afterwards. Time reveals character. Paul has just laid down a careful procedure, test them first (3:10), do not be hasty (v. 22), require witnesses (v. 19), and now he admits the procedure will not catch everything. Some appointments will go wrong despite proper care. He does not pretend otherwise, and he does not respond by tightening the rules further. What he offers instead is the assurance underneath the whole thing: nothing stays hidden. Sins that do not appear now will appear later, if not in this life then at the judgement. That is why haste is unnecessary as well as unwise: a man who waits is not risking that the truth will never come out.

Good works are conspicuous. Then verse 25 turns it round, and this is the kinder half. Some goodness is visible and gets its recognition.

Cannot remain hidden. Much goodness does not get noticed, and Paul says it cannot stay hidden either. Good works done quietly will eventually come to light (Matthew 6:4). Timothy should not overlook a modest, faithful man because his virtues are not on display; patient observation will reveal them. Think back to the widow of verse 10 with her lifetime of unrecorded work: children raised, guests fed, feet washed, sick people sat with. Nobody wrote any of it down. It is not lost. Hold that, if your faithfulness has gone unnoticed, and if you have watched someone else get the credit. Both columns are being kept, and both will be read out.

Brought to light by Christ Jesus. Paul knows who will do the revealing. God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus (Romans 2:16), and the Lord, when he comes, will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness (1 Corinthians 4:5). The eyes that will finally read both columns are the eyes of the risen Christ, which John saw like a flame of fire (Revelation 1:14; 2:23). That is sobering for the hypocrite, who has hidden his sins from every church committee but not from him. And it is deep comfort for the faithful whom nobody noticed, because the Judge is the same Lord who watched a widow put two small coins into the offering box and said she had put in more than all the rest (Mark 12:41–44).

If all my sins will come to light, should I be afraid of the judgement? Not if you are in Christ. For the believer, the sins that will be exposed have already been judged, at the cross, and there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1). The light of that day will show what grace forgave, not a debt still owing. That is why the best thing to do with hidden sin is to bring it into the light now: confess it to God, and where it is wise and fitting, to a trusted believer (James 5:16; 1 John 1:7–9). Hidden sin festers; confessed sin is cleansed. What should alarm us is not the light but the hope that we can keep anything from it.

On a Tuesday. Is there something you are hoping will never come out? Bring it to the God who has already covered it in Christ, and if it involves someone you have wronged, begin to put it right.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>Do not rebuke an older man but encourage him as you would a father, younger men as brothers,<sup>2</sup>older women as mothers, younger women as sisters, in all purity.<sup>3</sup>Honor widows who are truly widows.<sup>4</sup>But if a widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to show godliness to their own household and to make some return to their parents, for this is pleasing in the sight of God.<sup>5</sup>She who is truly a widow, left all alone, has set her hope on God and continues in supplications and prayers night and day,<sup>6</sup>but she who is self-indulgent is dead even while she lives.<sup>7</sup>Command these things as well, so that they may be without reproach.<sup>8</sup>But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.<sup>9</sup>Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years of age, having been the wife of one husband,<sup>10</sup>and having a reputation for good works: if she has brought up children, has shown hospitality, has washed the feet of the saints, has cared for the afflicted, and has devoted herself to every good work.<sup>11</sup>But refuse to enroll younger widows, for when their passions draw them away from Christ, they desire to marry<sup>12</sup>and so incur condemnation for having abandoned their former faith.<sup>13</sup>Besides that, they learn to be idlers, going about from house to house, and not only idlers, but also gossips and busybodies, saying what they should not.<sup>14</sup>So I would have younger widows marry, bear children, manage their households, and give the adversary no occasion for slander.<sup>15</sup>For some have already strayed after Satan.<sup>16</sup>If any believing woman has relatives who are widows, let her care for them. Let the church not be burdened, so that it may care for those who are truly widows.<sup>17</sup>Let the elders who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching.<sup>18</sup>For the Scripture says, "You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain," and, "The laborer deserves his wages."<sup>19</sup>Do not admit a charge against an elder except on the evidence of two or three witnesses.<sup>20</sup>As for those who persist in sin, rebuke them in the presence of all, so that the rest may stand in fear.<sup>21</sup>In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels I charge you to keep these rules without prejudging, doing nothing from partiality.<sup>22</sup>Do not be hasty in the laying on of hands, nor take part in the sins of others; keep yourself pure.<sup>23</sup>No longer drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments.<sup>24</sup>The sins of some people are conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others appear later.<sup>25</sup>So also good works are conspicuous, and even those that are not cannot remain hidden.

6.title: Godliness with Contentment Is Great Gain
6.overview:
The last chapter ties the letter together. Slaves are to honour their masters, so that God’s name is not slandered. Then the root of the false teaching is exposed: these men thought godliness was a way to make money. Paul answers that “godliness with contentment is great gain”, since we brought nothing into the world and can take nothing out, and that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.

Timothy, the man of God, must flee all this and pursue what is good, fighting the good fight until Christ appears, the King of kings who dwells in unapproachable light. The rich are not told to give everything away, but to hope in God, who gives richly for enjoyment, and to be rich in good works. Finally: guard the deposit, and grace be with you all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul finishes his household instructions with Christian slaves, whose conduct is to keep God’s name and the teaching from reproach, including those whose masters are fellow believers.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Paul Does and Does Not Say

Paul gives slaves a reason for their conduct that has nothing to do with their masters' rights, the honour of God's name (v.1), and sets it beside his condemnation of slave-trading (1:10) and his plea for Onesimus (Philem 16): a principle planted inside the institution that would in time dissolve it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Equality in Christ, Paul says, should make a slave serve a believing master better, not worse (v.2).

Now: The strategy took far too long, and Christians defended slavery with verses like this while ignoring 1:10; yet abolition came largely from people arguing from this book.

verseByVerse.quote: Let all who are under a yoke as bondservants regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled. Those who have believing masters must not be disrespectful on the ground that they are brothers; rather they must serve all the better since those who benefit by their good service are believers and beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. 1 Timothy 6 closes the letter by returning to its two great concerns: the false teachers and the kind of man Timothy must be. It moves from slaves and masters (vv. 1–2) to the false teachers and the money behind them (vv. 3–10), then to the charge to Timothy and a doxology (vv. 11–16), a word to the rich (vv. 17–19) and a last plea to guard the deposit (vv. 20–21). At the centre of a chapter about slaves, money and quarrels, the letter rises into one of the highest descriptions of God in the Bible. Paul cannot talk about wealth for long without being carried up to the only One who is truly rich.

The setting. Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world; on some estimates as much as a third of the population of a city like Ephesus were slaves, though the figures are uncertain. It was not based on race, and many slaves were educated and skilled, could own property and could hope for freedom; but they were legally their masters’ property and could be cruelly treated. The church contained both slaves and masters, as brothers in Christ (Galatians 3:28; Philemon 16), and some slaves, as verse 2 shows, were owned by fellow Christians. Some may have thought that their new equality in Christ freed them from duty to their masters, perhaps encouraged by the false teachers. These verses need honest handling, because the New Testament’s treatment of slavery is one of the things most often held against it. A movement calling for immediate abolition would very likely have been crushed as sedition, as the great slave revolt under Spartacus had been, and the gospel would have been heard as a call to arms rather than as good news about Christ.

Under a yoke. “Under a yoke” (hypo zygon): the yoke was a picture of servitude and burden (Leviticus 26:13), and God himself is the one who broke the bars of Israel’s yoke and made them walk upright. “Bondservants” (douloi) are slaves. Paul does not pretend the condition is light; he names it a yoke.

Worthy of all honor. “Masters” (despotai) are owners, lords; our word despot comes from it. “All honor” (pasēs timēs) is full respect, owed even to unbelieving masters.

Not be reviled. “Reviled” (blasphēmeō) means slandered, blasphemed. If Christian slaves were rebellious or lazy, outsiders would say that Christianity destroys social order. The gospel’s reputation was at stake (Titus 2:9–10). But see what Paul does not say. The slave is not told to obey because his owner deserves it or because the arrangement is just. He is given a reason for his conduct that has nothing to do with his master’s rights. He is told that he is a witness: that the reputation of God is, astonishingly, in the hands of a slave. The man with the least standing in Ephesus is entrusted with the honour of the highest name in the universe.

Not be disrespectful. “Disrespectful” (kataphroneō) means despise, look down on. Some had reasoned, quite understandably, that equality in Christ meant the old arrangement no longer bound them: he is my brother, so I need not work hard for him. Paul’s answer is not to deny the equality. He affirms it in the same breath, calling the master a brother, believing and beloved. Spiritual equality does not cancel earthly responsibilities.

Serve all the better. “Serve all the better” (mallon douleuetōsan) means serve them even more; “benefit” (antilambanomai) means take part in, receive. And there is a quiet revolution in the word beloved. The slave is told to see his owner as one whom God loves; the owner, reading the same letter aloud in the same room, is being told that his slave is his brother.

Serving the Lord Christ. In his letters to Colossae and Ephesus Paul gives slaves the deepest reason of all: work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward, for you are serving the Lord Christ (Colossians 3:23–24; Ephesians 6:5–8). It is an astonishing thing to say to people who by law could inherit nothing. Their earthly owner was not their final master, and their work was not finally done for him. That is why a slave could serve without servility, and why his faithfulness could adorn the gospel: every honest day’s work was offered to a Lord who sees it and will reward it.

In the flow. These verses finish the household instructions that filled chapter 5, and one word ties them together. Widows are to be honoured (5:3), elders counted worthy of double honour (5:17), and now masters regarded as worthy of all honour (6:1). In every relationship Paul asks what will keep the gospel from reproach (5:7, 14; 6:1). Then the last words of verse 2, teach and urge these things, close the section and open the next: the false teachers who refuse such teaching, and the love of money behind them (vv. 3–10).

Where Christians differ: does the New Testament approve of slavery? Critics have accused the Bible of endorsing slavery, and slaveholders once used such texts to defend it. Verdict: The New Testament regulates an institution it did not create and could not abolish by decree, while planting the principles that would undermine it. It condemns slave-trading (1:10), tells slaves to gain freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21, on the most likely reading), commands masters to treat slaves justly and remember that they too have a Master (Ephesians 6:9; Colossians 4:1), and declares slave and free one in Christ (Galatians 3:28). Paul sends Onesimus back to Philemon “no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 16). The race-based chattel slavery of later centuries, built on kidnapping, was condemned by Scripture’s own law (Exodus 21:16). Christians who fought for abolition, like William Wilberforce, did so from these principles. That is the strategy: not a revolt that would have been drowned in blood, but a principle planted inside the institution that would eventually dissolve it. It took far too long, and Christians defended slavery for centuries by quoting verses like this one while ignoring 1:10 and Philemon. That is a grief and a shame to the church. But when abolition finally came, much of its moral force came from people arguing from this book.

Does this mean I must put up with an abusive boss? No. An employee today is not a slave: you are free to leave, to complain through proper channels, and to seek justice, and you should when you are mistreated (1 Corinthians 7:21 shows Paul valued freedom where it was available). What carries over is the attitude: honest work, respect for those in authority, no sulking, cutting corners or badmouthing behind their backs, so that your conduct commends Christ. But respect is not complicity. You must never do what is sinful because you are told to (Acts 5:29), and harassment, abuse or illegal practice should be reported, not endured in silence. Working well and standing up for what is right are both ways of keeping God’s name from being reviled.

What about slavery and trafficking today? Christians must oppose it with all their strength. Modern slavery, forced labour, debt bondage and sex trafficking are exactly the kidnapping that God’s law punished with death (Exodus 21:16) and the slave-trading that Paul condemns in this very letter (1:10). Nothing in these verses gives them any cover. In practice that means praying, supporting organisations that rescue and restore victims, asking where the goods you buy come from, and refusing to look away when something seems wrong in your community. The gospel that made Onesimus a beloved brother still sets captives free.

On a Tuesday. You already serve the Lord Christ, who bought you and sees what no manager sees; work today for him. The moment to watch is when you are tempted to do less because no one will check, or because your manager is a Christian and will understand. Do the job well, speak well of the people above you, and let your work be the sermon your colleagues actually hear.

For worship. The Lord of glory took the form of a doulos. He who owned the universe was sold for the price of a slave, thirty pieces of silver, and he washed feet, and he served all the better those who did not deserve it. He is the Master in heaven who shows no partiality, before whom slave and free, employer and employee, stand on the same ground. And he is the Redeemer, the One who buys slaves to set them free. In his house there are no slaves, only sons and daughters, and the slave who reveres his name in a Roman kitchen will sit at the marriage supper of the Lamb beside kings.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul traces the false teaching to its root, the love of money, and sets against it the real gain of godliness with contentment. The warning that follows falls on the desire to be rich, which has led some away from the faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Root Beneath the Quarrels

Beneath the Ephesian error was a business: ‘godliness is a means of gain’ (v.5), and its fruit was relational damage rather than doctrinal error (v.4). The love of money, a root of all kinds of evils (v.10), enables every sin rather than having one of its own.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul grants the false teachers their word ‘gain’ and attaches it to contentment (v.6).

Now: Verse 9 warns those who desire to be rich, a condition available at every income.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone teaches a different doctrine and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that accords with godliness, he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions, and constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A different doctrine. Paul returns to the false teachers one last time, and now he traces their error to its root, which turns out not to be intellectual at all. “Teaches a different doctrine” (heterodidaskalei) is the same word as 1:3, forming a bracket around the letter.

The sound words. “Agree with” (proserchomai) means come to, adhere to, attach oneself to. “Sound” (hygiainousi) is the medical word again: healthy, wholesome. “The words of our Lord Jesus Christ” are either the teachings of Jesus himself, or the apostolic gospel about him, which carries his authority. True doctrine is healthy; it produces spiritual health.

Accords with godliness. Teaching is measured by whether it accords with godliness, by what kind of life it produces. That has been the letter’s yardstick since 1:5.

Puffed up with conceit. “Puffed up” (typhoō) is the inflation word again (3:6): swollen with air, or blinded by smoke, conceited. “Understands nothing” (mēden epistamenos) means knows nothing. And the pairing is deliberate: maximum self-regard, zero comprehension.

An unhealthy craving. The Greek is a striking reversal. “Unhealthy craving” (nosōn) is literally being sick, diseased, the opposite of the sound teaching just named. Paul’s picture is of a man with an appetite that is itself a sickness: he does not merely tolerate argument, he needs it. “Controversy” (zētēseis) means speculative questions, disputes, as in 1:4. And “quarrels about words” (logomachias) are word-battles, fighting over terms: arguments about technicalities and hair-splitting, not substance (2 Timothy 2:14).

Envy, dissension, slander. Five words, and not one is a doctrinal error. They are all relational damage. “Envy” (phthonos) is jealousy. “Dissension” (eris) is strife, rivalry. “Slander” (blasphēmiai) is abusive speech. “Evil suspicions” (hyponoiai ponērai) are malicious suspicions, assuming the worst. “Constant friction” (diaparatribai) is mutual irritation, people rubbing against each other until the skin is raw. You can know a teaching by its fruit (Matthew 7:16–20). Paul judges the teaching by its wreckage: a congregation where people suspect each other and cannot stop arguing has a teaching problem, whatever is on its statement of faith.

Depraved in mind. “Depraved” (diephtharmenōn) means thoroughly corrupted, rotted. “Deprived” (apestermenōn) means robbed, stripped. They once had access to the truth, but have been robbed of it, or have turned from it.

A means of gain. Then the root. “Means of gain” (porismos) is a source of profit, a money-making scheme. Beneath the genealogies and the quarrels about words was a business. These men had discovered that religion pays: that a reputation for spiritual insight brings money, standing and a following. Like the teachers Paul warns Titus about, they taught for shameful gain (Titus 1:11; compare 2 Peter 2:3). Paul puts the financial motive at the bottom of the whole Ephesian trouble, and the next verses are about money because of it. And the question reaches closer to home than Ephesus. Religion can be used for gain without any fee: for a reputation, for a sense of being better than others, or for a quiet bargain that if I am good, God owes me a good life. That too treats godliness as a means of gain, and the gospel ends it, because Christ is not a means to something else but the treasure himself (Philippians 3:8).

The words that make peace. The standard is not Paul’s own teaching but the words of our Lord Jesus Christ. The apostolic gospel is Christ’s own word, carried by the men he sent, so that to hear them was to hear him (Luke 10:16). Those who teach otherwise are not quarrelling with Paul’s opinions; they are refusing the words of the Lord. And set those words beside the five that verse 4 lists. Jesus blessed the peacemakers (Matthew 5:9), washed his disciples’ feet, commanded them to love one another as he had loved them (John 13:34), and prayed that they would be one (John 17:21). A teaching that leaves envy, suspicion and friction behind it has wandered far from the One whose words make peace.

How can I tell the difference between defending the truth and loving controversy? Look at three things. The subject: is it something Scripture treats as central, such as the person of Christ, the gospel, the authority of the Bible, or is it a speculation Scripture does not settle? The manner: are you gentle, patient and willing to listen, or do you enjoy winning and look for the next fight (2 Timothy 2:24–25)? And the fruit: does the conversation leave people closer to Christ and to each other, or does it leave envy, suspicion and friction? A healthy defender of the faith would rather not argue, and does so for the sake of others. A lover of controversy argues for the pleasure of it, and would be lost without an opponent.

How do I recognise a teacher who is using religion for gain? Watch the money and the message together. Be wary when giving is tied to promised returns, when a teacher’s lifestyle is lavish and unaccountable, when pressure is applied to give more, or when the message flatters the wealthy and fits suspiciously well with what the teacher needs. Ask whether there is real accountability: elders, published finances, a church that can correct him. Gain need not be money; it can be fame, a platform or power over people. A faithful teacher can be paid (5:17–18), but he is not driven by it, and his teaching makes you want Christ, not him.

verseByVerse.quote: But godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world. But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great gain. Paul takes their phrase and turns it inside out. They imagined godliness was a means of financial gain; Paul says godliness is great gain, but only when combined with contentment. The word they wanted is granted, there is real profit here, but it is attached to something they had no interest in. “Contentment” (autarkeia) is a Stoic word; Paul used its adjective at Philippians 4:11 and filled it with different content. For the Stoic it meant self-sufficiency, independence from circumstances through inner strength, needing nothing outside yourself. For Paul it means having enough because of who supplies you: sufficiency in Christ, being satisfied with what God provides (Philippians 4:11–13; 2 Corinthians 9:8).

We brought nothing. Paul gives two arguments, and the first is unanswerable. Job said it (Job 1:21), and so did the Preacher (Ecclesiastes 5:15; compare Psalm 49:17). It is not a religious claim at all but an observation anybody can verify. We arrive naked and leave naked, and whatever a person accumulates is held for the middle stretch only: nothing crosses either boundary. Why stake your life on what you cannot keep?

Food and clothing. Then the second argument: two items. Not comfort, not security, not a modest sufficiency by local standards: food and covering. The word (skepasmata, coverings) can include shelter, so perhaps three. The basic necessities. When we have these, we have enough to be content. Jesus taught the same: do not be anxious about food and clothing, for your Father knows you need them (Matthew 6:25–33). This should not be softened into a general commendation of simplicity. Paul has set the bar at survival. He is not saying it is wrong to have more; he will tell the rich in verse 17 that God gives us everything to enjoy, which rules out asceticism. He is saying that everything above food and clothing is surplus, and that a Christian should know it is surplus. And contentment is not a matter of income: anyone can name a figure at which they would be content, but the honest question is whether contentment arrived when the last increase did.

The Lord who lived inside the bracket. The Son of God kept these two verses more completely than anyone. He came into the world with nothing, laid in a manger because there was no place for them in the inn (Luke 2:7), and he left it with nothing, while soldiers divided his clothing among them (John 19:23–24) and he was buried in another man’s tomb. In between he said that his food was to do the will of the One who sent him (John 4:34). He is the proof that a life with little more than food and covering can be the richest life ever lived. And he is the secret Paul learned: I can do all things through him who strengthens me, he wrote, at the end of a sentence about being content with plenty or with hunger (Philippians 4:12–13). Godliness with contentment is great gain, because the godly have God.

How do I actually learn contentment? Paul says he learned it (Philippians 4:11–12); it is not a temperament but a trained habit of the heart, and its secret is Christ, through whom he could do all things. Practise gratitude daily, naming specific gifts, because thanksgiving and discontent cannot live long in the same heart. Notice what feeds your wanting, the adverts, the scrolling, the comparisons with friends, and starve it. Give generously, because giving loosens the grip of things. Remember the bracket: you will leave with nothing. And above all, feed on what does satisfy: the God who has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you, which is the very reason Hebrews gives for being content (Hebrews 13:5).

Is it wrong to want a better job, a pay rise or a nicer home? Not necessarily. Wanting to provide better for your family, to use your gifts more fully, or to have room for hospitality can be good desires. Paul assumes people may improve their situation. The question is what the wanting is doing to you. Ask: am I anxious, envious or restless about it? Would I be at peace with God if it never came? Am I prepared to sacrifice integrity, family or church to get it? If you can want it with open hands, pray for it and work for it. If it has become the thing you cannot be happy without, it has become an idol, and contentment means laying it down.

On a Tuesday. Contentment rarely arrives as a feeling; it usually arrives as noticing. The meal in front of you, the coat on the hook, the bed you will sleep in tonight: food and covering, and more besides. When the familiar thought comes, if only I had that, it can be brought to God by name, and set beside something you already have that you once longed for. Often the thing we could not live without last year is the thing we now barely notice.

verseByVerse.quote: But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who desire to be rich. The warning is not for the rich: Paul will address them separately in verse 17, and does not tell them to divest. “Desire” (boulomenoi) means want, resolve, set their will on: those determined to become rich, whose goal in life is wealth. The danger is in the desiring, which is a condition available at every income.

Into a snare. The verbs describe a descent. “Fall” (empiptō) is to fall into, as into a pit. They fall into temptation (peirasmos) and a snare (pagis), the bird-trap word from 3:7, something that closes on you before you have seen it. The pursuit of wealth exposes people to endless temptations: dishonesty, neglect of family, idolatry, oppression.

Senseless and harmful desires. Many desires (epithymias, cravings, lusts), senseless (anoētous, foolish, unreasonable) and harmful (blaberas, injurious, damaging), which arrive in company, because wanting one thing teaches you to want others. Greed breeds other cravings, and none of them satisfy.

Ruin and destruction. Finally these plunge people (bythizō), a verb used of a ship going down, dragged under, sinking to the bottom. “Ruin” (olethros) and “destruction” (apōleia, perdition, eternal loss) together describe total, final ruin, in this life and the next (Matthew 16:26; Luke 12:20–21). The rich fool built bigger barns and was told, this night your soul is required of you.

The love of money. The line is famously misquoted. Three corrections in one sentence. It is not money but the love of it (philargyria, love of silver, avarice); money is a tool and Paul is about to tell wealthy Christians what to do with theirs. It is not the root but a root (rhiza: Greek has no article here, and most translators rightly render it a root); Paul is not claiming every sin traces here, and pride and lust do fine without it. And it produces all kinds of evils (pantōn tōn kakōn) rather than every single evil; the point is the variety. There is almost no wickedness that money-love cannot eventually produce: theft, murder, adultery, war, lies, broken families. And at bottom it is idolatry (Colossians 3:5; Matthew 6:24). You cannot serve God and money.

Wandered away. “Craving” (oregomenoi) is reaching out for, stretching toward. “Wandered away” (apeplanēthēsan) means been led astray. Wandered, not renounced. Nobody sets out to leave Christ for money. The word suggests drifting off the path while looking at something else, which is exactly how it happens. The love of money has led some to abandon the faith, perhaps including the false teachers: like Judas, who sold his Master for silver (Matthew 26:14–16), and Demas, who loved this present world (2 Timothy 4:10).

Pierced themselves. The verb (peripeirō) is violent: run through, impaled, as on a spit. And the reflexive is the sting. Nobody did this to them. “Pangs” (odynais) are pains, griefs, sorrows: anxiety, guilt, broken relationships, emptiness, regret. The griefs money-love produces are self-inflicted, and they come to the person who got what he wanted.

The temptation he refused. In the wilderness the devil showed Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and offered them for one act of worship (Matthew 4:8–10). It was the desire to be rich in its purest form, the whole world as the price of a divided heart, and he refused it with Scripture: worship the Lord your God and serve him only. Where others reach for wealth and are dragged under, the Son of God turned down everything and kept his Father. That victory is the believer’s hope. The love of money is not overcome by a stronger grip on ourselves but by a greater love. What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul (Mark 8:36)? The One who refused the world is worth more than all of it.

Where Christians differ: does God promise wealth to the faithful? The prosperity gospel teaches that God wants every believer to be rich, and that faith, giving or positive confession will produce wealth. Verdict: This passage directly refutes it. Paul warns that the desire to be rich is a trap that leads to destruction. Jesus warned against storing up treasure on earth (Matthew 6:19–21) and said it is hard for the rich to enter the kingdom (Mark 10:23–25). God promises to provide what we need (Philippians 4:19), not wealth. Teachers who promise wealth are precisely those who think godliness is a means of gain (v. 5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean money itself is evil, or that wanting to provide for one’s family is wrong (5:8). Nor does “wandered from the faith” mean that a true believer can be finally lost: Christ’s sheep are held in his hand (John 10:28–29; see on 6:21). If you see a drift towards money in yourself and it grieves you, that grief is not the mark of an apostate but of the Spirit at work, and the way back is open (1 John 1:9).

How do I know if I love money? Love shows itself in what you think about, what you fear losing, and what you will sacrifice for. Ask: Do I think about money more than about God? Am I anxious when it is short, proud when it is plentiful? Do I resent giving, or give only what I will not miss? Would I bend the truth, cut a corner or neglect my family to get more? Do I envy those who have more? Does the prospect of losing it terrify me more than the prospect of losing fellowship with Christ? Nobody answers all of these well. The cure is not guilt but a better love: look at Christ, who though he was rich became poor for you, and give something away today as an act of worship.

Is it wrong to save, invest or have a pension? No. Scripture commends the ant that stores up in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8) and the wise who plan ahead (Proverbs 21:20), and providing for your family includes thinking about the future (5:8). Saving becomes sin when it is driven by fear rather than faith, when it becomes the place your security truly rests, or when it crowds out generosity. The rich fool’s problem was not that he had barns but that he built bigger ones for himself alone and was not rich toward God (Luke 12:16–21). Save wisely, give generously, and hold it all loosely, remembering whose it is.

For worship. We pierce ourselves with griefs we chose; the Son of God was pierced with griefs that were never his, wounded for our transgressions, so that by his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). Money promises everything and leaves its lovers sinking; Christ, who had no silver, is the treasure hidden in the field, and those who find him sell all they have for joy (Matthew 13:44). He drags no one under. He is the Lord who reached out his hand to Peter sinking in the waves (Matthew 14:31), and that hand still lifts the drowning and holds them fast.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Against the false teachers stands the man of God. Paul charges Timothy to flee, pursue and fight, and to keep the commandment until Christ appears; and the thought of that appearing carries him into a doxology to the God who will bring it about.
verseByVerse.theology:
Titles Thrown at Idols

‘Only Sovereign’, ‘King of kings and Lord of lords’, ‘who alone has immortality’ (vv.15–16) are aimed at Artemis and the emperor; and the God who dwells in unapproachable light is reached only through the one mediator (2:5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Timothy confessed Christ among friends; Jesus confessed before Pilate, who could kill him (vv.12–13).

Now: Flee and pursue (v.11): some temptations must simply be run from, and a man who only avoids will eventually be caught.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for you, O man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O man of God. The contrast is emphatic (sy de, but you). Against the men who imagine godliness is gain, against those who desire to be rich, stands one person, addressed directly. And the title is striking. “Man of God” (anthrōpe theou) is the Old Testament’s standing description of the prophets and leaders: Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1), Samuel (1 Samuel 9:6), Elijah (1 Kings 17:18) and Elisha (2 Kings 4:9), men who stood for God against a drifting people. It marks a person who belongs to God, represents him and speaks for him. Paul lays that mantle on a young minister in Ephesus who has been having a difficult time of it, and in 2 Timothy 3:17 he uses it of anyone whom Scripture equips for every good work, which many read as every believer.

Flee these things. Then two verbs, and the Christian life is in both. “Flee” (pheugō) means run away from, escape, and it is present tense: keep fleeing. “These things” are the love of money, pride, controversy and greed (vv. 3–10). It is the word used of Joseph leaving his garment in her hand rather than staying to argue with Potiphar’s wife (Genesis 39:12). Some temptations are not to be engaged, reasoned with or managed. Distance is often the only reliable tactic, and a man who stays to test his own strength has usually decided how it ends (1 Corinthians 6:18; 10:14; 2 Timothy 2:22).

Pursue righteousness. “Pursue” (diōkō) is the word used of hunting and of persecution: chase it down, run after it. And the pairing matters. Fleeing alone leaves a vacuum, and a man who is only avoiding things will eventually be caught by one of them. You have to be running toward something. Six virtues, and they fall into three pairs. Righteousness (dikaiosynē, upright conduct) and godliness (eusebeia, devotion to God): right living toward people and toward God. Faith (pistis, trust, faithfulness) and love (agapē): the inner life of a believer, the two that have run through this letter since 1:5. Then steadfastness and gentleness, which is the interesting pair: hypomonē, the staying power that does not buckle under weight, and praupathia, a rare word meaning meekness, mildness of temper. Those last two together are the answer to what this chapter has described. A man dealing with quarrelsome teachers and constant friction needs to be immovable and unaggravated at the same time: to face opposition with endurance and without harshness, to hold the ground without becoming like the people pushing him. ## Running towards a person. Paul’s flee-and-pursue pattern has a centre elsewhere in his letters. In Romans he tells believers to cast off the works of darkness and then, instead of a list, gives a name: put on the Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 13:12–14). The six virtues here are not a self-improvement programme; pursuing them is pursuing likeness to him. That is also why the man of God is not left to his own strength. The One he is running towards has already run the course, and lives in him by his Spirit. Every step towards gentleness or steadfastness is a step towards his Lord.

What does fleeing look like in practice? It means arranging your life so that the temptation has less access to you. For money: unsubscribe from the shopping emails, stop browsing what you cannot afford, avoid the friendships built around getting and spending. For sexual sin: filters and accountability, no being alone where you know you are weak, leaving the room or switching off at once. For controversy: closing the thread, not reading the comments. Fleeing is not cowardice; it is wisdom about your own weakness. And it is always paired with pursuing: put something good in the space you have cleared, or the old thing will come back with friends (Matthew 12:43–45).
verseByVerse.note: “Man of God” is an Old Testament title for prophets such as Moses, Samuel and Elijah.

verseByVerse.quote: Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called and about which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good fight. The verb (agōnizou) comes from the arena: contend, compete, struggle, strain. It is the root of our word agonise, and it is present tense: keep fighting. Paul has used the military and athletic images throughout (1:18; 4:7–8), and the image here may be athletic, a race or wrestling match, as much as military. “Good fight” (kalon agōna) is the noble contest. Note the definite article: the good fight of the faith. Not any struggle a Christian happens to be in, and not merely a private battle with a besetting sin. Paul means the one contest that matters, waged over the faith itself, the deposit he will name in verse 20: a contest for the faith, the body of truth, and in faith, trusting God. Paul uses the same words of his own life at its end: I have fought the good fight (2 Timothy 4:7).

Take hold. The verb (epilabou) means to seize, grasp, lay hold of, and here it is a simple, urgent command: take hold. That sounds odd applied to eternal life, which Timothy already has as a gift (John 5:24). But this is Paul’s regular pattern: what God gives, you are then told to lay hold of; work out your salvation because God works in you (Philippians 2:12–13). The possession is secure and the grip is still commanded. Eternal life must be grasped, lived in, and pressed toward as the prize at the end of the race (Philippians 3:12–14).

To which you were called. “Called” (eklēthēs) is God’s effectual call, which brought Timothy to faith (Romans 8:30; 2 Timothy 1:9). Effectual means that it does what it says. A general invitation can be refused; this call creates the response it asks for, which is why Jesus says no one can come to him unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). The call is God’s act; our grasping is the response his grace enables. Timothy did not wander into eternal life; he was summoned into it by the voice that raises the dead.

The good confession. “Confession” (homologia) is a public declaration, an acknowledgement. The good confession was probably made at Timothy’s baptism, when he publicly confessed Jesus as Lord (Romans 10:9–10), or perhaps at his ordination: a public occasion where he said in front of people what he believed. “Many witnesses” are the congregation who heard it. He must live up to what he declared before them. Paul does this repeatedly in these letters. When a man is flagging, he sends him back to what was said over him and by him at the beginning (1:18; 4:14). That is a practical kindness. Feelings about ministry come and go; the fact that you stood up in front of witnesses and confessed Christ does not, and on the days when nothing else is steady it is a fixed point you can put your weight on.

Laying hold of the One who laid hold of you. Eternal life in the New Testament is not a thing apart from Christ. This is eternal life, Jesus prayed, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3); and God gave us eternal life, and this life is in his Son (1 John 5:11). So to take hold of eternal life is to take hold of Christ. And Paul knew which grip comes first. He pressed on to make it his own, he said, because Christ Jesus had made him his own (Philippians 3:12). Timothy’s grasp is weak and must be renewed every day. The hand that holds him is not weak, and it does not let go.

What is the fight, for an ordinary Christian? It is the daily contest to keep believing and living the gospel against everything that pulls the other way. Inwardly, it is the fight against unbelief, doubt and the sins that would choke faith. Outwardly, it is holding to the truth when the world, or even a church, drifts from it, and speaking of Christ when it costs you. Its weapons are those God supplies: the Word, prayer, the fellowship of the church, the Lord’s Supper (Ephesians 6:10–18). It is not fought by aggression toward people; Paul has just told Timothy to pursue gentleness. And it is a good fight: one that ends in victory, because the Captain has already won it.

Why does it matter that I made a public confession? Because faith in Christ is not meant to be private. Jesus said that whoever confesses him before men, he will confess before his Father (Matthew 10:32). For a believer, baptism is the appointed place for that first public confession, made before witnesses who can later remind you of it and hold you to it. If you are a believer and have never been baptised, this verse is an invitation: speak to your pastor. This commentary holds believer’s baptism, because the baptisms of the New Testament follow hearing and believing (Acts 2:41; 8:12); many godly Christians who were baptised as infants, and whose churches see baptism as the covenant sign given to believers’ children, would point instead to the day they publicly owned their faith, and both agree that faith in Christ must be confessed openly. If you have been, look back on it when faith feels weak. You did not imagine it. You stood before God and his people and said Jesus is Lord, and the God who called you then has not changed his mind.
verseByVerse.note: The “good confession” was probably made at Timothy’s baptism or ordination.

verseByVerse.quote: I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, to keep the commandment unstained and free from reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the presence of God. The second solemn charge in God’s sight in the letter (compare 5:21), and both witnesses are chosen for the occasion. “Charge” (parangellō, command) is the keyword of the letter (1:3, 5, 18). “Gives life” (zōogoneō) means preserves alive, gives life to. God is the giver and sustainer of all life, which is precisely what a man needs to remember if the charge might cost him his own. The God who gives life to all things is the God who will raise Timothy if he dies for his faith.

Before Pontius Pilate. Before Pilate, he declared that he was a king, whose kingdom is not of this world, and that he came to bear witness to the truth (John 18:33–37; Mark 15:2). He did so knowing it would cost him his life. Timothy made his good confession before many witnesses, in a room full of friends. Jesus made his before a magistrate who could kill him, and did. Paul sets the two side by side without comment. Confession before a supportive congregation is real; confession before a hostile authority is the same act with the price attached, and Timothy is being told which one he is signed up to.

Suffered under Pontius Pilate. Paul anchors the confession in a datable event. Pontius Pilate is a name from provincial administration, known from Tacitus, Josephus and Philo and from an inscription found at Caesarea, and the later creeds would keep it in the words suffered under Pontius Pilate. The faith Timothy is charged to keep is not a philosophy but something that happened at a particular hour in front of a particular official.

Keep the commandment. “Keep” (tērēsai) means guard, preserve, obey. “The commandment” (tēn entolēn) is probably the whole charge Timothy received, the gospel and its demands, all that Paul has entrusted to him (1:18; 6:20), which he will call the deposit in verse 20.

Unstained and free from reproach. Two adjectives describe how it is to be kept. “Unstained” (aspilos) means spotless, without blemish. “Free from reproach” (anepilēmptos) means irreproachable, as of elders (3:2). These may describe the commandment (keep it pure, uncorrupted) or Timothy (keep it so that you are spotless), and in practice both are true, because a man’s life can put a mark on the message he carries. No minister has ever kept it perfectly. The One who did is Christ, who kept his Father’s charge without a stain and in our place, and his obedience is counted to all who are his (Romans 5:19); so Timothy guards it as a man already accepted, and his failures, confessed, do not undo that.

Until the appearing. “Appearing” (epiphaneia) means manifestation, glorious appearance: a word used in the Greek world for the appearance of a god or the arrival of an emperor. The Pastoral Letters often use it for Christ’s return (2 Timothy 4:1, 8; Titus 2:13). And the timescale is the whole of it: not until the trouble in Ephesus resolves, or until Paul arrives, but until Christ appears. The assignment has one end date, and it is not in Timothy’s diary.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul knew Christ would return within Timothy’s lifetime; he leaves the timing to God, who will bring it about “at the proper time” (v. 15). It means the return is the horizon of faithful ministry.

What will Christ’s appearing be like? Public, visible and glorious. Scripture describes one return of Christ at the end of the age, not a secret coming: he will come on the clouds with power and great glory, every eye will see him, the dead will be raised, and he will judge the living and the dead and make all things new (Matthew 24:30; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; Revelation 1:7). Many Christians, especially in churches that teach a rapture, expect Christ to come secretly for his people some years before a later visible return; this commentary reads the coming of 1 Thessalonians 4, with its shout and trumpet, as that same loud and public final return, while gladly owning those who see it otherwise as brothers who love his appearing too. It will be terror to those who rejected him and unspeakable joy to those who love his appearing (2 Timothy 4:8). We do not know the day, and we are not told to calculate it. We are told what Timothy was told: keep faith until then, and live so that you would be glad to be found doing what you are doing.

What if I am afraid to confess Christ before people who could harm me? Look at the One who went first. Christ did not ask Timothy to do anything he had not already done, before a far more dangerous judge. Fear is not itself sin; it is the soil in which courage grows. Pray for boldness, as the apostles did (Acts 4:29). Remember that the Spirit gives words in the hour of need (Matthew 10:19–20). Use wisdom: you are not commanded to court danger needlessly. And if you have failed, as Peter did in the courtyard, remember that the risen Lord restored him and later gave him courage to die for him (John 21:15–19). The God who gives life to all things holds yours.

For worship. He stood bound before the governor of Judea, the true King before a man who thought he held the power of life and death, and he told the truth knowing it meant the cross. Pilate asked what truth is while the Truth stood in front of him. Christ did not deny us when we would have denied him. He was crucified under Pontius Pilate, dead and buried, and on the third day he rose again; and the God who gives life to all things has given him the name above every name. One day he will appear, and every knee will bow, the governor’s among them.

verseByVerse.quote: which he will display at the proper time—he who is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the proper time. The mention of Christ’s appearing sets Paul off, and the letter breaks into its second doxology (compare 1:17). It may well be something the churches already sang. “Display” (deixei) means show, bring about, reveal. “At the proper time” (kairois idiois) means in his own seasons, as in 2:6. God the Father will bring about Christ’s appearing at the moment he has appointed (Acts 1:7; Mark 13:32). Nobody hurries it and nobody delays it.

The blessed and only Sovereign. Then the titles, and every one of them is a stone thrown at an idol. “Blessed” (makarios) is the word from 1:11: perfectly and self-sufficiently happy. God is not a lonely or needy being who made us to fill an emptiness; he is supremely happy in himself, Father, Son and Spirit, and he creates out of fullness. “Only Sovereign” (monos dynastēs) means the only ruler, the only potentate, and the only is pointed, in a city with a temple to Artemis and a cult of the emperor. All earthly rulers, including the emperor who claimed divine titles, are under him.

King of kings. Literally King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule. This was royal vocabulary. Eastern monarchs used the formula of themselves (Ezra 7:12; Daniel 2:37), and in Paul’s day the emperor in Rome claimed divine honours of his own. Paul takes the highest title available in the political world and says it belongs to someone else. It is a title of the supreme God (Deuteronomy 10:17; Psalm 136:2–3), and in Revelation 17:14 and 19:16 it is given to Christ, the Lamb who conquers. Timothy is to keep his charge until that King appears.

Who alone has immortality. “Immortality” (athanasia) is deathlessness. Not merely that God happens to live forever, but that deathlessness belongs to him by nature and necessarily, and to nobody else in that way. God alone has life in himself (John 5:26). All other beings, including angels and human souls, continue because he sustains them; he continues because of what he is. Believers will receive immortality as his gift at the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:53–54). If, as many think, the false teachers spun speculations about angels and other spiritual beings out of their genealogies (1:4), Paul cuts beneath them all: there is one immortal.

Unapproachable light. “Unapproachable” (aprositon) means inaccessible. God’s holiness and glory are like blinding light that no creature can approach on its own (Exodus 33:20; Psalm 104:2; Isaiah 6:1–5). And the paradox is deliberate. Light is what makes seeing possible, and here it is what prevents it: not darkness keeping God hidden but excess of brightness.

Whom no one has seen. God in his essence is invisible (1:17; John 1:18). We see him only as he reveals himself, supremely in Christ: whoever has seen me has seen the Father (John 14:9), the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). In glory, believers will see him in Christ (Matthew 5:8; 1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:4). And that is where the doxology lands in a letter about false teachers claiming special access. Nobody has seen him, nobody can, and no technique will get you nearer. Which makes the line Paul has already written the more astonishing: there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (2:5). The unapproachable light came out to meet us.

Honor and eternal dominion. “Dominion” (kratos) is might, power, rule. The proper response to such a God is worship, and Paul does not argue for it; he simply gives it. Theology that does not end in doxology has not yet understood its subject.

What it does not mean. “Who alone has immortality” does not mean human souls cease to exist at death. Humans have an immortality given by God; God alone has it by nature. Scripture teaches a conscious intermediate state and the eternal existence of all people (Luke 16:22–26; Matthew 25:46). Nor does “no one can see” contradict the promise that the pure in heart will see God; we will see him as he reveals himself in the glorified Christ.

If God dwells in unapproachable light, how can I pray to him? Through Christ. On your own you could not approach this God for a moment; Isaiah, seeing only the edge of his glory, cried that he was undone. But the One who dwells in that light sent his Son into our darkness, and through his blood we have confidence to enter the holy places by the new and living way he opened (Hebrews 10:19–22). So you come not in your own name but in his, and you are welcomed as a child. Hold both truths together when you pray: the awe of verse 16, which keeps prayer reverent, and the access of the gospel, which makes it bold (Hebrews 4:16).

Why does Paul break into praise in the middle of instructions? Because for Paul doctrine and worship are one thing. He cannot mention Christ’s appearing without being carried up to the God who will bring it about. It is a lesson in how to read the Bible and how to live: every truth about God is meant to end in adoration. If your study of Scripture never moves you to praise, slow down and ask what the passage shows you of God. And it is a comfort in hard places: Timothy, facing false teachers and difficult elders, is reminded that the One he serves is the only Sovereign, and that every throne in Ephesus is beneath his.

Is a God who wants honour not simply vain? No, and the difference matters. When a human being demands praise, he is asking for more than he is worth. When God receives it, he is being given exactly what he is worth, and nothing he lacks, for he is blessed in himself and needs nothing (Acts 17:25). Praise is also how joy completes itself: we naturally praise what we delight in, a view, a piece of music, a person we love, and the praise finishes the enjoyment. So when God calls us to honour him, he is calling us to the one delight big enough to bear the full weight of our love. A God who did not want our worship would be leaving us to worship lesser things.

On a Tuesday. Pray these two verses back to God phrase by phrase this week: blessed, only Sovereign, King of kings, alone immortal, dwelling in light. When the news makes some earthly ruler seem all-powerful, or the future makes you anxious, remember who sets the proper time.
