verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul gives the wealthy a charge for using what they have, then makes a last plea to Timothy to guard the deposit, and ends with grace for the whole church.
verseByVerse.theology:
Guard the Deposit

The paratheke of verse 20 is property left for safekeeping, to be returned exactly as received, not developed or made more interesting, and guarded against ‘what is falsely called knowledge’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul does not tell the rich to divest but to hope in God, who gives everything to enjoy (v.17), and to get rich in good works (v.18).

Now: The closing grace is plural (v.21): after pages addressed to Timothy, Paul turns to the whole room.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy. They are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share, thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rich in this present age. Now Paul turns to the rich in the congregation, and what he does not say matters. He does not tell them to divest, and he does not treat wealth as a sin requiring repentance. He gives them instructions for handling it. These are those who are already wealthy, as distinct from those who desire to be (v. 9). “In this present age”: their riches belong to this passing world only. There were wealthy believers in Ephesus, a prosperous commercial city.

Not to be haughty. Two dangers first. “Haughty” (hypsēlophronein) means high-minded, arrogant, thinking oneself superior, and it is the natural drift of money: it quietly persuades a person that he is a different sort of human from the people who do not have it, and that he does not need God (Deuteronomy 8:11–17).

The uncertainty of riches. “Set their hopes” (ēlpikenai) means fix their hope. And the phrase is exact: not on uncertain riches but on the uncertainty of them (adēlotēti, unreliability). Wealth’s defining property, for the purposes of hope, is that it might not be there. Riches can sprout wings and fly away overnight (Proverbs 23:5; Luke 12:16–21). They are a foolish foundation for hope.

God, who richly provides. This is a generous sentence, and it comes from the man who has just said food and clothing are enough. “Richly” (plousiōs) is a play on the word rich: the truly rich one is God, who gives abundantly. And the purpose named is enjoyment (eis apolausin): not merely use, not bare sufficiency. God is not stingy; he gives good things for our pleasure. This is the final answer to the ascetics of chapter 4 who forbade marriage and food. The God who gives us things means us to be glad of them. Wealth is not evil; it is a gift to be enjoyed with thanks (4:4), not trusted.

Rich in good works. Then four things for the rich to do, and they build. “Do good” (agathoergein) is the general instruction. “Be rich in good works”: and there is the deliberate wordplay. They are rich in one currency, and Paul tells them to get rich in another.

Generous and ready to share. “Generous” (eumetadotous) means ready to give, liberal, open-handed. And “ready to share” (koinōnikous) is a further step, from the fellowship word: not merely willing when asked, but holding what they have as common property with people who need it.

Storing up treasure. “Storing up treasure” (apothēsaurizontas) means laying up in store; “foundation” (themelion) is the base a building stands on. The image is Christ’s own: treasure in heaven where moth and rust do not destroy (Matthew 6:19–21; Luke 12:33; 16:9). And it turns the whole thing round. Giving money away is here described as an investment, the only one whose returns are guaranteed.

Truly life. “Truly life” (tēs ontōs zōēs) is life that is really life; some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read eternal life, but the earliest read truly life. It is the same verb as verse 12, and the same implication. What the rich are currently holding is not, in Paul’s estimate, quite life. Life measured by possessions is not real life (Luke 12:15). There is a realer thing available, the life of God, now and forever, and the way to lay hold of it is to let go of the other.

The rich man who became poor. The truly rich man of the New Testament does not live in Ephesus. Paul reminds the Corinthians of the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, who was rich and for their sake became poor, so that by his poverty they might be made rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). That is the pattern behind every instruction here. He did not hoard heaven; he shared it, taking our lot so that we might have his. And the life that is truly life is not a vague idea but a person: whoever has the Son has life (1 John 5:12). The rich lay hold of it the way everyone does, by letting go of what they were trusting and holding on to him.

In the flow. Why do these verses come after the doxology rather than with verses 6–10? Paul has finished the charge to Timothy and the praise of God, and now he comes back to the rich who are actually in the room. Verses 9–10 warned those who want to be rich; verses 17–19 instruct those who already are. And the doxology stands between them for a reason: the blessed and only Sovereign, who richly provides, is the only safe place for a wealthy person to rest his hope.

Does generosity earn heaven? No. Good works are the fruit of saving faith (Ephesians 2:8–10), and the reward is God’s grace. Paul is telling the rich to use their wealth for others because they have something better to hope in. He sets no fixed amount; the measure is a generous heart and a ready hand (v. 18).

Am I rich? Most readers of this probably are, by any global or historical measure. If you have regular meals, a home, clothes beyond what you need and some money left at the end of the month, you are among the rich in this present age, even if you feel stretched compared with those around you. That feeling is itself one of the dangers: we measure ourselves against people who have more, and so never notice we are the ones Paul is addressing. Read verses 17–19 as written to you. Not to make you guilty, but to free you: from pride, from false security, and into the joy of using what God has given for others.

How much is generous? The New Testament sets no fixed percentage, but it gives a direction and a spirit. Paul’s charge to the rich here is not a figure but a habit: be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (v. 18). Give regularly and in proportion to what God has given you (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give cheerfully, not reluctantly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7). Give first to the church that feeds you (5:17–18; Galatians 6:6), and to the poor, especially fellow believers (Galatians 6:10). Many Christians find the Old Testament tithe a helpful starting point and then grow beyond it; for some on very low incomes, faithful giving will be smaller. The test of verse 18 is not the amount but readiness: a hand that opens quickly, and a heart that enjoys it.

On a Tuesday. Do both halves of verses 17 and 18 on purpose: give a gift you will notice to someone who needs it, and then sit down to a good meal and thank God for it without guilt. Generosity and enjoyment are not rivals; both say that God is the Giver.

verseByVerse.quote: O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you. Avoid the irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called "knowledge,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Timothy. The letter’s last direct address, and the vocative gives it the sound of a hand on the shoulder.

Guard the deposit entrusted to you. “Guard” (phylaxon) means keep safe, protect, like a sentry. The word for deposit is parathēkē, a technical term from banking and law: property placed with someone for safekeeping. In a world without secure storage you left valuables with a trustworthy man, and the obligation on him was absolute: not to invest it, improve it or use it, but to return exactly what he received. That is Paul’s picture of the gospel and of Timothy’s job. The deposit is the gospel, the apostolic truth (2 Timothy 1:12–14). It was entrusted to Paul (1:11) and now to Timothy, who is not its owner but its guardian. He must not add to it, subtract from it, or let it be stolen or corrupted. He must hand it on intact (2 Timothy 2:2).

Irreverent babble. “Avoid” (ektrepomenos) means turn away from. “Irreverent” (bebēlous) is godless, profane, as in 4:7. “Babble” (kenophōnias) is empty sounds, empty chatter. The false teaching was all noise and no substance.

Falsely called knowledge. “Contradictions” (antitheseis) are opposing arguments, counter-claims; our word antitheses. “Falsely called” (pseudōnymou) means falsely named. And “knowledge” is gnōsis, the word from which the second-century movements now called Gnosticism take their name, with their promise of secret understanding available only to the spiritual elite. Whether or not developed Gnosticism existed yet, the instinct plainly did, and Paul names it: falsely called. It advertises knowledge and does not have any. Against this, the Christian gospel is public, open to all, and centred on the historical Christ.

The whole letter in one verse. Set the two halves together. On one side a deposit: fixed, received, handed on, not yours to alter. On the other an endless production of new material that sounds impressive and is empty noise. Every generation faces the same choice, and the second is always the more exciting of the two. And note what guarding requires. Not aggression: Paul has ruled out the quarrelsome man (3:3) and the craving for controversy (6:4). A guard does not chase; he stays where he was posted, and the thing he was given is still there in the morning.

The knowledge that has a name. Against knowledge falsely so called Paul sets a person. In Christ, he told the Colossians, are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:2–3), hidden not as a secret for initiates but as riches laid open to everyone who comes to him. The deposit Timothy guards is the gospel of the glory of the blessed God (1:11), and at its centre is the saying the letter has already given him to keep: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1:15). Every promise of a deeper knowledge that moves past Christ is moving away from where the treasure is. To guard the deposit is to keep Christ at the centre, and to let nobody sell the church a wisdom he does not hold.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should avoid learning or scholarship. True knowledge of God is commanded (2 Peter 3:18). The problem is false claims to secret or superior knowledge that contradict the gospel.

I am not a pastor. How do I guard the deposit? Every believer has been entrusted with the gospel, and you guard it first by knowing it: read the Bible whole, learn a sound confession or catechism, and be able to say clearly what the gospel is. Guard it in your home by teaching it to your children. Guard it in your church by supporting faithful preaching, asking questions when something sounds wrong, and being slow to embrace new ideas that cannot be found in Scripture. Guard it in your own life by holding to it when it is unfashionable. And pass it on: tell someone else. The deposit is guarded best not by being buried but by being faithfully handed to the next person (2 Timothy 2:2).

Are there modern forms of falsely called knowledge? Yes. Any teaching that claims a secret key to the Bible, a hidden message only insiders can see, or a spiritual experience that lifts some believers above ordinary Christians follows this pattern. So does the claim that the church misunderstood Jesus until some recent discovery or theory, or the idea that real spirituality lies in techniques beyond the Word, prayer and sacraments. Scripture is sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17); it is not a code for an elite but light for all God’s people. When a teaching makes you feel you must get past the plain meaning of the Bible to find the real truth, turn away.

For worship. His truth is not kept for an elite. He hid these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children, for such was his gracious will (Matthew 11:25–26). And the deposit is safe, not finally because Timothy guarded it, but because God does. Paul knew whom he had believed, and was convinced that he is able to guard what has been entrusted until that day (2 Timothy 1:12). The gospel has passed through twenty centuries of hands, many of them weak, and it reaches us whole, because the Lord of the gospel keeps his Word.
verseByVerse.note: “Knowledge” may point to early forms of the teaching later called Gnosticism.

verseByVerse.quote: for by professing it some have swerved from the faith. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Swerved from the faith. The letter ends where it began. “Swerved” (ēstochēsan) means to miss the mark, to go astray, the same word as 1:6, where certain persons had swerved and wandered into vain discussion. The mechanism: by professing it (epangellomenoi, claiming, promising, making a show of). Not by studying it or being tempted by it, but by claiming it. The moment a man announced he had this knowledge, he was committed to a position, and the faith had to be adjusted around it. Public claims have a way of taking their maker where he did not intend to go. The warning is sober: it can happen.

Grace be with you. Then the last words, which no letter of Paul’s is without. And the you is plural (meth’ hymōn). Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read the singular, with thee, and add Amen; the earliest have the plural, which most modern Bibles follow. Much of the letter has addressed Timothy personally, O Timothy, guard the deposit, and at the very end Paul turns to the room. This letter was always going to be read aloud to the congregation, and he knows it. The elders being assessed, the widows on the roll, the rich being charged, the slaves with believing masters, and the men who wanted to be teachers: grace to all of them. This has been a demanding letter: qualifications, disciplines, warnings, a list of the lawless, two men handed over to Satan. It closes with the only thing that was ever going to make any of it possible.

The grace that is in Christ Jesus. The grace Paul leaves with the church is not a general goodwill. The letter has told us where it lives. The grace of our Lord overflowed for Paul, the foremost of sinners, with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus (1:14–15), and in his next letter he tells Timothy to be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus (2 Timothy 2:1). Those who swerved missed the mark because they aimed at knowledge; the mark was always a person. To be kept in the faith is to be kept in him, and the last word Paul writes is a gift from the Saviour’s own hand to everyone in the room.

What it does not mean. It does not mean those who are truly in Christ can finally fall away. Those who swerve from the faith show that they did not truly belong (1 John 2:19). But we must take the warning seriously, for it is one of the means by which God keeps his own. This is the Reformed teaching called the perseverance of the saints: God keeps to the end those he has truly called (Philippians 1:6). Many faithful Christians in Arminian churches (which hold that saving grace can be resisted and finally abandoned) read such warnings differently, and they take them seriously too. And if you fear you are swerving, the fear itself is a sign of life: those who have truly left the faith are rarely troubled at having left it.

Someone I love has swerved from the faith. Is there hope? Yes, while they live there is hope. Some who wander are true believers in a season of backsliding, and the Shepherd goes after his lost sheep (Luke 15:4–7); Peter denied Christ and was restored. Others were never truly converted, and the God who raises the dead can still call them. You cannot tell from outside which it is, and you do not need to. Keep praying for them by name, without giving up. Keep loving them and keep the door open, without pretending all is well. Speak of Christ when there is an opening, gently. And entrust them to the God who is mighty to save. Grace is the last word of this letter, and it is not too late for grace.

On a Tuesday. Read the whole of 1 Timothy again this week in one sitting, as the church at Ephesus would have heard it. Then pray for your church as Paul did: for its leaders, its widows, its rich and its poor, its teachers and its young. And end the day as the letter ends, by asking grace for the people you have found hardest to love.

For worship. Grace, to a difficult church, from an apostle on the road, about a deposit that had to be carried one more generation. It was. And it has been carried every generation since, not because the carriers were strong, but because the grace was. The God of all grace called us, keeps us, and will bring us home. The first word of the gospel is grace, and so is the last. Grace be with you all.
verseByVerse.note: “You” here is plural: the letter was meant for the whole church to hear.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Let all who are under a yoke as bondservants regard their own masters as worthy of all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be reviled.<sup>2</sup>Those who have believing masters must not be disrespectful on the ground that they are brothers; rather they must serve all the better since those who benefit by their good service are believers and beloved.<sup>3</sup>If anyone teaches a different doctrine and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and the teaching that accords with godliness,<sup>4</sup>he is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy and for quarrels about words, which produce envy, dissension, slander, evil suspicions,<sup>5</sup>and constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain.<sup>6</sup>But godliness with contentment is great gain,<sup>7</sup>for we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world.<sup>8</sup>But if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content.<sup>9</sup>But those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin and destruction.<sup>10</sup>For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs.<sup>11</sup>But as for you, O man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness.<sup>12</sup>Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called and about which you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.<sup>13</sup>I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession,<sup>14</sup>to keep the commandment unstained and free from reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ,<sup>15</sup>which he will display at the proper time—he who is the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords,<sup>16</sup>who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.<sup>17</sup>As for the rich in this present age, charge them not to be haughty, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who richly provides us with everything to enjoy.<sup>18</sup>They are to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share,<sup>19</sup>thus storing up treasure for themselves as a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of that which is truly life.<sup>20</sup>O Timothy, guard the deposit entrusted to you. Avoid the irreverent babble and contradictions of what is falsely called "knowledge,"<sup>21</sup>for by professing it some have swerved from the faith. Grace be with you.
